It was 2013, and future Helix Sleep co-founders Adam Tishman, Jerry Lin and Kristian von Rickenbach had a simple mission: to find a comfy new mattress that wouldn't break the bank.

But instead of an enjoyable shopping experience, the trio were faced with confusing online cliches, or pricey mattresses from brick and mortar stores.

Quickly, an opportunity sprung up in front of them: to disrupt a tired industry and subsequently create one of America's leading sleep brands.

Fast forward to present day and Helix Sleep is making some of the best mattresses we've tested, chief among them being the Helix Midnight Luxe, which is currently 25% off at Helix.

In an exclusive interview for Tom's Guide, Helix co-founder Jerry Lin talks us through the conception, creation and rebirth of the Midnight Luxe, our top-rated mattress for side sleepers, and what the future looks like for this award-wining bed.

The Midnight Luxe is always included in the monthly Helix mattress sale, but this month's discount is higher than normal. For Black Friday you can save 25% on every size, with a queen costing $1,874 (was $2,498). You'll also get a year's sleep trial, lifetime warranty, and free shipping.

Tishman, Lin and von Rickenbach identified three big problems when trying to buy a new mattress:.

In a recent development, the trio started working with sleep PHD researchers in Europe to design a line of mattresses that weren't one-size-fits-all, but instead distinguishable by sleep position. (And by looking closely at our sleep DNA, the brand name Helix was born.).

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

When Helix Sleep finally debuted in 2015, they did so with a direct-to-consumer model. They sought to demystify the mattress buying process by creating bespoke mattresses based on your answers to the Helix Sleep quiz.

After thousands of online orders, in 2017 the brand mined the sleep quiz data to roll out a basic range of mattresses that catered to every major sleep position.

Soon after, the original Helix Midnight entered the online marketplace. Now the entry level bed in the brand's expanded range, the Core Midnight is designed to meet the needs of a typical side sleeper; cushioning at the shoulders, hips and knees, and support at the lower back.

It has been revealed that in terms of mattress firmness, we'd rate the Core Midnight as a medium. It was a great start for improved side sleep comfort, but the best was yet to come...

In 2018, Helix Sleep introduced the Luxe Collection. Maintaining its philosophy of mattresses tailored for every individual sleep need, this newly introduced and more luxurious range of beds aimed to elevate the comfort of the Core mattresses to appeal to customers seeking a truly indulgent sleep.

The original inspiration was straightforward: take the medium-feel of our original Helix Midnight and elevate it with the comfort, materials, and craftsmanship you'd expect from a luxury hotel mattress.

“The Helix Luxe Collection is our most popular mattress line, with the Midnight Luxe consistently ranking as our best-selling model,” reveals Lin, a Wharton MBA who began his career in investment banking.

“The original inspiration was straightforward: take the medium-feel, side-sleeper-friendly design of our original Helix Midnight and elevate it with the comfort, materials, and craftsmanship you'd expect from a luxury hotel mattress, but at a much more accessible price point.".

The timing of the 2018 launch couldn’t have been better. With original mattress-in-a-box brands Casper and Purple disrupting the traditional brick-and-mortar mattress industry, Helix and its Luxe line became an integral part of the growing boxed bed revolution.

Then, just two years later, many parts of the States found themselves under stay-at-home orders as part of Covid-19 quarantine measures.

One of Helix's biggest competitive advantages is that we manufacture our own foam.

With 'work from bed' the upcoming normal for many Americans, and with little else to spend hard-earned cash on, the e-commerce mattress industry boomed.

Some even reported that the Helix Midnight Luxe was the only thing helping them sleep during those uncertain times.

With the bed-to-door industry on fast forward, Helix wanted to keep the Midnight Luxe ahead of the curve. The answer lay in doubling down: improving the mattress from base to quilted cover.

The Midnight Luxe stands at 13.5" tall and is crafted from a combination of coils and comfort foam.

Each layer serves a specific purpose for its overall sleep comfort.

From top to bottom, let's take a closer look at the Luxe's overall structure:.

A soft, breathable cover sits above two layers of premium quilting foam (1.5 lb and gel-infused 1.8 lb), creating a plush sleep surface that's both comfortable and durable. The standard cover is made with TENCEL fabric.

An additional layer of gel memory foam provides targeted pressure relief, particularly around the shoulders and hips, making the Midnight Luxe especially well-suited for side sleepers. This gel memory foam has an IFD (Indentation Force Deflection) of 10-18 and a density of 1.8-4.0 PCF.

It has been revealed that helix's signature titanium, graphite, and copper infused memory foam delivers deeper contouring and is engineered for temperature management and long-term durability. It has a 4lb foam density, which is more than double the 2lb density of many foams used by standard brands.

Next, A firmer transition layer, with lower density foam, creates a gradual shift from the plush comfort layers to the supportive coil system underneath. This helps prevent the sensation of sinking too deeply into the mattress.

Up to 1,000 individually wrapped eight-inch coils provide responsive support, with enhanced reinforcement in the lumbar region to help promote healthy spinal alignment. Reinforced perimeter coils also improve edge support, making the full surface of the mattress more usable. Each coil is made from tempered steel and wrapped in polypropylene non-woven fabric.

Recent findings suggest that the Helix Midnight Luxe is a luxury hybrid mattress. While the coils are in vital factor in the bed's overall comfort layer, it is the proprietary foams that help set this boxed bed apart from many competitors.

While most brands use pre-poured foams from third party suppliers, Helix manufacture their own foam (more on this below). This should allow them to fine tune its construction until the optimal level of comfort is achieved. A feat I think they've pulled it off.

As someone who sleeps predominantly on my side and occasionally on my back, I feel as though the Helix Midnight Luxe has been crafted specifically for me in way that I haven't experienced while testing another mattress.

The foams provide just the right amount of body-contouring support across the shoulders, hips and knees, while holding the spine in healthy alignment with the rest of the body.

It has been revealed that in 2022, Helix merged with sleep brand Brooklyn Bedding. Now operating from its own factory in Arizona, Helix began experimenting with pouring and manufacturing its own mattress foam, alongside its own coils.

This decision proved to be a pivotal moment in the development of the Midnight Luxe.

“One of Helix's biggest competitive advantages is something most consumers never see: we manufacture our own foam,” explains Lin, who built the finance and operations backbone behind Helix’s growth and helps steer the brand’s product innovation and retail expansion.

Sources indicate that “Many mattress brands are essentially assemblers. They source foam, coils, and other components from third-party suppliers and combine them into a finished product.

Industry observers note that “At Helix, we take a different approach. We manufacture our core components ourselves, giving us significantly more control over material quality, performance, and cost.

“A perfect example is the proprietary memory foam we developed specifically for the Luxe Collection.”.

We developed a high-density, 4lb memory foam infused with titanium, graphite and copper.

“For the latest Midnight Luxe, we developed a high-density, 4lb memory foam infused with titanium, graphite and copper,” explains Lin. “This is one of the most notable innovations in the redesigned mattress.”.

It has been revealed that foam density is an key factor in overall durability. Higher-density memory foams can offer greater resistance to daily use, wear and compression, helping the Midnight Luxe to maintain its comfort and support through years of use.

And with a queen costing in the region of $1,900 when not on sale, durability is crucial.

However, as someone who has tested both versions of the Helix Midnight Luxe, it's worth noting that the trade off of this durability is that the 2025 redesigned model is slightly firmer.

"At 4lb per cubic foot, this is a premium-density memory foam engineered for long-term performance," explains Lin.

For context, many luxury manufacturer's use foams under 2lb in density, with 1.8lb considered an acceptable density.

Industry observers note that helix also incorporates three distinct materials into the foam formulation, each selected for its specialist properties. These are:.

By manufacturing its own foam, the brand can refine density, responsiveness and body-cradling characteristics until it's achieved the desired balance.

For the Midnight Luxe in particular, that means "deep pressure relief without sacrificing the support that makes the [mattress] so comfortable," indicates Lin.

"It's a level of material customization that would be much more difficult if we were simply purchasing off-the-shelf foam.".

“While the deeper comfort layers are vital, we also paid attention to the part of the mattress you feel first: the quilted pillow top,” says Lin.

"The plush pillow top is a quilted comfort system made with two layers of high-density foam, a 1.5lb layer and a 1.8lb gel-infused layer.

“These layers are designed to provide immediate cushioning and pressure relief, particularly around sensitive areas like the shoulders and hips.".

While pressure relief is a crucial feature of any mattress designed specifically for side sleepers, there was another reason the brand invested in higher-density materials at the top — durability.

Recent findings suggest that "The uppermost layers of a mattress experience significant daily compression and wear," explains Lin. "Using higher-quality foam in these layers helps the Midnight Luxe to maintain its comfort characteristics over time.

"By incorporating 1.5lb and 1.8lb foams, we're making a deliberate investment in materials that go beyond what's commonly used in the industry.".

For context, both the Saatva Classic, the highest-scoring mattress we've ever tested, and the DreamCloud Classic, our second highest ranking mattress overall because of its superb value for money, use a foam density of 1.4lb in their Euro top covers, which are inherently different by design to the plush pillow top on the Midnight Luxe.

According to recent reports, the Helix Midnight Luxe rolled out in 2018 as a luxury hotel-style upgrade to the original Midnight (now marketed as the Core Midnight). It has a plush pillow top and zoned lumbar support for back pain relief.

"Those features helped establish the Luxe Collection as our most popular mattress line," claims Lin.

"But as our manufacturing capabilities evolved, we saw an opportunity to make more meaningful improvements to the mattress itself.".

In 2025, Helix introduced the most significant redesign of the Luxe Collection since its launch.

Rather than focusing on cosmetic changes or additional features, they sought to reengineer the mattress from the inside out.

"These improvements reflect how we think about product development at Helix," states Lin.

"We're constantly looking for ways to improve the actual sleep experience, whether that's through better pressure relief, more consistent support, improved temperature regulation, or materials that maintain their performance longer.

"Ultimately, our philosophy is simple: a luxury mattress should be defined by the quality of what's inside it, not just how it looks or how much it costs," concludes Lin.

"That's what guided the latest Midnight Luxe redesign, and it's what continues to drive our approach to mattress innovation.".

Offering support for iPhone and Android’s tracking networks, the latest Kodak SlideTag offers the neat added functionality over an AirTag of being able to show your photos and more on an E-Ink display.

In a recent development, the Kodak SlideTag is inspired by classic 35mm slides from Kodak cameras, and is built by the same organization, Reto, that rolled out a keychain digital camera inspired by old Kodak cameras too. The tracker’s E-Ink display is designed mainly to showcase your photos, with storage built-in for up to 12 photos, but also the ability to show lists and QR codes.

The SlideTag’s extra features are controlled by the Kodak Memory Link app, while tracking is handled in the Find My app on iPhone just like an AirTag (and the Find Hub app on Android phones).

There are nine total styles for the SlideTag, all sold in a blind box format. You can order one tracker for $35 with the whole set also available for purchase.

Eight of the styles have a one-in-eight chance of finding, while the ninth style is only found in one out of every 64 boxes.

Kodak SlideTag is available today from Amazon.

#120697. Macrohistory in Six Facts

Macrohistory in Six Facts

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Basilhalperin

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that joe Stiglitz: “Economists spend enormous energy providing refined testing to their models.
  • In a recent development, can we condense down the most vital lessons we’ve learned from macro and macrohistory to a minimal set of facts?
  • According to recent reports, what I have here on the X-axis is GDP per person, adjusted for inflation and cost of living differences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that joe Stiglitz: “Economists spend enormous energy providing refined testing to their models. Economists often seem to forget that some of the most important theories in physics are either verified or refuted by a single observation, or a limited number of observations (e.g. Einstein’s theory of relativity, or the theory of black holes).”.

In a recent development, can we condense down the most vital lessons we’ve learned from macro and macrohistory to a minimal set of facts? Here is one attempt: macrohistory in six (plus or minus) facts.

According to recent reports, what I have here on the X-axis is GDP per person, adjusted for inflation and cost of living differences. On the Y-axis is life satisfaction, based on going around and asking people, ‘on a scale of zero to ten, how satisfied are you with your life’.

In richer countries, on average people are happier.

Or – in richer countries, on average people live longer:.

Or – in richer countries, fewer babies die:.

Recent findings suggest that are all these good things just coming from people working more? No – in richer countries, people work less; and as countries become richer over time, people work less:.

More intangible things, too. You can ask people how much they trust their neighbors. In richer countries, people trust their neighbors more:.

Of course, we know market capitalism has its flaws – for example, richer countries emit more CO2 per person:.

And all of this is correlation not causation.

But we’re going to run with this, and use GDP per person as our measure of how well we are doing.

This is the most key fact about human history.

We are ∼10 times richer than our great-great-great grandparents, who themselves in turn were ∼2 times as rich as Jesus of Nazareth.

Recent findings suggest that everyone used to be poor. This is the most important fact about macro history.

Why did we used to be poor? We lived in a Malthusian hellscape:.

This shows the real wage of workers in England since 1250.

Prior to the Industrial Revolution, any time wages rose, more babies would survive to adulthood, parents would have more babies, and the population would rise until wages were driven back to subsistence.

We lived in a Malthusian hellscape. Until:.

The Industrial Revolution was the single most key event in human history.

We went from 0.01% growth per year, up to 0.1% with the Industrial Revolution around 1750, to 1% with the Second Industrial Revolution around 1870, to the modern 2% growth rate.

The Industrial Revolution was the single most crucial event in macro history. It also brought about:.

The growth explosion from the Industrial Revolution did not take place everywhere and all at once. Many countries did not see faster growth and rising GDP per person until much later – and many still have not seen these much at all.

But let’s talk first about the frontier.

Recent findings suggest that this is the most important fact in modern macro. Growth at the technological frontier – measured here as GDP per person in the United States – has been a shockingly steady 2% per year for the last 150 years.

You can see a temporary blip down for the Great Depression, but otherwise the trend has been remarkably constant.

Running water, electricity, automobiles, computers, the web – all show up here as a continuation of a steady 2% per year trend.

What about the rest of the world?

Sources indicate that the figure here has on the X-axis, income per person per day. You can see, for example, that even the poorest 11% of people in the United States have on average a higher income than the median person in Bangladesh or Ethiopia.

According to recent reports, income varies enormously across countries. Those of us born in the United States are so, so lucky.

Well, are we stuck with these enormous differences? No:.

Here again we see the United States up top as the frontier.

Japan and South Korea, at the turn of the 20th century, were ∼as poor as sub-Saharan Africa is today. But Japan and South Korea caught up close to the United States. There are growth miracles.

But there are also growth disasters. Argentina at the turn of the 20th century was one of the richest countries in the world. But it has stagnated, relative to the frontier. A classic basket case.

And there are countries like Nigeria, which have never experienced much sustained growth at all.

What should we expect of the future? This takes us to the most fun fact, the most speculative:.

Over the long sweep of history, aggregate GDP growth is speeding up.

In a recent development, what I have plotted here is how long it takes for world GDP to double. This goes back to 1 million years ago. Measuring GDP in 1 million BC is hard, but for our purposes I feel good about these numbers.

We’ve gone from doubling every 100,000 years down to a modern doubling time of every 35 or so years.

Now, to the natural question: what should we expect about growth in the future?

I think it really comes down to: which prior do you want to anchor to?

Do you want to anchor to the last 150 years or so, with our constant 2% growth and doubling every 35 years?

Or do you want to anchor to the long sweep of macrohistory, where growth has been speeding up?

Walking around outside, I think we should really feel bombarded with this fact, every day. All these buildings? All these people? All this stuff?

In a recent development, this is all kind of crazy. It’s all a little bonkers. Compared to the grand sweep of macrohistory, we live in a weird time.

I found these “Six Substantial Facts of Macrohistory” particularly useful as framing when teaching my undergrad macro course for the first time last fall: teaching GDP construction (fact 0), the Malthusian model (fact 1), the theories of the Industrial Revolution (fact 2), the Solow model (facts 3-5), and the endogenous growth model (fact 6).

It was pedagogically very useful to have this catechism of the Six Facts to review at the start of many classes, to anchor the students to where we were in the course.

In a recent development, it was also useful for me, for setting a target for the bare minimum that students might remember in a decade. Do I expect them to remember the capital accumulation equation of the Solow model? No. Or even the idea of income vs. substitution effects? For the vast majority – no, not really.

Can I hope that they pick up a gut-level sense, in their bones, that everyone used to be poor? That’s an extremely notable idea, a realistic goal, and yet an idea that the vast majority of people do not know or have not properly internalized.

It has been revealed that I also think the Six Big Facts of Macrohistory is a useful attempt to condense “what should any well-informed civilian know about macro and macrohistory”. E.g. my microeconomist wife, or my parents.

It has been revealed that what are the runner-up facts not listed here? Structural transformation and urbanization? The demographic transition? Women’s emancipation or rising health would be the natural top candidates, but are captured (if perhaps buried) in Fact 0.

Again, underlying these figures is the astounding work of generations of economic historians, demographers, national statistical agencies, and others.

Initially, Fielder planned to film her watching some of the documentary footage he’d shot so far.

Industry observers note that “It was fascinating,” Seyfried stated, adding that “we kept organically deciding to do more things.” Fielder eventually convinced Seyfried to play Holmes again during reenactments in the film. “It was weird,” Seyfried said of returning to the character.

She remarked it was especially challenging because she couldn’t watch the documentary footage unless she was present on the set and the script was only accessible via “five-factor authentication” the night before. “I was so insecure about it,” Seyfried said. “The Dropout is fiction based on real things. This is based on what we know.”.

Seyfried added, “What an experience. I haven’t processed it fully because it was meta at a point.”.

Sources indicate that she also admitted that she had a hard time keeping her role a secret. “I’m the most indiscreet person I’ve ever met in my life,” Seyfried told Fallon. “How the hell did I manage to keep it under wraps? I told a lot of people. But I guess I could trust them all.”.

Seyfried recently told Rolling Stone that she agreed to be part of You Can See Everything without telling her team. Why Do We Allow Politicians to Trade Stocks?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollingstone

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earlier this year, before coming on to Rolling Stone’s staff full time, I sold some stock.
  • Industry observers note that donald Trump, however, has no such qualms.
  • Recent findings suggest that this week, after exerting a considerable amount of political pressure, Trump convinced the board of Nvidia, the most valuable firm in the world, to reinstate its disgraced CEO Jensen Huang after an absurd scandal that revealed Huang was potentially complicit in helping one of his mistresses buy up advanced Nvidia computer chips on behalf of the Chinese government.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this year, before coming on to Rolling Stone’s staff full time, I sold some stock. Back in the early 2000s, my grandmother had willed me a handful of shares of Disney stock, which sat around appreciating value and were worth a few grand. I told myself I was selling off the Disney stock for ethical reasons — many places I wrote for as a freelancer asked employees to sign contracts that attest that they won’t buy, sell, or hold stock in individual companies they cover. Really, though, I just needed the cash.

Industry observers note that donald Trump, however, has no such qualms. Nor does he really need a little extra cash. In his time as president, he has made billions of dollars, some of it through the sale of stock in companies that his policies have directly affected.

Recent findings suggest that this week, after exerting a considerable amount of political pressure, Trump convinced the board of Nvidia, the most valuable firm in the world, to reinstate its disgraced CEO Jensen Huang after an absurd scandal that revealed Huang was potentially complicit in helping one of his mistresses buy up advanced Nvidia computer chips on behalf of the Chinese government. Huang’s ouster — and the whole selling super computer parts to a Chinese spy thing — had tanked Nvidia’s stock in recent weeks, dragging most of Wall Street down with it, which was not something that Trump wanted. But now, Huang is back as CEO, and the numbers are once again going up — including Trump’s own. According to financial disclosures from September, Trump owns hundreds of thousands of shares in Nvidia — which could have gained as much as $15 million in value in the past 48 hours alone, since Huang’s reinstatement.

The scale of Trump’s corruption and grift in office is something we have truly never seen before, but elected officials making big money off the stock market is nothing latest. There are no provisions prohibiting politicians from investing in private companies — only limp guidelines passed in 2012 that force them to disclose their positions online and promise not to use privileged information. Shockingly, that hasn’t stopped many of them from taking advantage of their position for years. The numbers don’t lie: There are even indexes that often out-perform the S&P 500 and multiple major hedge funds just by mirroring the exact trades that former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi makes. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Recent findings suggest that trump, of course, has taken this to its extreme end, at times appearing to manipulate markets on behalf of his friends and political allies, while enriching himself through everything from stock sales to pump-and-dump crypto scams. In 2025 alone, the president’s annual earnings were more than $2.2 billion, which makes Pelosi’s millions look like the take from a podunk coin laundromat. But ultimately, the discrepancy is beside the point. Why do we let any of these people trade stocks at all? Why is a cub reporter at a newspaper held to a higher standard than someone holding federal elected office? Why are members of Congress allowed to pass legislation pertaining to companies they have a financial stake in? Why is the president of the United States allowed to wheel and deal on Wall Street as he makes decisions that can turn the global economy on a dime?

According to recent reports, in a functioning democracy, this would all be banned. And I mean all of it: a total ban on owning individual stock for any elected representative. Hell, ban their staff and consultants too, but start with the electeds. The point of representative democracy is for the public to appoint someone to serve as their avatar in government. That person’s job, then, becomes representing their constituents. They should have no other occupation, no other outside interests. I’d go as far as to say that they should have to sell off any equity in businesses they themselves started (and get rid of this nonsense of “blind trusts”). If they must hold stocks, they should have to dump their portfolio into a mutual fund or market index, and be prohibited from buying or selling at all until they leave public office. These people are supposed to work for us. Related Content Thomas Markle Indicted on Charges of Having Child Sex Abuse Material Cher’s Victory in Royalties War Under Fire as Mary Bono Pushes for Reversal Hollywood Heavyweights Urge Dems to Dump Schumer Nick Carter Loses Bid to Dismiss Sexual Battery Claim From Melissa Schuman.

That doesn’t mean the job is easy. Freshmen members of Congress who don’t come from money often have to get roommates when they come to D.C., because their base salary of $174,00 a year (in the House) can’t keep up with the cost of living their new life in politics. So increase their pay! I have no problem with every member of Congress, every major elected official, making a salary of a million dollars a year. That’s barely more than the league minimum for a rookie in the NFL, and I’m pretty comfortable saying that more people depend on the job performance of the former Speaker of the House than they do on the quality of the third-string offensive lineman for the San Francisco 49ers (no offense to Enrique Cruz Jr., who has a bright career ahead of him). Pay them all a million bucks, two million bucks, whatever — but strip them of everything else.

Recent findings suggest that it’s clear, too, that the American people are fed up with this. In exit polls following the 2026 midterms, 90 percent of voters remarked that corruption was a crucial issue to them. Many of the country’s political failings stem from a lack of trust — in leaders, in institutions, in the building blocks of society and social contract. It’s hard to rebuild those with leaders who are so blatantly helping themselves to a bigger share of every pie that comes across their table. Democrats, newly poised to take charge of the House and Senate, have pledged to bring their investigative might down on Trump and his children, but my fear is that the rot will remain even if the most corrupt president in history is taken down. Trending Stories Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Cher’s Victory in Royalties War Under Fire as Mary Bono Pushes for Reversal Don Was Pays Tribute to Bobby Weir by Reimagining a Classic Dead Album Amanda Seyfried Admits She ‘Told a Lot of People’ About Elizabeth Holmes Documentary.

Trump is a particularly egregious offender, but he didn’t create the system he exploited. There are 15 members of Congress with net worths in the hundreds of millions, and dozens more with millions in play. As the system is at the moment constructed, they’re all going to continue trading stock — an act that benefits no one but themselves. Hakeem Jeffries, Pelosi’s assumed successor as House Speaker, has pledged to make banning stock trades a priority next year, but it’s unclear how the push will play out with Trump unlikely to sign such a ban — at least as long as it includes the president — and if Democrats will be as motivated to pass it when he leaves office.

In a recent development, running for office should be a selfless act. The point should be to subsume your own sense of self into the collective will of the people who elected you. If you want to get rich in America, go ahead and get rich, but know that we elect our leaders to serve, not rule. It’s time we started making sure they do so with both clear eyes and empty pockets.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it.
  • Just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not.
  • It has been revealed that at its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that cupertino is one of those TV shows that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

It has been revealed that at its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

It has been revealed that the film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

It’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a big-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

If you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a significant payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

In a recent development, the true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the company lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

When in Doubt, Flail About

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Seangoedecke

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you’re working in an unclear situation — you have no clear guidance, or you don’t know what will help — the best course of action is often just to flail about.
  • Sources indicate that this is definitely dangerous advice.
  • Trying a lot of different things is the key to the other two points as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you’re working in an unclear situation — you have no clear guidance, or you don’t know what will help — the best course of action is often just to flail about. This sounds counter-intuitive. Wouldn’t it be better to be cautious and wait until you have a better understanding of what’s going on? Typically not.

Sources indicate that this is definitely dangerous advice. Flailing badly is a great way to damage your reputation at a tech company. We’ve all worked with engineers who seem to have nothing but bad ideas, and who are constantly pushing one stupid plan or another1. But if you do it right, flailing about is the best and quickest way to get that understanding and become useful.

Trying a lot of different things is the key to the other two points as well. First, the entire point of flailing is to get direct contact with as many different bits of reality as you can. Think of yourself as a caveman learning how to use an iPhone: the first step is to just hit all the buttons and see what happens.

Second, you need to try lots of things because most of your plans will suck. You’re flailing because you don’t know enough to just do the right thing, after all. If you just try one thing, it will probably be a bad idea; if you try ten things, one of them might turn out to be good. Because you’re not equipped to judge which is which, you need to be extremely sensitive to feedback2.

Recent findings suggest that third, trying many things also ensures that you’re not over-invested in them. If you only have one plan, you’ll want it to succeed. If you have ten aims, you only care about one of them succeeding, so you can drop plans that are failing. Since most of your plans will suck, this is critical.

Coincidentally3, there are also three types of flailing that most engineers will encounter.

Recent findings suggest that the first is product flailing. When you’re working on a feature that doesn’t really have product-market fit yet, everyone is in a state of uncertainty. You will typically have some central idea about where the value is, but there’s a lot of room to wiggle (i.e. flail) around the margins. When I worked on GitHub Models (now retired) I built a lot of features or integrations that didn’t really work. However, one of those — allowing AI inference to run from a GitHub Actions token — was surprisingly sticky, and turned out to be the seed of “Continuous AI”. If you’re working on a brand-latest product and you’re not flailing, you’re likely investing a ton of effort into ideas that were always doomed. Far better to flail around until you find something with traction, then commit hard to that.

The second is engineering flailing. Sometimes a system is so difficult that it’s hard to see where you’d even begin improving it: either it’s so tangled up, or it’s already so optimized, or it’s just so large and unknown. Some engineers like to sit down and carefully work their way through the entire system before recommending changes. I think this is foolish. Modern large software systems are too complex and are changing too fast to do that. Instead, I recommend making a bunch of speculative changes4 and just seeing how it looks (or how it performs). If it doesn’t seem like an improvement, drop it immediately; if it does, dig in and figure out why.

The third — the one most relevant to senior and staff engineers — is organizational flailing. Often I’m put in a situation where the problems are not technical: usually two teams aren’t talking to each other, or some team is unhappy and the director/VP isn’t quite sure why. What do you do then? Well, I recommend flailing! Just try a bunch of things that you think might help5: automate pieces of manual work, volunteer to take over tasks, suggest long-term looks that could conceivably make things much better, and so on. Most of these won’t be useful, but it at least reveals that you’re trying, which can go a long way in situations like this. A note of caution: this is the case where it’s most critical to be sensitive to feedback. If you instantly drop some blueprint of action that is failing, you can build trust; if you miss that feedback and press on, the people you’re helping will start to point their anger and unhappiness at you.

Recent findings suggest that why am I calling this “flailing” when it sounds like a sensible approach? Because it feels like flailing from the inside. Your manager will (hopefully) look at you and see a proactive engineer experimenting with solutions, but you will feel like you’re repeatedly failing: acting with insufficient information, trying a bunch of stuff that doesn’t work, and in general making a fool out of yourself. This feeling is normal, but you must ignore it.

Recent findings suggest that the unpleasant sense that you’re flailing is one of the many psychological barriers6 you need to push through in order to be an effective engineer. Knowing ahead of time that it’s going to feel like flailing can help you recognize the emotion and treat it as a positive signal instead of as a sign you’re in trouble. So long as you’re sensitive to feedback and willing to instantly drop plans that aren’t working, flailing can be an incredibly effective approach to difficult engineering and organizational problems.

Working around people like this is one of the cardinal social skills of succeeding in substantial tech companies.

It has been revealed that both from the people around you with more expertise and from reality itself (which plan actually lowers latency, increases user metrics, etc). Ideally you’re dropping any plan that isn’t getting “wow!” feedback.

In a recent development, it really is a coincidence. I tried to come up with a fourth or cut it down to two to avoid the appearance of symmetry but couldn’t.

Recent findings suggest that AI agents help with this a lot. You can just ask for five different refactors and skim them to see which one is most promising, for instance.

If you haven’t done this kind of work much you might be thinking “why not just ask people what they’re unhappy about and fix it?” In my experience, situations where that is possible get quickly solved on their own, and situations where other engineers get parachuted in are ones where nobody can articulate what change they’d want, or where that change is impossible for other reasons, or where everyone disagrees, and so on.

Sources indicate that others include the valley of engineering despair, taking a position even when you’re uncertain, or shipping code that isn’t perfect. “Many engineering problems are actually psychological problems” is a recurring theme on this blog.

Doesn’t that make it impossible to get started? I get a lot of emails from engineers who are struggling with this problem. They go like this:.

I work with a strong senior engineer. I feel like my manager structures work so that strong engineer always gets the visible work, and the more they do, the more opportunities they get, while I sit on the sidelines. Thank You, Jensen Huang

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollingstone

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even if one lives a long and daring life full of adventure and passion, it is unlikely one’s sexual activities will become the nexus of a geopolitical crisis, let alone the tipping point in a scandal with the potential to doom or save American democracy.
  • One of the more unsettling features of modern life is its resonance with an earlier American epoch, a Gilded Age when the sordid lives of tycoons and power-brokers were not simply tabloid fodder, but persistent causes of concern for national security.
  • On November 12, Jensen Huang, the billionaire founder of the semiconductor manufacturer Nvidia, resigned as CEO of the tech giant he created after admissions of several extramarital affairs — including one with a Chinese national suspected of cooperating with intelligence officials in her home country.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even if one lives a long and daring life full of adventure and passion, it is unlikely one’s sexual activities will become the nexus of a geopolitical crisis, let alone the tipping point in a scandal with the potential to doom or save American democracy.

But alas, not everyone can say this.

One of the more unsettling features of modern life is its resonance with an earlier American epoch, a Gilded Age when the sordid lives of tycoons and power-brokers were not simply tabloid fodder, but persistent causes of concern for national security.

On November 12, Jensen Huang, the billionaire founder of the semiconductor manufacturer Nvidia, resigned as CEO of the tech giant he created after admissions of several extramarital affairs — including one with a Chinese national suspected of cooperating with intelligence officials in her home country.

This affair was especially concerning to American national security officials, as the woman involved, Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), was heavily involved with a Singapore-based tech firm called Megaspeed. That company was under investigation for transferring export-controlled technology to China, namely the kind of advanced semiconductors produced by Nvidia required for the most sophisticated artificial intelligence (AI) applications.

Recent findings suggest that even more concerning is that Ms. Huang, it seems, had direct connections with China’s top intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security, or MSS.

It has been revealed that markets did not react well to the news that Nvidia might have been compromised by China. The company is a critical component of the burgeoning AI industry, the promise of which has kept stock indices growing strong since 2024 amid what was otherwise a maelstrom of macroeconomic ordeals.

Nvidia lost more than $1 trillion dollars in market value after Huang’s departure. The tech-oriented NASDAQ fell 11 percent, and the S&P 500 dropped 9 percent, reflecting the reality — apparent to anyone examining their 401k — that exposure to AI was pervasive across sectors. Some analysts began to speculate the “AI bubble” was entering its terminal phase and panic would soon ensue, dragging markets sharply downward. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

Then President Donald Trump intervened.

According to the president, he convinced Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang. Investors — those fickle creatures, as skittish as peccaries — rejoiced and plunged their money back into Wall Street and Nvidia with gusto.

Trump assures the public that national security concerns have been “addressed.” But he provided no details, apparently expecting Americans simply to accept that there are no further risks, even as investigations are still underway and further details continue to emerge about China’s targeting of Nvidia.

Although it is absurd to imagine the MSS will willingly divulge its clandestine activities, there is reason to believe that a thorough investigation may yield further details both about this specific case, and China’s wider corporate espionage and technology theft programs.

Indeed, market reaction is just one of the many threads to pull on in the Nvidia saga, and the Trump administration’s precipitous effort to pressure a corporate board to reinstate a disgraced founder has breathed a spark of life into America’s erstwhile somnolent legislators.

Sources indicate that one might even begin to hope that each loose thread, when tugged, will begin to unravel the tangled skein of corruption, incompetence, and lawlessness that defines this administration. Here are five key questions lawmakers — and law enforcement — can ask to untangle the mess.

Recent findings suggest that first: How and why did the president insert himself into the corporate governance of a publicly traded company? Such behavior is typical of state-run firms under the worst forms of authoritarianism, whether communism on the left or fascism on the right. Recent findings suggest that second: What precisely has been the impact on national security? Industry observers note that third: Who directly benefited from Huang’s reinstatement? The public must know if members of the administration, or anyone in the wider government, had advanced knowledge Trump was going to interfere with Nvidia, or acted on it in a manner that benefited them financially.

Fourth: How widespread is Chinese intelligence penetration of the U.S. tech sector? Nvidia and Jensen Huang are in many ways a unique vulnerability, but they are far from the only targets.

In a recent development, fifth: Is Congress meeting its Constitutional responsibilities when it comes to regulating high tech, especially AI? Corporations cannot be expected to strike the correct balance between profit and national security on their own, nor should they be left to operate without clear guidelines when it comes to critical tech that could benefit adversaries if it falls into the wrong hands.

Strangely, it is the answer “No” to this final question that should offer a glimmer of hope to Americans enervated by the president’s nonstop abuses of power. The senator isn’t alone, either, with GOP colleagues in the House of Representatives providing further cover.

According to recent reports, “The NVIDIA [sic] board’s brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed,” a group of Republican representatives wrote in a joint statement. “We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities.”.

The glitch at stake is not merely the future of a single company. A technological edge is one of the United States’ global advantages, and the security of strategic assets must be regulated by law, not subject to the whims and undue influence of individuals, no matter how rich and powerful they are.

It’s becoming clear that the Nvidia saga may present a unique opportunity for savvy politicians — one remains hopeful that such persons still exist in America — who ought to be able to make hay out of such a verdant crop of scandal. #120687. GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
