GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our GPT‑6 family of models can design fresh protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
  • An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks.
  • In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs revealed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our GPT‑6 family of models can design fresh protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.

An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.

In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs revealed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.

The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.

In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Industry observers note that proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Recent findings suggest that scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

Industry observers note that using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept newly introduced kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

It has been revealed that our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested.

We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.

Industry observers note that the model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together.

With our research partner, Onava⁠(opens in a fresh window), we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein revealed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.

Recent findings suggest that our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.

Sources indicate that we gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.

In a recent development, to turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.

Sources indicate that GPT‑6.2 designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to chosen targets. Specialized models then proposed amino acid sequences—the order of the proteins’ chemical building blocks—and helped select designs for our research partner Onava to make and test in the lab.

Recent findings suggest that we tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target. We found 5 hits for PD-L1 (a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system), 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. The original RFdiffusion study⁠(opens in a latest window) reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. Nevertheless, our results provide early evidence that we can turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins that bind to their intended targets in the lab.

An internal research model designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to the target proteins shown in gray. The colored shapes compare each design with a computational prediction of how the protein would fold and fit against its target.

Recent findings suggest that we tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose new ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab.

For three targets, we started with computationally predicted structures of confirmed minibinders whose sequences Onava had collected from earlier studies. In our initial lab screens, we saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). The amino acid sequences proposed by GPT‑6.2 also often differed significantly from the original minibinder sequences, with a median of 50% for VEGF-A, 43% for MDM2, and 15% for PD-1.

We also asked GPT‑6.2 to design upcoming sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes it had generated earlier: two targeting PD-L1 and one targeting IL-7Rα. A specialized model, ProteinMPNN, had already supplied one sequence for each shape, and proteins made from those sequences had shown binding in the lab. Of the 107 proteins made from GPT‑6.2’s new sequences, 14 (13.1%) showed binding.

Given an unpublished structure, GPT‑6.2 had come up with two substantially different sequences that both showed signs of binding to the same target. For the same PD-L1 minibinder structure, GPT‑6.2 designed two sequences different from the original in 52 and 58 out of 90 total amino acids. The two also differed from each other at 44 positions, nearly half the sequence.

Industry observers note that the unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give us strong evidence that GPT‑6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. The results also suggest we could use GPT‑6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence.

Industry observers note that researchers often redesign an antibody’s binding loops to help it grip its target more tightly, a process called affinity maturation. They may also want it to bind more selectively, so it’s less likely to attach to similar proteins. We tested a first step toward those goals by asking our models to design new loop sequences that preserved binding to the original target.

Industry observers note that we started with six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind to the same protein, IL-4Rα. For each antibody, we gave GPT‑6.2 its predicted three-dimensional structure and most of its amino acid sequence, leaving out the three loops that help the antibody grip its target. We asked the model to design newly introduced sequences for them. Of the 182 designs we tested, 128 (70%) showed signs of binding to IL-4Rα.

It has been revealed that we then tested how precisely we could guide the model’s changes to existing therapeutic antibodies. This time, we gave the model the original sequences and asked it to change about half the amino acids in each of three binding loops while keeping the rest of the sequence intact. We tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab. Of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) revealed binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1.

A long-term goal of programmable structure-based design is to let researchers specify structural constraints in natural language. In our computational evaluations, our models consistently designed minibinders that contacted the required locations on the target. We could also specify the minibinder’s structural class (all helices, all strands, or a combination) and control the number of coils and strands with near-perfect fidelity. The same approach lets us express more detailed requirements for the binding interface, such as which target amino acids should be buried upon binding or whether the minibinder and target should interact through specific interactions such as “β-sheet–β-sheet”. As our model’s reasoning capabilities improve, we envision researchers guiding protein structure generation much as they guide image generation today, by describing the features they want.

Our model was asked to design small proteins with specified shapes: mainly coils (orange), mainly strands (blue), or a mix. Some instructions also specified how many coils or strands to include. The designs are intended to attach to PD-L1 or PD-1, shown in gray.

Most enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. When designing a upcoming enzyme, researchers may know how a few key amino acids need to be arranged at the site where the reaction happens. Those amino acids can lie far apart along the protein chain. The challenge is to design the rest of the protein so that, as the chain folds, it brings them together and holds them in place.

We tested our models on 30 challenges from MotifBench⁠(opens in a new window), including examples drawn from enzymes and from sites where proteins bind to one another. We gave the models a specific three-dimensional arrangement of amino acids, called a motif, and asked them to use coding tools to design the rest of the protein around it. This task is called motif scaffolding.

Recent findings suggest that for each design, we used ProteinMPNN to propose eight possible amino acid sequences, and ESMFold⁠(opens in a fresh window) to predict how each would fold. We counted the design as a success if at least one predicted structure both preserved the motif and closely matched the overall structure the model had designed.

Recent findings suggest that in a preliminary analysis, 43.7% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model met both criteria, compared with 27.8% for RFdiffusion. While laboratory experiments are needed to find out whether these proteins could carry out the intended function, such as speeding up a particular reaction, this provides strong computational evidence of our models’ intrinsic protein capabilities.

An internal research model designed protein structures around a small region whose shape had to stay fixed, shown in gold. The colored shapes compare the model’s designs with computer predictions of how the proteins would fold. Panels showing only gold had no design that passed the computer checks.

In a recent development, in motif scaffolding, we specified how a few amino acids should sit relative to one another. We then determined whether we could also guide the design of an entire protein by specifying its overall fold. We gave our models a chain length and a code from CATH⁠(opens in a upcoming window), a system scientists use to classify protein structures. The models then had to work out where each amino acid should go in three-dimensional space.

Recent findings suggest that many designs captured the broad layout we asked for. The harder part was getting the chain to follow the right path through it. Two proteins can have several coiled stretches packed together in a similar bundle, for example, yet differ in the order in which the chain connects them.

We counted a design as a success if at least one amino acid sequence was predicted to adopt the requested fold and closely match the model’s three-dimensional design. Across 200 challenges, 18.9% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model passed, compared with 17.1% for Proteina, a specialized protein design model.

An internal research model was asked to design proteins with specified overall shapes, such as bundles of coils or layers of strands. The colored shapes compare selected designs with computer predictions of how they would fold, showing examples where the two closely match.

According to recent reports, many medicines, including aspirin, are small molecules, chemical compounds much smaller than the proteins they act on. Predicting where a small molecule binds to a protein and how it fits there is called docking. These predictions can help researchers decide how to modify a drug candidate so it binds more tightly to its target. To test our models, we started with experimentally determined structures of small molecules bound to proteins. We digitally removed each small molecule and gave the models the protein structure along with a text description of how the molecule’s atoms were connected (a sequence of characters called SMILES). We then asked the models to predict where the molecule had been bound and how it was oriented.

For our first docking test, we used the PoseBusters dataset⁠(opens in a new window), a collection of three-dimensional structures that show how small molecules bind to proteins. Researchers determined these structures experimentally, giving us a way to check the models’ predictions. Without being told where on the protein each molecule had bound, the models had to predict both where the molecule fit and which way it faced. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the molecule’s observed position and orientation in 93% of scored predictions, compared with 96% for our latest internal model and 50% for DiffDock-L, a specialized docking model.

In practice, researchers may already know something about how a molecule binds. One major advantage of a GPT model is that we can give additional information directly in the prompt. We tested this on 179 structures from the Scarpino dataset⁠(opens in a latest window), where each protein structure forms a chemical bond with a small molecule, tethering the two together. We told our models which two atoms formed the bond and asked them to predict how the rest of the molecule fit against the protein. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the experimental structure in 92% of scored predictions⁠(opens in a new window), and our latest internal model did so in 97%, while DiffDock⁠(opens in a new window) reached 60%.

Recent findings suggest that an internal research model predicted where and how small molecules would fit against proteins, shown in gray. Purple reveals the model’s predictions, and teal shows the molecules’ positions determined in earlier experiments. In these examples, the predictions closely match the experimental structures.

Sources indicate that where an antibody binds can help explain whether it blocks another protein from attaching to the same site. We tested how accurately successive generations of GPT could predict where an antibody binds and which way it faces. For hundreds of pairs of antibodies and targets, we revealed the models the two proteins separately and hid some of the atomic detail (all side chains) on their surfaces.

With the side-chain details hidden, the mean DockQ score (a commonly used metric in which higher values indicate a closer match to the experimentally observed arrangement) increased from approximately 0.05 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.28 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.81 for our latest internal model, at each model’s highest evaluated compute setting.

Because these structures were public, the models may have seen the same antibody-target pairs or similar ones during training. Even so, each generation of our models predicted more accurately how the two proteins fit together, even with all side-chain positions hidden. That progress gives us reason to be optimistic about harder docking problems.

Recent findings suggest that each row compares four models’ predictions of how an antibody attaches to its target protein. Colored shapes show the model’s prediction; dark gray reveals the position observed in experiments. Results improved with each successive generation of model.

In a recent development, we can design far more proteins on a computer than we can make and test in the lab. Even after we settle on a promising structure, we may have many amino acid sequences to choose from. We tested whether our models could help researchers decide which versions to make first by predicting how changes to a protein’s sequence would affect its stability, activity, or ability to bind to a target.

In a recent development, we drew on four public datasets from experiments in which scientists had replaced one or more amino acids in a protein and measured the effects. For each test, we gave our models the sequence of the protein the scientists started with and the sequences of 50 modified versions. We told the models what the scientists had measured, withheld the results, and asked them to rank the 50 versions without using coding tools, by reasoning only.

According to recent reports, in one study of protein stability, we asked the models to rank 50 versions of a protein by how likely each was to be folded at room temperature. We compared the predicted order with the order observed in the lab using a measure called rank correlation. A value of 1 means the rankings match perfectly, 0 means there’s no consistent relationship, and −1 means the order is exactly reversed. Across 265 sets from the stability study, each model generation improved, from 0.41 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.52 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.66 for our latest internal model.

In each of the four datasets, GPT‑6.2 and our latest internal model produced more accurate rankings on average than ESM2-650M, a specialized protein model.

Earlier, we relied on specialized models to predict whether an amino acid sequence would fold into the structure our models had designed. We wanted to see how close our models are to making that prediction themselves. We gave our models the amino acid sequences of proteins with known three-dimensional structures. Using only basic coding tools, the models predicted how each chain would fold in three dimensions. We evaluated their predictions using a measure called TM-score. A score of 1 means a perfect match to the real structure, and scores above 0.5 generally indicate that the prediction captures the overall fold.

It has been revealed that the biggest gains are visible in individual examples. For some proteins, our latest internal model closely reproduced folds that earlier models missed. Across the full test, the average score rose from 0.16 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.26 for GPT‑6.2 and 0.38 for our latest internal model. The specialized model ESMFold2 averaged 0.93, so there’s still a substantial gap in how reliably our models can predict a whole protein’s structure from its sequence alone.

What if researchers already know most of the structure and want to fill in a missing piece? We tested this on 100 antibody fragments. For each one, we gave our models the amino acid sequences and the surrounding three-dimension structure, hiding the six loops that help the antibody recognize its target. Our latest internal model often predicted both the shape and position of those loops quite accurately. ESMFold2 was still more accurate overall, even working from the sequences alone.

Sources indicate that each model was given the same protein sequence—the order of its chemical building blocks—and asked to predict its 3D shape. The colored shapes show the predictions, and dark gray highlights the structure measured in experiments.

It has been revealed that each model was given a partial structure and tasked with predicting the missing regions corresponding to the antibody CDRs. The colored regions show predictions from the internal model and ESMFold2 compared with the experimentally determined structures.

Sources indicate that it is vital to note that our protein design campaign relied on specialized structure prediction models such as Boltz-2, OpenDDE, and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. Our results show that GPT models have intrinsic capabilities comparable to specialized models at two stages of the workflow: backbone generation, where researchers commonly use RFdiffusion; and sequence redesign, where they commonly use ProteinMPNN. Our results therefore do not yet establish that our models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end in a zero-shot setting without help from specialized models.

According to recent reports, our work demonstrates yet again the jagged capability frontier. Predicting a complete protein structure from its amino acid sequence remains substantially harder for our models than several of the component tasks above. On that task, even our best internal models remained well behind specialized structure-prediction models.

Industry observers note that some benchmark results also require careful interpretation. In tests that asked models to infer amino acid sequences from protein structures, unusually high accuracy may partly reflect memorization or patterns left by the process used to generate those structures. Those results alone do not establish reliable performance on unfamiliar proteins.

The laboratory results provide a more direct test of whether proposed designs can work, but binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish properties such as specificity, stability, and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications.

This work is an early step toward programmable molecular design at OpenAI. Our goal is to let scientists describe what they want a molecule to do in plain language and use our models to help design candidates to test in the lab. To make that approach useful for developing medicines, we want to make progress in three areas.

It has been revealed that find minibinders for harder targets. We want to design molecules that bind to targets where our attempts so far have fallen short.

Design for what happens after binding. We want to test whether the molecules we design can produce a specific biological effect, such as killing a cancer cell. We also want to design molecules that bind selectively to their intended targets and are practical to manufacture.

Industry observers note that design a wider range of molecules. Our lab experiments focused on small protein minibinders and antibody fragments. We’d like to extend that work to molecules that bind to several targets at once, RNA, and small molecules, including a class called PROTACs that direct a cell to break down a particular protein.

It has been revealed that as we work to accelerate scientific progress safely and responsibly, we also seek to evaluate and reduce risks, particularly those related to biosecurity. The same capabilities that help scientists design proteins for upcoming medicines could also be misused. Our Preparedness Framework⁠ guides how we assess these risks and test safeguards to reduce them.

It has been revealed that while lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of new biotechnologies and new medicines.

Industry observers note that the BirdBuddy has been one of the most popular smart bird feeders since it hit the market a few years ago, but even with Black Friday discounts, the BirdBuddy Home is still a pricey $199. However, the manufacturer recently came out with a cheaper alternative: the BirdBuddy Nook starts at $169, but can be found for as little as $99 for Black Friday.

I’ve been testing out the BirdBuddy Nook for the last few weeks in my yard, and I think it’s a fine budget option for those who want to get into smart bird watching.

It has been revealed that the BirdBuddy Nook Solar has a 2K HDR camera with a 135° wide-angle view that can be rotated horizontally or vertically. It has a capacity of 3.8 cups (0.9 L) of birdseed.

According to recent reports, the larger of BirdBuddy's feeders, the Home can be filled with up to 6 cups / 1.4 liters of birdseed. It can be pole- or wall-mounted, and comes with a metal attachment to hang it from a branch.

In a recent development, the BirdBuddy Nook regularly costs $169 and $189 for the BirdBuddy Solar. For Black Friday, the base model has been discounted to $99, and the Solar model to $129. If you can afford the solar model, go for it — it’ll save you from having to recharge the camera module. I’ve been using the Solar model, and not once have I had to plug it in.

You can also find the older BirdBuddy Pro Solar for sale at Amazon for $179, but that camera is locked to a vertical orientation.

So what’s the difference between BirdBuddy’s feeders, other than the price? Mostly it comes down to capacity. The BirdBuddy Home ($299; on sale for $199) can fit more seed than the Nook, so you won’t have to fill it as often, unless you have ravenous squirrels in your yard, like I do.

The other major difference is in how you fill the feeder. The entire roof of the Nook hinges upwards so that you can fill its innards; the Home has a smaller opening in its rear. I found it’s very easy to accidentally overfill the Nook, especially if it’s mounted on a pole.

Otherwise, the Nook has the same camera as the BirdBuddy Home, which, while not as good as the now-discontinued BirdBuddy Pro, delivers more than respectable 2K videos and photos. Like the Home, the Nook’s camera can be rotated so you can record either portrait or landscape videos. I’m still not a fan of how the camera has a bit of lens distortion, so that objects near the edges are elongated.

It has been revealed that birdbuddy claims that the Nook’s smaller shelf is better at deterring squirrels. I initially set it up with the perch extender, which may have been a mistake, as it gave the little furry creatures an easy spot to clean out the feeder. Don't get this attachment if you have problems with squirrels.

It has been revealed that given that the cameras on the BirdBuddy Home and BirdBuddy Nook are identical, I would definitely opt for the cheaper Nook; yes, you’ll have to refill it more often, but it’s $110 less expensive. During Black Friday, the price difference is just $70, but that’s still pretty significant.

As I mentioned earlier, get the model with the built-in solar panel. It’ll save you the hassle of having to schlep out to your yard in the middle of winter just to see the squirrels raiding your supply.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are certain Neil Young stories that have been repeated so many times they now feel like folktales. They include his decision to head to a musical “ditch” after scoring a middle-of-the-road hit with “Heart of Gold”; his “More Barn!” command to crew members who wired one set of speakers to his house and another to a barn while he listened to Harvest on a rowboat floating between the two; and the rock of cocaine lodged in his nostril during The Last Waltz that had to be removed frame by frame by Martin Scorsese’s editing team at tremendous expense.

These are all true, but let’s focus on the latter one, since the Last Waltz concert took place 50 years ago today, and the cocaine incident requires some context. First off, Young was hardly the only one using cocaine during The Last Waltz or just about any other major rock concert of that time. The drug was everywhere back then, and most people didn’t fully understand the dangers.

According to recent reports, secondly, cocaine was likely one of the only substances on earth that could have gotten Young onto the Last Waltz stage, considering his psychotic schedule over the previous few weeks, and that day alone, which he started with a 1 a.m. concert more than 2,000 miles away in Atlanta before jetting across the continent to play with the Band at their last show with Robbie Robertson.

The Last Waltz was the culmination of the craziest touring year of Young’s career. It began with a run of dates in Japan and Europe in March 1976, chronicled on the live LP Odeon Budokan, that promoted Zuma and introduced audiences to latest Crazy Horse guitarist Frank “Poncho” Sampedro.

It has been revealed that these were stellar gigs, arguably some of the best Young ever played. They began with solo acoustic sets where he combed through his already vast catalog and dug out gentle songs like “Mellow My Mind,” “A Man Needs a Maid,” and “Too Far Gone,” before bringing out Crazy Horse after an intermission for fiery renditions of “Like a Hurricane,” “Down by the River,” and “Cortez the Killer.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

After somehow traveling all across Japan and then hitting Norway, Denmark, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, England, and Scotland in the course of a single month, Young flew to Miami to finish work on the collaborative album he had begun with Stephen Stills earlier that year. Buffalo Springfield were a distant memory at this point, and Young had already abandoned plans for the CSNY reunion LP Human Highway following their 1974 reunion tour, but he felt he had unfinished business with Stills.

The result was Long May You Run, credited to a newly introduced entity he called the Stills-Young Band. Young agreed to a summer tour with Stills three months before Long May You Run came out, even though Crazy Horse had assumed they were going to keep working with him on the road. “Neil doesn’t turn corners, he ricochets around them,” Sampedro told Rolling Stone in 2012. “So you just have to hold on to your hat.”.

In a recent development, the Stills-Young Band hit indoor arenas and outdoor amphitheaters in June and July of 1976. Without Graham Nash and David Crosby, Young had to work extra hard on the harmonies. The result was totally unique renditions of CSN/CSNY standards like “Suite: Judy Blue Eyes,” where Young’s voice is very prominent instead of buried in the back or absent completely.

According to recent reports, the tour didn’t last very long. In a 2020 interview with Rolling Stone, drummer Joe Vitale recounted how it ended much earlier than anyone imagined, especially the fans with tickets for the later indicates and the promoters who had signed contracts.

“We had finished a show in South Carolina,” he remarked. “We sold it out, a major arena. We got on the plane and flew to Atlanta, Georgia. We got to the hotel. Remember, this is 1976. They were using telegrams in 1976. When we got there, we got our room key, our room list, and a telegram. We were like, ‘What?’ I’d never received a telegram in my life. It said, ‘Funny how things that start spontaneously end the same way. Oh well. Each a peach, love Neil.’ It said ‘eat a peach’ because we were in Atlanta, Georgia, the peach state. Everyone’s telegram read the same. I still have mine.” Related Content 50 Years Ago Today: The Beach Boys Play Pivotal ‘Brian’s Back’ Concert in Cincinnati Inside the Wild Nights of Martin Scorsese and Robbie Robertson’s 1970s L.A. Adventure Neil Young Sues Trump Committee for $10 Million Over Use of ‘Rockin’ in the Free World’ 50 Years Ago Today: Paul McCartney Wraps Up the Greatest Tour of His Post-Beatles Career.

Industry observers note that A furious Stills brought in Chris Hillman from the Byrds to try and finish out the tour. “We tried to salvage the demonstrates, but when Neil Young bails, so does the audience,” Vitale said. “The same thing would have happened if Stephen Stills had bailed. Both those guys were major ticket sellers individually. But together they were huge ticket sellers.”.

The bad news for Stills was a blessing for Crazy Horse, since Young agreed to a U.S. fall tour with them, kicking off with a series of unannounced warm-up gigs at California bars. It began officially at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion in Los Angeles on Nov. 1. They stuck to a single continent this time, but it was still a punishing schedule in which he often played two lengthy concerts in a single evening.

Near the end of the run, he played four concerts at Latest York’s Palladium in three days, went up to Boston for two shows in a single night, and then traveled down to Atlanta on Nov. 24 for an early show and a late show. “A special Thanksgiving eve concert!” read an ad in the paper that listed ticket prices as $7.00 and $8.00. “Two shows! Advance tickets available at all Tic-X-Press outlets.”.

A tape of the early show has circulated for years, minus “Give Me Strength,” “Pocahontas,” and “A Man Needs a Maid” from the acoustic set. But the entire show is in Young’s vault, and he released “The Old Laughing Lady” and “The Needle and the Damage Done” on the 2018 live LP Songs for Judy.

In a recent development, it’s called Songs for Judy because of a rant that a delirious Young delivered early in the second show, which began around 1 a.m. “I saw Judy Garland down there tonight earlier,” he stated, talking about the orchestra pit. “She was wearing a red dress with red lipstick and she had a little bit of music with her, one of those music folios. It said ‘Somewhere Over the Rainbow.’ Had a picture of her as a little girl looking up at me with the blue sky behind her. And there she was, Judy Garland, with a red dress with a piece of music, and she looked up and said, ‘How’s the business, Neil?’ You don’t have to believe me.”.

It’s hardly surprising Young was hallucinating at this point, considering what he’d put his body through over the previous few weeks. “Neil and the band had imbibed and were on a particular plane, so the midnight show started around 1 a.m. in the end,” Joel Bernstein, Young’s longtime photographer and archivist, told Uncut in 2018. “It was an extremely rambling affair; I don’t think any of the Tonight’s the Night shows I saw were as drunken as this one.”.

But Young was still able to dig deep at the late show and rip through “Down by the River,” “Cinnamon Girl,” “Cowgirl in the Sand,” and many other classics. A complete recording of the show is also in Young’s vault, but he’s only released “The Losing End,” “Here We Are in the Years,” “Pocahontas,” and “Sugar Mountain” from the acoustic set, and nothing from the electric one.

The show must have ended sometime after 3 a.m. It’s lost to history exactly when Young got on a plane in Atlanta and flew to San Francisco for The Last Waltz, but the three-hour time difference worked in his favor, and the show didn’t begin until 9 p.m. Trending Stories Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Cher’s Victory in Royalties War Under Fire as Mary Bono Pushes for Reversal Don Was Pays Tribute to Bobby Weir by Reimagining a Classic Dead Album Amanda Seyfried Admits She ‘Told a Lot of People’ About Elizabeth Holmes Documentary.

Recent findings suggest that with all of this in mind, the only surprise about the infamous cocaine rock was that he didn’t have another lodged in the other nostril. And when you watch him play “Helpless” and “I Shall Be Released” with that glazed look in his eyes, remember what he was doing at 1 a.m. that same day. He was probably seeing Clara Bow, Lillian Gish, and Douglas Fairbanks all seated in the first few rows of the Winterland Ballroom. He’s lucky he didn’t start talking to them.

It has been revealed that it’s easy to understand why Young decided to have a very mellow year in 1977, playing only club gigs with his bar band, the Ducks. They did 20 indicates in the summer of 1977, and every last one of them took place in Santa Cruz, California. After the wild year he had in 1976, he was more than ready to stay put in a single place. When you start having visions of Judy Garland seven years after she died, it’s time to come home for a while.

The Best Last-Minute Gifts That Don't Feel Last Minute

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give.
  • With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful.
  • Sources indicate that and focus on presentation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we’ve all experienced gift panic—that sinking feeling when you realize you need a present in an hour and you just don’t have one to give. Whether you spent all year chasing the “perfect” gift or simply procrastinated, your time is nearly up. But don’t panic. The clock may have nearly run out, but your options haven’t. Before you resort to re-gifting something from the back of a closet, here’s how to pull off a last-minute gift that is effortless but feels elevated and worthy of the person you’re giving it to.

With the right presentation, even the most last-minute gift can read as thoughtful. Any performer will tell you that the difference between a good show and a bad one comes down to commitment and confidence. The same is true for last-minute gifts: If you act like your gift is thoughtful and intentional, they’ll think it is. The biggest mistake people make is apologizing as they hand over a present—nothing ruins a vibe faster than, “Sorry this is so last-minute.” So give with confidence.

Sources indicate that and focus on presentation. A handwritten note that contains a shared memory or personal joke can elevate a present. Use simple but personal wrapping; craft paper and twine, or a reusable gift bag that looks like you planned ahead. Add a small flourish, like a sprig of holly or a fancy bow. Small touches can make it seem like you’ve carefully prepared. What you don’t want are obvious panic gifts that scream, “I grabbed this on the way here.” The goal is effortless, not frantic.

According to recent reports, digital gifts are your friends. You can order something in minutes that arrives instantly online, and with a little thought, will still read as personal and intentional. The trick is choosing a present that speaks to the recipient’s tastes, hobbies, or quirks, and pairing it with a small note to show you remember what they love. From e-books to streaming subscriptions, these gifts hit the sweet spot of thoughtful and last-minute. Here are some suggestion:.

When time is running out, gift cards are your secret weapon. They arrive instantly online, don’t require shipping, and with the right presentation, they can feel surprisingly thoughtful. The key is to pick a card that fits the recipient’s interests and add a personal note. The more specific you are, the better. If your giftee is into Italian food, get them an Eataly gift card. If they're a PC gamer, get them a Steam card. If they're into education, a membership to Skillshare is perfect. There's a gift card out there for just about any interest, and all you have to do it google it and email it.

Generic gift cards can be a last-minute lifesaver that can still seem a little personal if you give them the right way.

Pick a theme or design: Many online cards, like Amazon, Etsy, or Starbucks, let you choose designs. The right visual makes the card feel more intentional.

Include a warm, personal message: Even one line can make a digital card feel thoughtful—something like, “I couldn’t pick just one thing for you. Hope this helps you treat yourself.”.

Send strategically: Deliver the card by email or text, but consider printing the email or screenshotting it in a small envelope so it feels like a “real” gift.

In a recent development, sign someone up for a subscription service, write a note explaining you want to keep giving them presents all year, and you're golden. Here are some suggestions:.

SnackCrate: This service sends a different snack from around the world every month.

Sources indicate that spiceClub: For the culinary adventurer on your list. A subscription to RawSpiceBar’s Spice Club delivers a curated selection of spices every month.

In a recent development, mocktail Club: Booze-free fancy drinks delivered once a month? Sign me up.

Thera Box: If you know someone in need of some self-care, this once-a-month box is packed with wellness and relaxation items.

Loot Crate: If your giftee is geeky, consider this monthly surprise box of pop culture treasures.

Sources indicate that cameo is a platform where celebrities, influencers, musicians, and performers create personalized video messages for fans. If someone on your list is a fan of someone on Cameo, you can set up a session, and give a card with a mysterious note like "Keep an eye out for a special message." They'll be delighted with a personal message from wrestling legend Mick Foley or terrified when Chris Hansen appears on their screen; your choice.

I have enough crap in my house, so I love getting experiences instead of things. The challenge with experience gifts is usually timing: Many require reservations or coordination, but there are plenty of options that let your giftee schedule the time, making them perfect last-minute gifts.

Museum membership cards: Many institutions sell digital gift memberships that the recipient can activate whenever they like.

Movie tickets: Your local multiplex probably has a gift certificate you can buy online.

Local attraction passes: Some city attractions offer gift cards or “anytime admission” tickets that don’t expire immediately.

Pair these with a note explaining why you chose the experience, or, if you have that kind of relationship, something like, "I want to take you to the Museum of Modern Art." Just make sure you follow through and actually go.

Sometimes, there’s literally no time to order, wrap, or even think about a gift. If you’re scrambling out the door and need something now, you might be able to fake your way through, even if you're stopping at the liquor store on the way to the Christmas party.

In a recent development, flowers or a small potted plant: Give a seasonal bouquet or a small indoor plant. Add a handwritten note, even a single line, and it might come off as thoughtful.

Gourmet chocolates or candy: Specialty chocolates from a local shop or grocery store display can feel luxe with a little ribbon or bag.

Wine, craft beer, or non-alcoholic beverage: A bottle with a clean label or interesting packaging immediately elevates your gift. Ask the clerk at the liquor store to help you find something unique.

Lottery tickets: Who wouldn't appreciate a bunch of scratch-off lottery tickets?

Hard cash is the most impersonal gift of all, but the only one you know will be used. This gift really depends on the person getting it, so be aware of whether they're likely to think "Just what I wanted!" or "Wait, I'm not poor." If you give cash, make sure it's crisp bills in a nice card, with a personalized note.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground.

Recent findings suggest that ask any Philadelphian about Wawa, and they won’t just tell you about the Pennsylvania-born chain of convenience stores known for their freshly prepared foods, coffee, fuel services, and surcharge-free ATMs. They’ll tell you a story about that time they ran into their childhood best friend at Wawa and caught up while waiting in line for their morning cup of coffee. They’ll tell you their favorite hoagie and a story about which location they were standing in the first time they tried it. They’ll talk about that last Wawa rest stop before arriving at their family’s annual beach trip and how their mom would always buy a few extra bags of chips to keep the kids happy on the last stretch of the journey.

Recent findings suggest that that’s because Wawa is more than a convenience store. It’s a way of life for those who know it. So, there were no two better longtime customers to meet up at Nashville’s first-ever in-town Wawa store than Pennsylvania native Joseph Hudak, host of Rolling Stone’s Nashville Now podcast, and Philly-raised Devon Gilfillian, a singer and songwriter now based in Music City.

It has been revealed that it was a homecoming of sorts for the two, who toured the upcoming location with all the excitement of a couple of kids on Christmas Eve, the day before the store’s grand opening. As Gilfillian enjoyed his meatball hoagie and Hudak reveled in an Italian Shorti, the two talked about the importance of finding community, putting down new roots in Music City, and, of course, all things Wawa.

Recent findings suggest that “Community is everything to me. That’s why I’m here in Nashville,” Gilfillian noted. Having moved to town in 2013, the singer-songwriter claims the city’s inclusive spirit has played a significant role in his evolution as an artist. Unlike some of the competitive environments he’s seen in other major music cities, Nashville offered something different.

Sources indicate that “It’s supportive. It’s collaborative,” he claims. “They put their egos away when it comes to Nashville.”.

For Gilfillian, that willingness to work together is part of what makes the city’s music scene so special. Regardless of genre, he believes musicians are better when they support one another rather than compete. “We’re stronger together,” he notes, echoing a sentiment that extends well beyond the recording studio. Since relocating from the Philadelphia area, Gilfillian says his musical tastes and songwriting skills have expanded, allowing him to reach fresh audiences along the way. He recently wrapped a five-week tour in support of his latest album, Time Will Tell, released in June, performing the new material with his four-piece band.

Nashville has become a home for more than just his music. Gilfillian’s parents have also relocated to Middle Tennessee, where his father has found his own musical community. Every Wednesday, he plays congas in a jam session at Flamingo Cocktail Club in the city’s Wedgewood-Houston neighborhood. It’s a fitting example of the connections that can grow when people find their place in a newly introduced city.

And just like the musicians who move to Nashville to find their own creative community, Wawa is focused on putting down meaningful roots in each of its new locations — be it inside the store or out in the community. The firm’s investment in Tennessee and its people is apparent. Since opening its first store in the state in June 2026, Wawa has expanded to six cities across six counties. With each store employing an average of 35 associates, the Southern expansion has created more than 250 long-term jobs for Tennesseans.

As part of each of the seven grand openings in the state, Wawa and The Wawa Foundation have contributed more than $27,000 to support Special Olympics Tennessee athlete programs, USO morale programs at Fort Campbell (which straddles the Tennessee/Kentucky state line), Second Harvest Food Bank of Middle Tennessee hunger relief efforts, and Monroe Carrell Jr. Children’s Hospital at Vanderbilt child life programs. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone people when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently confirmed four newly introduced features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

One of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface. The new interface makes it much easier to switch between different cards during the checkout flow on websites and in apps.

In the newly introduced design, you can easily swipe between cards on the main Apple Pay checkout screen. You can also tap on a card to view a grid of all your available Apple Pay cards.

The design also makes it easier to see information about individual cards, including rewards, balances, pay later options, and more.

Industry observers note that iOS 27 was released to everyone last week. You can enhancement in the Settings app on your iPhone.

Apple and American Express recently announced a new partnership that lets you pay with American Express rewards points.

When shopping online or in apps with an American Express card, you’ll see a fresh “Use Rewards” option alongside your available Membership Rewards points balance. You can apply points to cover all or part of your purchase, right in the Apple Pay checkout flow.

American Express points redeemed via Apple Pay are valued at 0.7 cents each. For example, this means 10,000 points can be redeemed for $70 applied towards your purchase.

In iOS 27, Apple is adding a new “Tap to Share” feature that integrates with Apple Pay on iPhone for in-store shopping.

This feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:.

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

It has been revealed that iPhone customers with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

This one isn’t really a upcoming feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has revealed that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.

As of November, Walmart’s roll out of Apple Pay across the United States is complete.

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

In a recent development, how often do you use Apple Pay? What are your favorite Apple Pay features? Let us know down in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looks like Tame Impala’s Kevin Parker just got an early Christmas present.

Recent findings suggest that this week, Seal released a video of himself nailing an acoustic cover of Tame Impala’s “Upcoming Person, Same Old Mistakes,” the defining song from the group’s hit 2015 album Currents. “You sang mine, Tame Impala. Had to sing yours,” the “Future Love Paradise” wrote on Instagram. “Felt a bit rude not to return the honour.“.

Industry observers note that “Finally taking flight/I know you don’t think it’s right,” Seal sings at Malibu’s Dragonfly Creek, turning Parker’s signature smooth synth into a soulful jam. “I know that you think it’s fake / Maybe fake’s what I like.”.

Industry observers note that seal’s not the first person to recognize the hypnotic draw of the Tame Impala song. Rihanna famously also recorded a version of “Upcoming Person, Same Old Mistakes” for her 2016 album ANTI. But this specific tribute comes after Tame Impala covered Seal’s “Kiss From a Rose” on Triple J’s “Like a Version” series.

It has been revealed that in his Triple J interview, Parker revealed that the song held some incredibly beloved childhood memories for him — mostly because “Kiss From a Rose” was included on the Batman Forever soundtrack. There were nerves at first, but Parker noted the group promptly focused on the task at hand. Trending Stories Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Cher’s Victory in Royalties War Under Fire as Mary Bono Pushes for Reversal Amanda Seyfried Admits She ‘Told a Lot of People’ About Elizabeth Holmes Documentary Don Was Pays Tribute to Bobby Weir by Reimagining a Classic Dead Album.

“It was the first CD I bought. So I knew every song on it. I used to listen to it back to back,” Parker said. “Once we accepted that none of us sound like Seal — like, none of us have the insane voice that he does, once we were content with, ‘Oh, it’s us, it’s a bunch of Aussie blokes doing it’ — then I think we were at peace with it. We’re gonna do the best we can.”.

Industry observers note that it’s the best kind of musical crossover: a cheeky musical appreciation from two top-tier artists. And who knows how fans could benefit from this? What’s that saying — first comes cover, then comes collab?

In a recent development, ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. It also summarizes utility records from a major regional ice storm. Finally, it outlines how to choose corridors, plan restoration and keep crews and the public safe around covered conductors.

In a recent development, the 80-minute musical, chronicling the days before the U.S. president’s assassination from the point of view of his alcoholic, cabaret-fanatic spouse, is a breathless romp with dance numbers, growling and some belt-out show tunes — all in a wig and corset.

Recent findings suggest that it took Adefope a couple of performances to realize it wasn’t do-or-die each night. “At first I was like, ‘This has to be all of my energy in every single second of the show,'” she begins to The Hollywood Reporter. “If you’re going to do one major show at Wembley Stadium, then yeah, you can let it all out. But it’s just not sustainable for the body to be under extreme tension for an hour-and-a-half. In the beginning, I was just kind of doing it like a panic attack. And then after a while I was like, ‘You can actually chill.'”.

Recent findings suggest that it tracks that Adefope performs Oh, Mary!‘s absurdity with the precision of a surgeon. She’s been described as the best part of everything she’s in — and it’s true. The South Londoner might be globally recognizable for roles in Hulu comedy Shrill or even the canceled-too-soon Franchise, but here in the U.K., she’s a titan of the British comedy circuit and possesses the kind of make-it-look-easy talent that some performers spend their entire careers searching for. Never is that more on display than in the BBC‘s Ghosts, where Adefope ascertained household-name status with her scene-stealing portrayal of Kitty, an adorable Georgian noblewoman who also happens to be dead.

Industry observers note that “I think it came naturally to me,” states Adefope about character comedy and her early stand-up aspirations. “It was probably a good thing that I didn’t really have people in my life who were doing stand-up. It was all just a very class clown vibe, listening to lots of Radio 4 comedy, watching [comedy duo] Mitchell and Webb and absorbing comedy on Nickelodeon and Disney Channel.” It wasn’t until late into her teens that Adefope thought she could make a living out of it. “I had an idea that I wanted to be a comic actor,” she says, “but that felt like a made-up thing.”.

Industry observers note that what does any young person with dreams of making a career out of cracking everyone else up do? Hit the Edinburgh Fringe Festival, of course. The must-stop for aspiring stand-ups and comedy performers has taken over the Scottish capital every August for 79 years, and served as a springboard for some of the most famous creatives in the business, such as Phoebe Waller-Bridge, Richard Gadd, Emma Thompson and Graham Norton. “It’s this one month where you get to live with all your friends and see your friends’ demonstrates and when I was doing it, I was like, ‘I wish this was what real life was like!'” remembers Adefope. “Sadly, it’s not.”.

But it did land her an acting agent, and with that came one of her first paid gigs: Josh Widdicombe’s 2014 sitcom Josh. “The character’s name was Catherine or something. But in the beginning,” says Adefope, “it was called, like, ‘Annoying Girl at Party.’ And I was like, ‘Sign me up!'”.

The more she acted, the more Adefope believed she thrived in that space — particularly character work. It was on the game show Taskmaster and a slew of other now-non-existent British panel indicates that her profile rose even higher. But it was a 2017 sitcom with Jim Howick, Loaded, that crucially got her acquainted with a member of theater collective Them There. “Jim called me and he was like, ‘We’re making this taster of this show. It’s called Ghosts,'” she recalls. “‘Would you want to be in it?'”.

Them There, comprised of Howick, Mathew Baynton, Simon Farnaby, Martha Howe-Douglas, Laurence Rickard and Ben Willbond, raised a generation with the still meme-spawning series Horrible Histories, a sketch show depicting caricatured versions of England’s most prolific historical figures.

They had a new pitch for the British broadcaster — a quasi-flat-share comedy in which a couple inherits an enormous stately home filled with the ghosts of those who spent time and died there throughout the centuries. Among the apparitions are a lightning-zapped caveman, a Regency-era poet shot in a duel, a boy scout counselor from the ’80s with an archery arrow through his neck, a victim of the Stuart era’s witch hunts, and a disgraced Tory minister who died mid-sex and is now destined to spend eternity without trousers on.

Recent findings suggest that five seasons later, and Ghosts stands in pride of place in the U.K.’s comedy hall of fame. Its unprecedented success has made superstars out of its cast, hatched versions in the likes of the U.S., Germany, and France, and accrued a cool $11.2 million at the British box office with last month’s release of a feature film Ghosts: The Possession of Button House, reuniting the beloved characters after the show’s end in 2023.

Since Katy Wix’s Mary ascended to a higher plane, or, as the ghosts say, got sucked off (“What can you do?” asks her former co-star with a faux pout), Adefope is the only performer who isn’t also a member of the writing team. She remains one of the show’s blindingly bright spots (of which there are many). “Kitty was pretty similar to how they first described her, but I think at first she was more stupid,” laughs Adefope about the initial conversations around her giggling, pop music-loving poltergeist. “But to this day, I’m like, ‘She’s the smartest ghost!’ I didn’t want it to be too two-dimensional — not that they would have ever written anything two-dimensional — but I am obsessed with Tituss Burgess [in Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt] and Jack McBrayer in 30 Rock; [the idea] that there’s something going on underneath the surface of this sweet character,” she says.

According to recent reports, indeed, it’s in Adefope’s immediate understanding of the smartest possible decision — a sly eye roll, sudden scream, or childlike outburst — that makes her work as Kitty so impressive. “I think a massive chunk of it is probably wanting to make the rest of the guys laugh,” says the star about keeping the rest of us guessing with Kitty’s mannerisms. “Part of it is probably having a background in doing live comedy — it’s quite good training for that kind of show because there are loads of us, and you don’t get hours to do a take. Sometimes you do just have to think: ‘What is going to make people laugh? What’s the unexpected thing?'”.

Industry observers note that she couldn’t have predicted the way the show would resonate with Brits. “It’s a very rare experience to make something that you love making and that people also love watching, because it’s sometimes one or the other,” indicates Adefope. But there certainly wasn’t any talk of a feature film after that fifth and final season wrapped up, or Adefope would have “really held onto that.”.

In the movie, the ghosts race to rescue a wandering spirit who’s possessed the body of a young boy before the child loses his life forever. “The writers always wanted to make sure that it wasn’t just a bonus, extra-long episode,” she indicates about the direction they took. “[They wanted it to feel] like it warranted being on a massive screen, and it’s so nice having people watch and validate that. […] It does deserve to be longer and bigger.”.

She would admittedly do “100 sequels,” but the group is facing some major continuity hurdles. “The ghosts aren’t meant to age, and every year we all think we look older,” she laughs. “We don’t know how long we could do it for, but I don’t think there are any intends to do a sequel. But there were no plans to make any more after the TV show, so who can trust what they say?”.

Industry observers note that adefope is certainly well-acquainted with the false hope of a fickle entertainment business. The Franchise, HBO’s satirical superhero comedy from Jon Brown, Sam Mendes and Armando Iannucci, got the axe after one season (though it did also earn Adefope a BAFTA TV Award nomination). She repeats THR‘s question with a knowing smirk: “Was it chopped down in its prime? It’s a great question. I was disappointed about The Franchise,” she begins. “I think it was so funny when the trailer came out for The Studio and it was so similar to the show we were making. And it’s won the most Emmys of any comedy ever [now],” she says about the Seth Rogen-led Apple TV hit. “So did we stand a chance?” The question lingers.

Sources indicate that another U.S.-based project, Aidy Bryant’s three-season Shrill, would take Adefope to Portland every year for 12 weeks. “That definitely felt like, ‘Whoa, this is actor lifestyle vibes,'” she says about playing Bryant’s British best friend and flatmate, Fran. “I loved Shrill so much, it was a dream,” she continues. “[But] because I’d done a show before that called Miracle Workers in Atlanta, there was a period of time [and] even now people say, ‘Where are you living at the moment?’ I’m like, ‘I do actually live in London,’ but after that I [thought], ‘Maybe I should try and do some British work just so that people don’t think I’ve left.'”.

It might not get much more British than the West End, where Adefope has set up camp for the first time in Escola’s Tony Award-winning show. Its transfer has denied the naysayers here in London, extending its run and consistently pulling enormous audiences, including to Adefope’s slot, which wraps up Dec. 5.

It has been revealed that she saw the Broadway version — ”I was so giddy” — and immediately told Escola afterward that they should consider bringing it to London. It never occurred to Adefope that she could take on Mary Todd Lincoln herself. “I have never really known where to start in the theater world,” she muses. “But Oh, Mary! is just so my humor and it felt like my comic sensibilities matched it quite well. I let the phone ring,” she adds. “I didn’t beg for the audition myself,” a glimpse of Kitty emerges in those fluttering eyelashes, “because I was too shy.”.

It might not be a shock to hear that Adefope is an electrifying First Lady, imbuing her portrayal with the no-holds-barred cheekiness the character necessitates. As is the joy of Oh, Mary!, seeing her version is an entirely different experience compared to her predecessors’. Adefope’s Mary is uniquely her own. “I feel so lucky to be able to put my spin on something and for it to feel like it fits really well,” she states. “Sometimes you get a script for something and you’re like, ‘It doesn’t quite match with how I see the character.’ But this [was] an amazingly lucky fit that I felt I could inhabit it.”.

In a recent development, after agreeing to take on the role, the nerves followed soon after. “I had these weird thoughts,” confesses Adefope. “I was like, ‘I’m going to forget to go to the theater.’ And they’re going to be like, ‘Where is she?'” But those jitters were swiftly reduced when she remembered it’s already a beloved, award-winning show. (The only tough part now is a hard-to-please audience, “[or] if they’re quiet when I’m doing my manic, physical comedy.” It’s a rarity, she assures us.).

Until December, Lolly Adefope has her kneepads on. “For the characters to get slightly further from myself is always fun,” she tells THR about what comes after. “I mean, Mary Todd Lincoln is quite far from myself, even though now I feel like she is me. But I’m doing lots of writing, and seeing where that goes, and [I’m] open to whatever comes next.” What that might entail is anyone’s guess, but one thing is for certain: this Ghosts alum will stay a pro at lifting spirits.

Nintendo notes that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in Upcoming York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials.
  • The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….
  • Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler says that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler says that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler notes, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

There’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting organization to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

According to recent reports, the best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera.
  • TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year.
  • The essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

The essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition).

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

Sources indicate that “The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”.

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in Newly introduced York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

The exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.
