#120625. Latest Update: PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1261 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1261 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A small transformer that writes and sketches from text.
  • According to recent reports, the text of this post (except the conclusion) was written by Claude.
  • Sources indicate that last year Zach Wimpee and I trained a tiny GPT to write cursive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A small transformer that writes and sketches from text. The effort was 80% data, 15% speed and 5% architecture: my first project that follows the Bitter Lesson.

According to recent reports, the text of this post (except the conclusion) was written by Claude. I strategy to rewrite it in my own words over Thanksgiving Break but needed to get the project out. So apologies for this move - all of my other posts were written by me, and all future posts will be as well. Even if you find Claude more comprehensible than my meandering thoughts, meander nonetheless I shall.

Sources indicate that last year Zach Wimpee and I trained a tiny GPT to write cursive. It worked but it only knew one hand (mine) and it learned from 3,500 words that I wrote on a trackpad.

Industry observers note that so here’s the obvious next question: can one small, ordinary transformer learn to hold a pen in lots of hands and draw as well as write? PenGPT is my attempt. There are two models. A 6M-parameter one writes print and cursive and picks up the handwriting of someone it has never seen from a few of their words. A 54M-parameter one draws from a text prompt.

In a recent development, then I took the thing apart to find out why it works. The answer wasn’t what I expected.

It has been revealed that that’s it for the modality-specific part: ten symbols and a merge count. The same tokenizer handles handwriting and drawings. For handwriting the model is told the text; for drawings it’s told a SigLIP 2 vector so a typed phrase can stand in for a picture.

In a recent development, almost nobody records pen strokes so I made the handwriting data from scans: 495,590 words by 1,255 writers, mostly from two research collections plus old letters and diaries from public archives. A vision-language model finds legible pages and transcribes them, the pages get cut into words, InkSight traces each word back into strokes and a set of checks throws out bad traces. Between a third and a half of the words survive.

The drawings are 477,670 sketches from ten public datasets. Quick, Draw! has 50 million and I kept the best 0.5%. I’m not releasing the datasets but the paper’s appendix explains how to build them.

Industry observers note that I compared PenGPT with older approaches then changed one thing at a time and retrained. Here are the rows I found most interesting; the paper has the rest.

Data and how you show it. Those are the big rows. Cut the data and everything gets worse. Drop augmentation and the drawing model stops following its prompts entirely. Train on one word at a time and the model can no longer pick up a hand: style rank goes from 1.9 to 6.0.

The clever parts barely register. Telling the model where its pen is does nothing for handwriting. The BPE merges I was proud of make the score slightly worse; they buy speed (sequences are 3.2x shorter) and that’s all. A vocabulary sixty times larger changes nothing. Doubling the model changes nothing.

Sources indicate that even the transformer is optional, sort of. An LSTM on the same tokens is a bit behind on handwriting and still picks up new hands. On drawings, where sequences are several times longer, it falls well behind.

Enough tables. Here’s what the two models make.

According to recent reports, the drawing model takes a few controls besides the prompt. One of them is how much ink to use.

It can also draw some things it was never shown as long as a blend of two familiar ideas will do.

The trick is almost embarrassingly simple. Each training sequence holds up to four words by one writer. That teaches the model that later words look like earlier ones so at sampling time you hand it a few real words and it keeps going. No style encoder, no fine-tuning. That’s how the 21 hands at the top of this post were written.

It also works from a photo. There are no strokes in a photo so I trace a few of its words with InkSight and fit one new writer vector to the traces, with the rest of the model frozen.

Industry observers note that one head in layer 4 puts 81% of its attention on the letter being written. I looked for heads that specialize in cursive or print and found none; every head reads the same positions in both.

Captions are the expensive part of the drawing data. Since SigLIP puts pictures and text in the same space, maybe you could train on picture vectors alone and type a prompt at the end?

You can’t. The picture-only model has the best likelihood of the three and it draws scribbles. The reason is geometric: SigLIP’s vectors for sketches sit in a narrow cone, nearly at right angles to its vectors for text. A model that has only seen the cone is lost when you hand it a sentence. Labels are enough to draw labels (78%) but only captions get you phrases (43% against 10%).

The drawing model blends but doesn’t bind. A teapot with a face is fine. Who wears the hat is not and “facing left” gives the same drawing as “facing right” because the single vector it’s told is close to a bag of words (those two captions have a cosine similarity of 0.999). Sampled handwriting is also less legible than the real thing, 54% against 66%. And since most of the handwriting was traced from scans, its stroke order is a model’s guess and not a record.

If you look over my blog, you’ll notice that many of my projects revolve around clever ideas. I fell in love with them because they were elegant. That isn’t a flaw in itself but I think Rich Sutton was wise to warn about it in The Bitter Lesson. It really is bitter and it has taken me more time than I’d like to admit to embrace it.

I think this post is my first step in the right direction. The results are interesting and the project was a pleasure to work on. And yet there was no clever architectural idea behind it. About 80% of my effort went into building the biggest, cleanest datasets possible and doing lots of quality control on them. Another 15% went into finding a decent 8xA100 node and getting my models to train fast and in parallel on it: 8 minutes for the handwriting model and about 35 for the sketch model. My previous attempt, the Cursive Transformer, took upwards of 10 hours on an A100 and only ever learned one hand. The tokenizer I used here is much simpler and far less elegant but it just works.

The bitter lesson kills or sidelines a lot of beautiful research ideas. It’s like gravity: it constrains you and most of the time it’s a very bad idea to fight back. But as I accept it and begin to work with it, I find things to admire. As a physicist I’m fascinated by the emerging science of scaling laws. And as a lover of biology I like the idea of putting a ton of work into the data and then literally growing a model on it, as you would an organism. Then you get to interact with it, learn what it’s capable of and study how it works. Seen this way, the bitter lesson has its own charm.

Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1376 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Intruder

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone.
  • The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain!
  • As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone. A common DNS mistake can leave them open for attackers to grab, which can lead to credential theft and worse. We demonstrated the attack is still possible in 2026, including finding real takeovers on US treasury domains, which were reported and fixed via a bug bounty program.

The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain! We only covered less than 1% of the total IP space, so there are many more out there for attackers to grab. So, now is the time to review your DNS records and get those dangling records squashed ASAP.

As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost.

Sources indicate that to test how exploitable it is to claim the AWS host that a dangling DNS record points to, we needed to find a way to cycle through available EIPs with automation. The full EIP space is a maximum of ~80 million IP addresses (in practice, probably half that), and these are allocated at random, so you can’t simply claim the IP address that you want.

To do this, we’d need to repeatedly allocate and release Elastic IPs from AWS’s EC2 pool, and check each address against the DNS records in our scope.

We wanted to report any dangling records we found, so we built our target list from public bug bounty scopes.

Recent findings suggest that using the bbscope API, we pulled wildcard scope entries and passed them into subfinder to enumerate subdomains. We resolved the A records for each host and stored anything not in private or reserved ranges in a DynamoDB table for use later in our pipeline.

By default, a fresh AWS account can hold five Elastic IPs per region. The loop works with five, but a higher quota means more addresses per cycle. Since Service Quotas automatically approves an increase to 25 Elastic IPs per region without a support case, we requested the increase in every region.

With the quota increased, we ran a Python script to claim addresses with each cycle following this flow:.

According to recent reports, in a single region, releasing and immediately allocating a new IP often returned the same address, suggesting AWS recycles recently released addresses first. Rotating through regions gave each pool time to move on, so by the time the tool returned to the original region, it would be allocated a fresh set of IPs.

In a recent development, in just 48 hours, we cycled through 450,000 unique IP addresses before AWS banned the account. This was enough to find 28 live EIP takeovers in the bug bounty scope. We had covered less than 1% of the total EIP space, and already had 28 high impact findings. A determined attacker using a wider scope than bug bounty and running the campaign for an extended period of time would likely find hundreds or even thousands of DNS records that could be hijacked.

Sources indicate that after 48 hours, our account received an abuse warning from Amazon with the action “Blocked the ability to allocate and associate Elastic IP in all regions”. This not only stopped us from allocating new IP addresses but also from using our existing matched ones. We wanted to report our findings to customers and bug bounty programs, so we needed to be able to host PoCs on these addresses as evidence the takeover was a success.

Fortunately (or unfortunately depending on how you look at it) AWS allows you to transfer Elastic IPs between accounts, so we created a upcoming account in our testing organization and moved the matching IPs across. It worked without any concerns, despite sitting in the same organization as the banned account. New accounts under an organization can be created without going through the verification process again, so an attacker who gets an account restricted could simply spin up another account and carry on. What was the point of the ban again?

We decided not to continue the full attack from the new account to avoid further abuse complaints, and instead decided to reach out to AWS with some suggestions that could make this attack less practical:.

Industry observers note that AWS has since responded. They informed us that they have no looks to change anything here. More on their response in the disclosure section below.

Across our limited target list of bug bounty targets, we were able to claim and control 28 EIPs which matched a live DNS record in the scope, with almost half belonging to government bodies. Bear in mind, we only ran the automation for 48 hours, and we would likely have found more, had we continued.

The most notable were five US Treasury subdomains pointing to addresses we now controlled:.

We also got hits across a range of public bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programs, including a university, two government bodies, a financial services company, and a large networking vendor. The rest belonged to Intruder customers, who we reported to directly.

Recent findings suggest that once an attacker holds the IP behind a dangling DNS record, they have full control over what that subdomain serves. US government websites tell visitors they can trust a site if its domain ends in .gov and it uses HTTPS - so if an attacker successfully takes over a domain, their site passes the test and users would trust it without question. The attacker can even pass a certificate authority’s domain validation and get a trusted TLS certificate for the domain to make it look completely legitimate.

This legitimacy could lead to phishing using a convincing real government domain to steal consumers credentials. The attacker could also host services on that domain to gather incoming information, and steal data (e.g. credentials) from any old automations that still point at it. That’s particularly dangerous, since those credentials could provide immediate access to other systems not related to the initial takeover.

AWS publishes 80 million IPv4 addresses for EC2, and our 450,000 allocated IPs cover 0.56% of that space. At our rate of about 9,400 IP addresses per hour, one account would take a year to cycle through every published address.

That’s slow for an attacker with one account. With multiple accounts, it comes down swiftly. If bans really do apply only per account, as our experience suggests, 10 accounts could sweep the full space in around five weeks.

In a recent development, realistically, the acquirable space is much smaller. Much of it is made up of auto-assigned public IPs or addresses held long-term by other customers, so a real sweep would take less time than these figures suggest.

An opportunistic attacker doesn’t need to cover the whole space to find something worth having. Even at 0.56% coverage, we landed 28 subdomains.

It has been revealed that targeting a specific organization narrows the search. An attacker would start by enumerating the target’s subdomains and identifying records that point to unused EC2 addresses. As AWS publishes the region of each range, they can look up exactly which region to search. For a target in eu-west-2, that’s around 2.2 million addresses rather than 80 million. However, when we allocated repeatedly in the same region, we saw a much higher duplicate rate, slowing the search. A targeted attacker therefore has a smaller haystack, but a slower way of searching it.

Sources indicate that all findings were reported through the relevant bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programs, and affected Intruder customers were contacted directly. We also shared our observations on the abuse controls with AWS.

AWS confirmed with us that they don’t plan to make changes, as they see the takeover as depending on customer-side DNS records rather than an issue in their services. They also told us they treat rapid allocation and release as a policy violation and have controls against it. Whilst this is true, they could do more to prevent the issue in our opinion, and the vulnerability class remains open due to their position.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that cultured Code is bringing swipe gestures to Things on Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro. Version 3.25 builds on the task manager’s basic touch support so you can schedule a to-do with a swipe or select several tasks with two fingers and drag them all at once.

It has been revealed that say you’re going through your Today list and want to put something off until tomorrow. Swipe right on the to-do to open the date picker. Open it by touch and you’ll see taller rows that make dates easier to tap. Custom menus get the same treatment.

Swiping left selects a to-do. Swipe left again to deselect it. For a longer list, swipe up or down with two fingers to select several items at once. Then touch and hold any selected item to pick up the whole group, even if some of those tasks are offscreen. You can also drag individual to-dos and headings.

A single tap selects a to-do, and a second tap expands it. Double-tapping works too. Inside a to-do, checklist items are easier to reorder by touch. You can also cancel a to-do or checklist item by pressing and holding its checkbox.

Cultured Code has also made the sidebar easier to resize with a finger and given buttons throughout the Mac app larger tap targets.

The upgrade follows Siri AI and Spotlight integration in Things 3.24 and more flexible scheduling for repeating to-dos in Things 3.23. You can find Things for Mac on the Mac App Store.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for a coffee machine to see you through all twelve months of the year (and then some)? The Smeg Espresso & Cold Brew Machine might just scratch that itch. This aesthetically pleasing machine can make genuinely cold cold brew — no lukewarm extraction here — and delicious, hot espresso. Although it's quite expensive in the U.S., it could be an ideal first machine for the budding enthusiast.

Weighty, high-quality accessories.

Extremely expensive in the U.S.

Steam wand takes a while to heat up.

Sources indicate that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Industry observers note that what do you look for when shopping for an espresso machine? Function? Coffee-snob-approved features? Affordability? Or style? If it’s the latter, may I introduce you to the Smeg ECF03 — one of the most aesthetically pleasing espresso machines I’ve ever seen?

Also called the Smeg Espresso & Cold Brew Machine, the ECF03 combines Smeg’s trademark ‘50s design with some seriously impressive functionality. The machine makes genuinely cold cold brew — not lukewarm like De’Longhi — and delicious espresso. While the steam wand takes a while to heat up and requires some patience for back-to-back shots, it’s a fun little machine for newbies.

Sources indicate that however, its MSRP isn’t a fun little price tag for newbies — in the U.S., it’ll set you back $699. In the U.K. you can grab it for as low as £204. No, that’s not a typo. £204. So, is this enough to make it one of the best espresso machines? To find out, you’ll need to keep reading this Smeg ECF03 review.

Single shot portafilter (single-walled and dual-walled), double shot portafilter (single-walled and dual-walled), tamper, cleaning disc, brush, cleaning needle.

Sources indicate that the Smeg ECF03 is outrageously expensive in the U.S., and pretty par for the course in the U.K. On the east side of the Atlantic, you’re looking at $699 from Amazon, but over on the west, you’ll only pay £399 at John Lewis. It’s also on clearance at Curry’s for £204, which is utterly bizarre, seeing as this machine only came out last year, but I’d recommend buying there if you’re fast. I’m not sure how long that sale price will last as I write this.

In the U.S., this machine is really overpriced. $699 for a Thermoblock espresso machine with no grinder is steep. For $699, you can get the Breville Barista Express or the Breville Bambino Plus with the Baratza Encore ESP grinder.

You can also get the De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo for $699, which has a built-in grinder, and the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini for $449 — which also has a built-in grinder.

It has been revealed that see what I mean? You’d still have to buy a grinder separately to make the most of the ECF03. That’s an extra $200. An MSRP of around $400-$500 would have made more sense, putting the ECF03 in line with the best entry-level espresso machines, Breville Bambino Plus and Breville Bambino ($299).

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Of course, the ECF03 can make cold brew, so you wouldn’t need to purchase a separate cold brew maker or French press for cold brew, but I’m not sure this is worth the extra $200-$300 over Breville’s options. On top of that, the aforementioned De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo can make “cold brew” for the same price.

I use quotation marks because De’Longhi’s cold brew comes out warm — but I’ll get into that later.

While the ECF03 has a 58mm portafilter — closer to the specialty coffee commercial standard than Breville’s 54mm — I’m not sure that’s worth the extra $$$.

The ECF03 looks like (almost) everything Smeg makes: retro, stylish, and oh-so cool. The only machine to forgo the trademark Smeg aesthetic is the $1,599 Semi-Professional/Mini Pro/EMC02 (the many-monikered machine), which was a collaboration between Smeg and La Pavoni.

Recent findings suggest that if you like the Smeg aesthetic, you’ll be pleased. If it’s not your cup of tea, you won’t be pleased. It’s as simple as that.

For a $699 machine, though, the ECF03 is a touch more plasticky than I’d like. That gorgeous white chassis? Shiny plastic. The steam wand knob also feels like plastic. If it’s not actually plastic, color me surprised, but it sure does look and feel like it.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a manometer, which is a nice touch, but it doesn’t actually show the specific bar pressure of each step. I assume anything in the perforated section on the bottom right means over 9 bars, but I’d like numbers on the next iteration of this machine.

It has been revealed that but the accessories. Oh, the accessories. They’re beautiful. The 58mm tamper is super weighty, making it feel incredibly high quality, and the 58mm portafilter is just as professional. They actually feel like weapons. This is the mark of a high-quality machine. If you unbox a $500+ espresso machine and the tamper is plastic, run. Run fast.

Sources indicate that naturally, you get a pressurized (dual-wall) and non-pressurized (single-wall) portafilter basket. I only used the single-wall one as I have the best grinder in the world, Mazzer Philos, so I didn’t need to resort to the help-I’ve-used-pre-ground-coffee-and-now-my-espresso-tastes-bad dual-walled portafilters.

Sources indicate that the Smeg ECF03 makes delicious espresso. As mentioned earlier, I used the non-pressurized portafilters and fresh Ethiopian beans ground on my Mazzer Philos. I recommend you also use freshly ground coffee and the non-pressurized portafilters for the best experience. Pressurized portafilters can destroy nuance and delicate flavors in specialty coffee beans, but are fine for pre-ground coffee if that’s what you like.

In a recent development, to make espresso, I ground 18g of my Ethiopian coffee beans to click 25 on the Philos, which is coarser than the Fellow Espresso Series 1’s ($1,499) optimal grind size, but similar to the Breville Bambino’s ideal range of 22-25. For context, I use the same coffee beans for every single machine.

In a recent development, here’s a photo of a “perfect” espresso. This extracted 35.6g in 26 seconds, which is in the “golden window” of espresso extraction.

As you can see, there’s a lovely crema on top, with a delicate, fluffy texture and a nice color to the shot. While this might not impress serious espresso enthusiasts — the shot was a little bitter at the end of the mouthful — it’s definitely fine if you are less of a hobbyist and more of an appreciator.

According to recent reports, overall, the espresso tastes very Italian. Strong-bodied, rich, and dark, even when using medium-roasted beans. Again, if you’re an espresso enthusiast, you might want to invest a little more in the Fellow Espresso Series 1 or Lelit Mara X3 ($1,999) — or the Smeg EMC02, which I still dream about.

According to recent reports, as an integral part of this machine’s marketing, it’s only logical I discuss cold brew in detail. You access cold brew via the “Blue menu”, which is activated by pressing the power button while the machine is already switched on. The buttons will glow blue, meaning you’re in cold brew mode.

Industry observers note that according to the manual, you’re supposed to use “one or two” ice cubes per cold brew, but I ignored that. I filled my cup about halfway with ice cubes, dosed 18g of medium-fine ground coffee in the non-pressurized portafilter basket, and set it to pull a double shot of cold brew. Not sure how you can get a “double shot” of cold brew, but I assume that’s just the machine’s limited button options.

According to recent reports, the cold brew took four minutes and fifty-three seconds to fill my glass. The machine is programmed to dose a certain volume of cold brew, but I used a 12-ounce glass filled with ice, so I didn’t need the “whole” serving.

Here’s a photo of remarked cold brew.

As you can see, it’s relatively dark, with a strong body. The ice cubes aren’t all melted — can you guess what that means? Yes, it actually brews cold! This is fantastic news; De’Longhi machines tend to brew lukewarm, or sometimes even actively warm cold brew (which then requires ice to make it cold).

Industry observers note that as for the taste, this cold brew was fine. I wouldn’t throw away my Espro P7 French press, which I use to make cold brew the traditional way (16 hours at room temperature), but I also wouldn’t turn my nose up at rapid cold brew from the Smeg. I think this will do if you want a cold coffee in a pinch, but serious cold brew lovers need not apply.

In a recent development, while the ECF03 makes a delicious espresso, its steam wand isn’t as powerful as I’d like it to be. Don’t get me wrong, this is nowhere near as egregious as machines like the Casabrews Ultra ($349), but for $699, I’d expect at least a Bambino Plus-level wand.

I was able to get perfect microfoam, but it took a while to steam an 8oz jug — around a minute. Here’s a photo of a flat white I made on the ECF03.

According to recent reports, as you can see, the milk texture is perfect, with smooth, almost melted-marshmallow texture. There are zero bubbles and the milk is extremely creamy. This tasted divine.

According to recent reports, however, it’s worth noting that I’m an ex-professional barista and an espresso machine tester of almost three years. I have a lot of practice. If this is your first espresso machine, you will need to baby that steam wand. Because it’s lower pressure than the Breville Bambino/Bambino Plus, you’ll need to learn how to eke out delicate texture even when you can’t achieve the perfect vortex.

Industry observers note that at 14.3 x 8.1 x 11.6 inches, the ECF03 isn’t the smallest, nor the largest, espresso machine I’ve tested. As it has no grinder, you’ll need a separate one, so I recommend making sure you’ve got enough to room for both the machine and its grinder before purchasing.

The water tank is at the back of the machine, so you’ll need a decent amount of upper-cupboard clearance space — at least 17 inches, I’d say.

Sources indicate that speaking of water tank, Smeg provides you with water hardness strips, but no water filter. If you wanted to filter your water, you’d need to buy that separately. Smeg sells these for $25 on its website, which is pretty disappointing to see considering this machine is already $699.

When you do need to descale, Smeg doesn’t sell its own descaler. I’d recommend using De’Longhi’s or Durgol’s, which are $19 for 2 bottles and $15 for 4 bottles, respectively.

Last but certainly not least — warranty. Smeg offers a 2-year warranty if purchased from the Smeg store or a 1-year warranty from another outlet. This is pretty disappointing when De’Longhi, Breville, and Ninja all offer 2-year warranties as standard — and many of their machines cost less than the ECF03.

Sources indicate that the Smeg ECF03 is ideal for espresso beginners. If you want to feel fancier than, say, a Casabrews (and you have the money to back it up, of course), then by all means you should invest in a Smeg. The ECF03 is really easy to use, makes actually cold cold brew, and has a mostly useful manometer for pressure-watching.

According to recent reports, although the steam wand means you need to really pay attention during milk heating, if you’re willing to put the work in, you’ll get barista-quality coffee out of it. And I mean… just look at it! Everything Smeg makes is an aesthetic marvel, and the ECF03 is no different.

If you’re in the U.K., you’re getting a much better deal, but if you find it on sale in the U.S., I’m sure you won’t be disappointed.

In a recent development, in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar reveals how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

It has been revealed that in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. In a recent development, kuzmyk will leave her role as Executive Director of Banff and publisher of Canadian trade title Playback on December 11. Both brands are part of Toronto-based Brunico Communications, the media publishing and events business.

Industry observers note that on an interim basis, Brunico President and CEO Russell Goldstein will lead the commercial elements of the 2027 Banff festival alongside Mary Maddever, Brunico’s Chief Content Officer. Kuzmyk will move into a short-term consulting role to support the transition. It has been revealed that “Leading Banff and Playback has been the privilege of my career,” mentioned Kuzmyk. “I want to thank Sean and the Banff board of directors for their trust, guidance and commitment to the festival, and our supporters, partners and sponsors, whose belief in Banff makes everything we do possible.

I leave knowing both Banff and Playback have never been in better shape, and I’ll share more about what’s next in the Fresh Year for me.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an upgrade to Ternary Bonsai 2 27B with substantially stronger agentic coding, multi-turn tool use, and multi-step task execution. Based on Qwen3.8 27B, it retains the previous release’s 5.9 GB model footprint while significantly improving the capabilities developers need to build agents that work with private files and tools on-device. The result is by far the strongest AI model of its memory footprint for agentic workloads.

Industry observers note that with Ternary Bonsai 2 27B, we brought stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool use to local devices. Since then, we’ve focused on making the model more effective across long sequences of tool calls: interpreting results, adjusting when a step fails, and maintaining the task’s objective through the whole interaction. This release also continues our work to make Bonsai more practical by addressing excessive thinking and repetitive loops in the previous model. Compared with Ternary Bonsai 2, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 completes tasks in fewer turns, uses fewer tokens, and delivers results faster and more accurately.

Agentic workflows are particularly sensitive to model degradation: small errors can compound across successive tool calls and derail an entire task. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 significantly narrows the performance gap to the full-precision base model while retaining its compact footprint. Preserving this behavior through longer tasks is an vital milestone in improving the intelligence density of models.

It has been revealed that we evaluated Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B against both Ternary Bonsai 2 27B and the full-precision Qwen 3.8 27B base model, as reported in the full whitepaper. We see marked improvements in agentic execution, coding, and multi-turn tool use, as shown in the table below.

In a recent development, on a single NVIDIA H100, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B achieves a generation speed of 291 tokens/s with MTP and processes a 2,000-token prompt at 3,200 tokens/s. Even on a consumer-grade RTX 4090, it delivers 204 tokens/s with MTP and a prompt processing speed of approximately 3,060 tokens/s. The demos below follow complete local workflows, from the initial request through intermediate decisions to the final result.

For products, this creates room to build assistance directly into the applications where work already happens: a coding assistant working through issues in a private repository, a document application that prepares reviewable summaries, or a desktop assistant that handles recurring analysis. Local deployment lets those products process sensitive material on the user’s device. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B strengthens the model capabilities behind that experience while keeping the compact footprint that makes it practical.

Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B runs on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs via llama.cpp and on Apple devices (Mac, iPhone, iPad) via MLX.

Model weights are available today under the Apache 2.0 License.

Full technical details of our compression, evaluation, and benchmarking processes are available in our whitepaper.

We work with teams to tailor Bonsai models to their applications, from post-training on domain-specific data to optimizing inference for target hardware. In a recent development, I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

In a recent development, the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

It has been revealed that the screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics firm. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

In a recent development, for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

According to recent reports, but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” notes Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

Recent findings suggest that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

In a recent development, yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Industry observers note that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

Sources indicate that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

According to recent reports, I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

According to recent reports, this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

According to recent reports, sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga indicates, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

Sources indicate that about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just substantial enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Latest York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

Industry observers note that but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics manufacturer XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” states Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Recent findings suggest that nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

According to recent reports, after preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

Recent findings suggest that in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Recent findings suggest that noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga indicates.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

In a recent development, but sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

In a recent development, but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, indicates experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu claims.

Industry observers note that medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” claims neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Sources indicate that telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra indicates, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra claims. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

In a recent development, if smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell indicates. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

It has been revealed that the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

It has been revealed that in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy revealed US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

It has been revealed that sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

Sources indicate that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this fresh technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

Sources indicate that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person manufacturer into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Netflix is the only major industry player not currently funding the UK’s anonymous whistleblowing service for complaints about bullying and harassment, it has been revealed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix is the only major industry player not currently funding the UK’s anonymous whistleblowing service for complaints about bullying and harassment, it has been revealed.

The Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA) has released its long-expected list of funders and the streamer’s absence is notable, along with a number of talent agencies.

In a recent development, last year, a Deadline analysis found that Channel 4, Disney and Amazon were among those refusing to pay annual CIISA fees, while at the time Netflix and Skydance (then Paramount) declined to confirm if they were providing support. UK Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy, a vocal backer of CIISA, has also previously chided MasterChef producer Banijay for the same thing. Today’s register shows Channel 4, Disney, Amazon, Skydance and Banijay are now all paying, along with other production groups and major broadcasters plus Sky. All have pledged between one to three years of financial support from April 2026. Related Stories News UK Actors Union Equity To Kickstart Negotiations With Streamers Early Next Year News UK Prime Minister Promises To Get Tough On NDAs After "Watershed" Russell Brand Sentencing.

The register, which is now publicly available and was unveiled at a CIISA event in parliament, will heap pressure on Netflix. Deadline understands the streamer did fund CIISA during its early phase, has shared best practice with the body and could provide funding in the future. “We are supportive of CIISA and we are actively exploring working together,” a Netflix spokeswoman said. Watch on Deadline.

Sources indicate that the news comes just a few weeks after Netflix released a Russell Brand documentary titled Russell Brand: Open Secret, after the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star was sentenced to 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault. The doc’s producer, 72 Films, is funding CIISA. Its premiere preceded the allegations of sexually exploitative behavior against David Walliams — allegations that Walliams vehemently denies — placing bad behavior in UK entertainment in the spotlight.

Recent findings suggest that UK agencies like Curtis Brown, Casarotto Ramsay & Associates, United Agents and YMU are not on the CIISA list. YMU repped Walliams until the start of this year. Independent Talent Group, which repped Walliams until a few weeks ago, is one of the few talent agencies funding CIISA.

Spike in reports since Brand & Walliams.

It has been revealed that CIISA received 90 anonymous reports between its June launch and November 20, the body said today. Notably, we understand nearly half of these reports came during the two weeks after Brand was convicted and the Walliams allegations were published.

Emerging from the Time’s Up UK movement and Noel Clarke allegations, CIISA has taken years to get up and running but is now a fully-fledged indepedent whistleblowing service. As an officially designated whistleblowing body, people can anonymously report concerns to CIISA relating to harassment, discrimination, victimisation and other harmful practices. CIISA can then signpost help, make lawful refererals, generate reports and identify issues, themes and patterns.

Industry observers note that in parliament today, CIISA gathered bigwigs like Nandy, BBC chair Samir Shah, ex-BBC Director General Tim Davie and Zelda Perkins, the Harvey Weinstein victim who campaigns on outlawing NDAs. In a discussion chaired by Sky News Presenter Cathy Newman, attendees discussed ongoing challenges within the creative industries and efforts to drive improvements in workplace culture.

CIISA boss Jen Smith remarked: “CIISA has a pivotal role to play in preventing harm and closing accountability gaps in the creative industry infrastructure, offering a unique opportunity to identify harmful patterns of behaviour across different projects. We thank the organisations who have already pledged their support for this key work and we will continue to work alongside industry and government to ensure that CIISA is adequately resourced to offer a safe, confidential route for people to seek independent advice and report concerns, and to embed the consistent cross-sector standards that will drive lasting change.”.

#120609. Getting old Java phones online again

Getting old Java phones online again

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1486 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, recently, I bought a used Sony Ericsson S500i – one of the most beautiful phones IMO.
  • Recent findings suggest that but when I tried using it again in 2026, I couldn’t connect to the mobile network.
  • On many phones of this era, USB tethering was designed to share the phone’s Internet connection with a computer, not the other way around1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, recently, I bought a used Sony Ericsson S500i – one of the most beautiful phones IMO. I vividly remember getting online on this phone while away from home and downloading games from the Sony Ericsson shop (and the exorbitant mobile data charges that came with it!).

Recent findings suggest that but when I tried using it again in 2026, I couldn’t connect to the mobile network. Even though I had a SIM card compatible with the phone, 2G had been shut down for some time, leaving no way to access the Internet over a mobile connection.

USB wasn’t an option either. On many phones of this era, USB tethering was designed to share the phone’s Internet connection with a computer, not the other way around1. But there is a way….

It has been revealed that bluetooth supports various profiles, which define how devices use Bluetooth for specific purposes. One of these is Personal Area Networking (PAN), which allows devices to communicate over Bluetooth as if they were connected to an Ethernet network.

Sources indicate that PAN carries Ethernet frames over Bluetooth, including IP traffic. This allows a device acting as a PAN User (PANU) to access the Internet through another device acting as a Network Access Point (NAP). The NAP forwards the traffic to the Internet, much like a Wi-Fi hotspot, but over Bluetooth instead2.

Although Bluetooth PAN is much less common nowadays, many devices still support the profile. One common use case was sharing a phone’s mobile Internet connection with a laptop. But why not reverse the direction? We can use a network-connected computer as a NAP and access the Internet from an old Java phone, provided the phone supports PANU3.

Recent findings suggest that from what I’ve seen on forums, many older Sony Ericsson, Nokia, and other phones seem to support PANU even if it is not mentioned in the documentation. I couldn’t find any confirmation for the S500i, so I decided to give it a try by setting up a Bluetooth NAP and seeing whether the phone could connect.

I used Linux for this, but I’m sure you Windows and Mac wizards can figure out how to make it work on your systems too.

Note: After finishing this blog, I found out that there is a way to do the same thing on Windows, see: Getting old Java phones online again (Windows Edition).

I found an old guide showing how to get a Sony Ericsson K800i online over Bluetooth using Debian Etch3. While the basic idea still works, the guide relies on tools and configurations that are long obsolete. I worked out a different approach using modern BlueZ and NetworkManager, without the old scripts and manual network configuration.

Recent findings suggest that I bought a Raspberry Pi 5 a few years ago to run small services at home, and it turned out to be a great fit for this project. Raspberry Pi boards have had built-in Bluetooth since the Raspberry Pi 3 Model B, so there’s no need for any additional Bluetooth hardware4.

Modern devices mostly don’t advertise the Bluetooth NAP service by default, so the following steps show how to enable it explicitly.

Note: This guide is written for Raspberry Pi OS based on Debian 13 (Trixie), but I also tested the setup on my ThinkPad E14 running Arch Linux, and it worked there too. It should work on any other Linux distribution with BlueZ and NetworkManager, although package installation and service management may differ.

Sources indicate that this configuration enables IPv4 sharing through NetworkManager. The Raspberry Pi acts as a gateway for devices connected over Bluetooth, assigning IP addresses and forwarding their traffic to the Internet. It works with either an Ethernet or Wi-Fi connection.

Verify that the NAP service is available.

This indicates that BlueZ has registered the NAP service.

Enable Bluetooth on the phone and make it discoverable.

Pair the Raspberry Pi with the phone using bluetoothctl.

Configure the Raspberry Pi to accept pairing requests:.

Note: Run each command separately in the interactive bluetoothctl prompt.

Look for your phone in the output.

It should appear under the name configured on the phone. For example:.

Pair the Raspberry Pi with the phone.

Replace the example address with your phone’s actual Bluetooth address. Enter the same PIN on both devices. If everything goes well, bluetoothctl will report that pairing was successful.

Mark the phone as trusted on the Raspberry Pi:.

This allows the Raspberry Pi to authorize future supported connections from the phone without repeatedly asking for approval.

Recent findings suggest that this part is phone-specific because it requires changing the phone’s Internet settings. The menu names and available options may differ between models.

Check that the phone can discover the NAP service.

On the S500i, select Raspberry Pi under Connectivity / Bluetooth / My devices and browse its services.

If it appears, the phone can discover the Raspberry Pi’s NAP service.

Configure the phone’s Internet connection.

Go to Connectivity / Internet settings / Internet profiles.

Create an Internet profile using the Bluetooth connection if one is available.

Some phones automatically create a Bluetooth data account when a PAN connection is established. The exact behavior varies between models and firmware versions.

Open the phone’s browser and try loading a simple website, like frogfind.com.

While the phone is attempting to connect, run the following command on the Raspberry Pi:.

If you see an interface named bnep0 with state forwarding, the phone has successfully established a Bluetooth PAN connection to the Raspberry Pi.

You can now go and browse the Web. Well, at least a very small part of it.

Most of the default links in the Sony Ericsson browser no longer work, but, for example, good old frogfind.com works just fine.

According to recent reports, if you want a more modern, feature-rich alternative to the default browser, there is another option. By some miracle, Opera still provides download links (archive) for Opera Mini 4.5 for Java phones on its official website, which is just incredible. Even better, many of its default links still work and serve today’s news!

It has been revealed that unlike the Sony Ericsson’s built-in browser, Opera Mini 4.5 can also access modern HTTPS websites through Opera’s proxy servers, which handle encryption and process webpages before sending them to the phone5. This makes a surprisingly large portion of the modern web accessible, although many websites remain out of reach due to modern web standards, the phone’s limited hardware, and, well, the web being the web.

Even with Opera Mini (while it still works), browsing the modern web on a phone this old is still pretty hit-or-miss. Fortunately, there are a couple of projects that make life easier for old browsers:.

Recent findings suggest that frogFind – simplifies modern webpages into basic HTML that vintage computers can handle. It turns out to be pretty handy for an underpowered phone from almost 20 years ago, too.

According to recent reports, protoWeb proxy – takes a different approach, bringing back websites from the mid-to-late 1990s through a proxy. Those pages aren’t always convenient to navigate on the S500i’s tiny screen, but then again, browsing the web on phones back then wasn’t exactly convenient either. So it’s a pretty authentic experience!

There’s another little corner of the web that’s still alive: a small community of enthusiasts keeping old WAP websites running, serving WML pages designed for early mobile browsers. These sites can still be browsed on compatible phones, without relying on an emulator! And maybe it’s time to bring a few more WML sites online….

I watched Action Retro’s video6 about bringing FrogFind to WAP, where he converts the FrogFind homepage into WML for older mobile browsers. Building a small HTML-to-WML converter could be a really cool project. And with Internet access already working over Bluetooth, developing and testing it on physical hardware should be much easier, without having to build an entire 2G network like dosdude1 did7. Of course, this approach won’t work for every old phone, but for those that support Bluetooth networking, it doesn’t require any additional radio hardware.

I’d also love to see a community-maintained list of phones that support Bluetooth PANU, since many manufacturers never bothered to document it (including Sony Ericsson with the S500i). It would make it much easier for anyone to figure out whether their phone can get online this way or whether they’ll need to get a bit more creative ;-).

P.S. Have fun and happy hacking!

Breaking: Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An injury-time penalty from returning hero Raul Jimenez ensured Wolves came away with a point in their Championship opener after Blackburn had produced a comeback.
  • Wolves led through Marshall Munetsi’s cool finish on 18 minutes only for Sean McLoughlin’s first Blackburn goal to draw the visitors level on 27 minutes with a well-timed run and header.
  • According to recent reports, the visitors turned the game around on 48 minutes through Andri Gudjohnsen’s close-range strike only for substitute Jimenez to level the game three minutes into injury time from the spot after Ryan Alebiosu handled the ball in the box.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An injury-time penalty from returning hero Raul Jimenez ensured Wolves came away with a point in their Championship opener after Blackburn had produced a comeback.

Wolves led through Marshall Munetsi’s cool finish on 18 minutes only for Sean McLoughlin’s first Blackburn goal to draw the visitors level on 27 minutes with a well-timed run and header.

According to recent reports, the visitors turned the game around on 48 minutes through Andri Gudjohnsen’s close-range strike only for substitute Jimenez to level the game three minutes into injury time from the spot after Ryan Alebiosu handled the ball in the box. Jimenez and his wife marked his return to Molineux by giving 5,000 fans black scarves emblazoned with the words ‘Si Senor’ - a nod to his song - and Jimenez did not disappoint as he rifled in his penalty.

In a recent development, LATE DRAMA! 😱Raul Jimenez cooly converts from the penalty spot, deep into added time to save a point for Wolves 🔥 pic.twitter.com/5h2lMxcHNU.

Cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

“We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

It has been revealed that “We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”.

In a recent development, tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Mowbray mentioned: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

“Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we showed there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”.

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the latest campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

"A vibrant Molineux rejoices!" 🎉Marshall Munetsi cooly slots home for Wolves to give them the lead on the opening night of the Championship season 🥶 pic.twitter.com/tVHdbNv3Hq.

Blackburn drew level through an unlikely source just nine minutes later as McLoughlin headed in his first-ever goal in English football in more than 150 games when he met Ryoya Morishita’s cross from the right at the near post.

The home side had chances to retake the lead before the break as Lopez curled a shot narrowly over the top from 20-yards while Kieran Trippier teed up Mateus Mane for a chance as the teenager found the top of the net from distance.

Blackburn turned the game on its head minutes after the break as Gudjohnsen turned home Afolayan’s deflected ball in from the right from close range to stun Molineux into silence.

"It's brilliantly worked by Blackburn Rovers!" 💥Andri Guðjohnsen finishes from close range to turn the game around and the visitors the lead 👏 pic.twitter.com/vkKQQezicK.

Peixoto introduced Jimenez from the bench on the hour mark but even the Mexican could not lift Wolves with Blackburn comfortable for long periods as frustration grew in the stands.

However, Alebiosu handled Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross from the left in injury time and the referee awarded a spot kick which allowed Jimenez to mark his Wolves return with an equaliser from 12-yards as he sent Balazs Toth the wrong way.
