The short age of dragon riders

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Atilloy

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that since approximately August of this year, the AI models available to the public have passed a threshold: in a proper harness, they are stronger than most theoretical physicists (myself included) at most technical tasks.
  • According to recent reports, concretely, the models are now able to carry out complex analytical calculations, work out lengthy proofs, turn well-posed problems into code, all with minimal input.
  • As of November 2026, the best public models still lack research taste.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that since approximately August of this year, the AI models available to the public have passed a threshold: in a proper harness, they are stronger than most theoretical physicists (myself included) at most technical tasks. What counts as “technical” exactly is blurry (and likely to expand) but I take it to include the bulk of what junior theoretical physicists were doing day to day during their PhDs.

According to recent reports, concretely, the models are now able to carry out complex analytical calculations, work out lengthy proofs, turn well-posed problems into code, all with minimal input. They iterate, correct their errors, launch simulations to verify their conjectures, and summarize their work. On my own problems, I have already seen the impossible being done several times, starting with Fable 5 in May (I reported some on X and LinkedIn). Those who deny this progress have just not tried hard enough (with the latest models), or are blinded by their ego.

As of November 2026, the best public models still lack research taste. They execute beautifully when given a clear goal but are worse than the best researchers at coming up with good questions, or at having the sparks of creativity needed to get out of a dead end. They do not have as much vision as the best humans.

This situation is unlikely to persist. Even if the whole internet has been exhausted to pre-train models, the availability of human data is no longer the bottleneck. Thanks to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), models can improve simply by solving new tasks, and are in no way bound by human intelligence.

At least in the immediate future, progress is thus predictable. First, the internal models at OpenAI and Anthropic have now solved countless open problems, showing that they are indeed a generation ahead of what the public at the moment has access to (which is already superhuman at many tasks). Second, computing power, the only bottleneck, has been increasing steadily, far beyond what was used to train the current best models. Unless the scaling laws surprisingly break down, we have two generations of improvements ahead of us without doing anything new. On top of this, recursive self-improvement is under way, at least in the weak sense that strong models already substantially help design the training environments of their successors. In a nutshell, as long as the datacenters survive kinetic strikes or a grassroots Butlerian Jihad, progress is not going to stop.

Like most scientists, I am conflicted. All the friction is gone; problems melt before we can even understand the solution. It is great, and also scary, leading some in the community to hate the models. I have always been a techno-optimist absolutist. It would be a betrayal to flip now that the wave of progress touches my craft. No, even if it burns me, I still think we should steal the fire!

Granted, the fire, this time, may come with existential risks for humanity. I think these risks are real, and to leading order, better understood by the nerds in Silicon Valley than by skeptics like Yann LeCun. Alignment research is certainly notable, and if slowing down training helps reduce existential risk, then we probably should.

Industry observers note that but I think it is too easy to reject AI progress for wrong, self-serving reasons, under the guise of a legitimate concern for mankind. And thus, while one should take these risks seriously, it is notable to also think about what is left for us in case they are solved.

Sources indicate that it is still too difficult for me to envision what the steady state may look like, or whether there will even be one. But I would like to discuss what I think we should do (or at least what I am doing) during the transient period of symbiotic human-AI discovery.

Industry observers note that the first step is to quickly go through the five stages of grief. Mathematicians, as Sylvia Serfaty recently noted in her talk at the IHP, at least seem to have gone through the denial phase. Physicists are likely only three months behind.

It has been revealed that prominent mathematicians, even those who were dismissing AI only three months ago, are no longer denying its power. However, the most visible public reaction, initiated by 25 Fields medalists, is terrible in a way that can only be explained by shock. The best problem solvers alive are now claiming that results, proofs, technical breakthroughs, which in many cases gave them their status and fame, were not really the goal. The goal was the friends we made along the way: the serendipitous discoveries, the mathematical community that got built, the long hours spent pondering in front of a blackboard. This enjoyment, this human understanding, for the community and by the community, is what had value all along.

I disagree. I think we deserve all the bad things that will happen to us if we react like such sore losers. Serendipitous discoveries are notable, but first, it is unclear that AIs will necessarily lead to fewer, and second, the end results clearly mattered and still matter. Seeing the process as an end in itself, rather than a means to an end, is profoundly self-serving, and sadly typical of academia.

We have to accept that many things we were doing, sometimes with joy, are already gone. I have spent days massaging an equation to bring it into a form that worked, proud of my virtuosity. I have made complicated calculations with pen and paper, covering entire notebooks to get an answer I could trust. I have spent weeks turning computations into code, and optimized the implementation over months, to be the first to extract certain results from theory. I have fine-tuned plots for hours until they looked pretty. Science was slow; all these steps were crucial and had to be taught. They were sometimes tedious, sometimes meditative, and tied to our identity. I was good at this, and enjoyed at least a fraction of it. But even if the models do not make any progress, which as I argued is highly unlikely, this is gone. Spending too much time on what is gone will soon be unprofessional, like bringing a coloring book to work.

Since AI is now needed to push the frontier of research and understanding, those who do not want to use it sometimes argue that the output of research is researchers themselves (and not so much the results they produce). Hugo Duminil-Copin, a French Fields medalist, explains (in a recent talk at the Société Mathématique de France) that no one really cares about or understands his proofs outside of a few experts (which is mostly true, although I personally enjoyed his lectures as a non-expert). As a result, he concludes, his main value for society lies in showing how far the human mind can be pushed with sustained effort and dedication. Hugo Duminil-Copin is an athlete of the mind, an example for the rest of society. If this is true, then indeed Duminil-Copin can never be replaced by AI, and he is right not to use AI too much. He has said he will digest the AI proofs to understand them and pass them on, a bit like chess players studying engine lines, while continuing his own research without AI.

Industry observers note that machines may progress to the point where this view (which I find self-serving) is the only reasonable one. But during the transient, I cannot accept it. At least after they are done with their PhDs, researchers are no longer the product of research; what matters is what they do.

I hold the naive view that the goal of research is to push toward new results, knowledge, applications, understanding that can be shared. Discoveries are usually a good thing, actually. I think there will still be joy in discoveries even if it is not only humans that push them. If the old ways are gone, at least I want to push to the stars!

In a recent development, as long as there are problems to solve, and as long as we bring something to their resolution, I think we should ride the AI dragon. We should enhance ourselves, move up in abstraction, and let the dragon deal with what it does better than us.

In a recent development, to do great things, we need to forgo some understanding of what is going on at lower levels, to focus on higher ones. This is still controversial in my field, and difficult to accept, but this has happened before: we no longer code in assembly, compute integrals manually with quadratures, or extract square roots with Newton’s method. The level of understanding we had was adapted to our tools; now that the tools have changed, what we need to understand fully also changes.

I doubt that riding the dragon can be a program for the steady-state ASI scenario (if there is one), but it can be a program for now. The dragon is getting bigger every three months. It may ride itself at some point, but so far few can ride it properly. Those who do not ride it now may never be able to ride it in the future, at least not to find new things.

Sources indicate that riding the dragon is fun but also exhausting, and in some ways humiliating. The best way to learn is just to do it, and to spend many hours looking the beast in the eye. It is not yet clear how to balance the time spent in front of the screen, actively prompting, with the time spent pondering the output during a walk in the park, to catch up with what the dragon found, and be able to productively point it in another direction next. I suspect we will never know what the right way is, as it changes too fast for us to find it. I certainly do not have a silver bullet, and I think some level of intellectual discomfort is worth it. Like many others, I try to push myself to the edge of psychosis, getting the most out of it while remaining sane. Discussing the output with other humans (ideally other dragon riders) also helps stay grounded. Sleeping the usual amount is vital, but increasingly difficult.

As in a bubble, I suspect the value of good dragon riders will increase exponentially until it collapses dramatically. At some point it will not be possible to raise the bar, stay above the wave, and it is plausible that nothing biological will be able to give valuable insights to the silicon. The dragon will know what to do. But we live now, not in three years.

As researchers, all that we hoped to be able to solve and find in a lifetime is probably going to be done in the next few years. We can remain bitter spectators of these great achievements, or ride the dragon to take part in them, for the honor of the human mind.

* I have given a bunch of talks defending this vision in the past months, the most recent one at the IHP (slides, video).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s nothing better than finding a newly introduced show to get stuck into, especially when you’re staring down a long list of streaming options and have absolutely no idea where to start. Thankfully, Prime Video’s latest top 10 chart is doing some of the hard work for us. There are plenty of returning reveals holding their ground, alongside newer arrivals that are clearly catching some attention. But as I always say to my fellow friends and family, just because a show is trending doesn’t necessarily mean it’s worth your time.

That’s why I’ve been digging through this week’s most-watched picks to find the ones that genuinely deserve a spot on your watchlist. I’ve narrowed things down to three shows I’d happily recommend to anyone, including an epic fantasy adventure reaching its season finale, a compelling sports drama charting the early life of one of the greatest boxers of all time, and a romantic drama packed with some awkward relationship complications.

This list is based on the Prime Video U.S. top 10 shows as of Wednesday, November 25, 2026.

Industry observers note that “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” is wrapping up its eight-episode third season, with the final two episodes now available to stream. There’s even better news for fans, as Prime Video renewed the series for season 4 ahead of the finale, so there’s more Middle-earth to look forward to. The show has certainly made headlines for its enormous budget and ambitious production, with Amazon originally committing to a five-season plan and involving the Tolkien Estate in overseeing the adaptation. It’s a fascinating chapter in the franchise’s television history, and thankfully, the story isn’t over yet.

Recent findings suggest that set five years after the fall of Eregion, the third season finds Middle-earth engulfed in war as Sauron’s (Charlie Vickers) armies continue their march across the land. With the Dark Lord establishing his stronghold in Mordor, he sets his sights on forging the One Ring, a powerful weapon that could secure his control over Middle-earth. Meanwhile, Galadriel (Morfydd Clark), Elrond (Robert Aramayo), Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) and their allies face mounting challenges as they attempt to unite the Elves, Dwarves and Men against him. As battles spread across the kingdoms, Sauron also works to enslave his ring-servants.

Watch "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that “The Greatest” is still holding strong in Prime Video’s top 10, a biographical sports drama following four formative years in the life of Cassius Clay as he goes from promising amateur boxer to heavyweight champion Muhammad Ali. Rather than focusing entirely on his career in the ring, the series also explores the personal, family and cultural pressures that shaped him along the way. This is a more intimate approach to Ali’s story, while the faithful recreation of historic boxing footage also helps bring the story to life. It’s an interesting watch even if you’re not a huge boxing fan.

Sources indicate that based on the early life of legendary boxer Muhammad Ali (Jaalen Best), this eight-part drama follows his journey from Olympic gold medallist to heavyweight title contender. Formerly known as Cassius Clay, the young fighter returns to his hometown of Louisville after winning gold at the 1960 Rome Olympics, ready to take the next step in his boxing career. As he prepares for a career-defining showdown with formidable opponent Sonny Liston (Amin Joseph), the series charts the pivotal moments that helped shape one of boxing’s most recognizable figures.

Watch "The Greatest" on Prime Video.

Romance fans should give “Love in Disguise” a spot on their watchlist this week. Adapted from a web novel by Lee A-yeon and Ryu Do-ha, this Korean romantic comedy-thriller stars Yim Si-wan from Netflix’s “Squid Game” alongside Seorina. It’s also the first time the two actors have shared the screen, which gives the series an extra appeal for fans of both. The pair have spoken about wanting to capture the spirit of the original novel while giving the story their own spin. With romance, comedy and thriller elements in the mix, it’s an interesting option if you're after something a little different.

The series follows Kang Jae-hee (Seorina), a former special forces operative turned detective who takes on an unusual undercover assignment. Disguising herself as a man, she lands a job as the personal secretary to Yoon Yi-jun (Yim Si-wan), the wealthy heir to the Taekang Group, who is suspected of murdering his previous secretary. While keeping a close eye on her latest employer and searching for evidence, Jae-hee finds herself caught up in the family’s complicated affairs. As Yi-jun begins to let his guard down, maintaining her cover becomes increasingly difficult, particularly as their relationship develops.

Watch "Love in Disguise" on Prime Video.

Before joining Tom’s Guide, Alix honed her skills as a staff writer with outlets like Screen Rant and Bough Digital, where she discovered her love for the entertainment industry.

She heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

Porting Rockbox to an Undocumented $9 Aliexpress 'YP3' MP3 Player with LLMs

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jayd

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that rockbox is a wonderful old custom firmware project for a variety of MP3 players and iPods.
  • Recent findings suggest that it seems like in 2026 there aren’t any cheap MP3 players that Rockbox supports though.
  • TL;DR: it ported Rockbox to a 512 KiB player, I was barely involved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rockbox is a wonderful old custom firmware project for a variety of MP3 players and iPods. Flashing rockbox to my Sansa E200 was a seminal moment for me: computers were everywhere, and if they didn’t do cool things, it was because no one had bothered to program them to do so. Looking back, that played no small part in my choice of career.

Recent findings suggest that it seems like in 2026 there aren’t any cheap MP3 players that Rockbox supports though. Reverse engineering an embedded platform like this is one of the hardest things I can think of, and I had decided to pay the big bucks for one of those delicious subsidized token plans to try and push it as hard as I could, and I did have a dirt cheap $9 Aliexpress MP3 player lying around.

TL;DR: it ported Rockbox to a 512 KiB player, I was barely involved. Then, I had it build a re-usable toolkit/set of skills for future ports based on what worked from the first attempt approach, and Claude was able to get Rockbox running on another MP3 player (TS47) in 4 hours.

I made a quick website for the project: https://rockslop.jayd.ml.

Here is the porting toolkit: auto-rockbox.

It has been revealed that this is an unbranded player, sold under a variety of fake consonant soup brands on Amazon as well as Aliexpress. You can order them wholesale from Alibaba for less than $7 or so each.

In a recent development, it calls itself a yp3_2.0.43 in the “About” menu as. This appears to be a listing for a YP3 - the original is gone. I paid $9.71 for mine, shipped.

NOTE: Before you run off and buy one, I have another rockbox port that is probably a week or two out, it is booting and stable, just needs more acceptance testing. This device is extremely similar but has 4 MiB PSRAM, so it has fewer compromises.

I also have a stack of other random MP3 players I intend to repeat this with.

See the project website: https://rockslop.jayd.ml.

If anyone gets credit for this rockbox port, it’s ilyakurdyukov - they figured out how to get it into ROM Download mode (Down + USB), and wrote a utility to dump / write flash. Then I could be a little slop kiddie and not have to use a soldering iron.

See the YP3 page on the project website for more info.

It has 512KiB of SRAM, and the smallest existing Rockbox target was 2 MiB, I was already scrolling Aliexpress for another one, but the LLM mentioned “trust me bro I can make it happen” and I decided to try its luck.

Industry observers note that after about a week it was booting a build of Rockbox on a crash diet - every single buffer had been cut to the bone, but it could start and play audio. Tuning, bug fixing, etc took another month or so.

I am not aware of anything that isn’t working hardware wise.

Recent findings suggest that the main feature you lose is concurrency while playing music and plugins. Codecs and plugins are already loaded and swapped around at runtime with normal Rockbox, but on this player there is one shared 128 KiB arena for both, so starting a plugin stops music playback.

The database has a newly introduced variant that is disk only and has synchronous, blocking updates (ie the player highlights a loading screen and stops music when it refreshes and doesn’t refresh in background). I think it also cut the “songs by letter” menu.

The database requests memory for its menus at runtime, and depending on the size of your theme it can refuse to open the menus.

Industry observers note that overnight Claude reverse engineered the bluetooth stack and wrote a bluetooth HAL for Rockbox. I asked it before I went to bed and it was working in the morning.

No binary blobs are shipped: the bt stack is burned into chip ROM (not flash), and the YP3 bluetooth driver calls into the stack.

Sources indicate that most of the codecs run from SRAM as normal. MP3, AAC, WMA, Vorbis and Opus, however, wouldn’t fit in our arena nicely, so they run from flash.

But, our XIP flash is dirt slow, so lots of very careful profiling was done to move hot code loops back into SRAM. This kind of profiling had to be done all over Rockbox to get hot loops into SRAM - font rendering, alpha blending, scrolling, etc. This is where most of the “weeks of polishing” went.

Sources indicate that largely comparable to stock. I hooked the player up to the PC’s line in or fake bluetooth sink and set it to repeat Daft Punks Random Access Memories. A script on the PC detected when it cut out.

Stock: 21.29 hours wired, 20.07 on Bluetooth.

Rockbox: 20.07 hours wired, 19.3 on Bluetooth.

There was some variation in the battery voltage at start, and this was just one run, so expect some variation.

Battery life is surprisingly impressive on this player,.

According to recent reports, I’m one of those software guys, I can’t solder or find UART pads to save my life. This was an entirely software only port; I haven’t ever opened mine up.

It has been revealed that I hooked up ghidra-mcp and let it start pulling the firmware apart. It figured out how to inject tasks into the running RTOS (FreeRTOS) in bootloader mode. This allowed it to probe the hardware and even write drivers before attempting a Rockbox boot.

Sources indicate that to be clear: this is 100% vibecoded. I have only glanced at some of the code it wrote. I contributed my approach to development and testing, was the PM and QA person, and the agent’s little meat robot to reboot it when it crashed or wander around my house with headphones on while it tuned the bluetooth radio. I haven’t doneC and firmware development for years.

In a recent development, initially I let the same agent do the reverse engineering as implementation. Later I had it go through and rip out anything that wasn’t a hardware fact (ie a register) and re-did the drivers with a cleanroom setup. One dirty agent with Ghidra, one referee agent in between to make sure nothing leaks, and the implementation agent. Subsequent ports used a variation of this setup from the beginning.

The most work I have done personally on this project is writing this blog post.

Webcam mic for bringing up the speaker.

(had to yell at Claude when it decided to start playing tones at 2 AM).

Headphone jack plugged into Line In on my PC (finally, I used it!!).

This allowed it to test and tune audio output.

This port was started with Codex/Sol 5.6. It was making progress, but was incredibly risk averse and slow. It took it 5 days or so and dozens of manual resets on my part until it felt ready to flash something and boot it.

According to recent reports, I should have told it how to figure out how to arm the watchdog and reboot into download mode itself sooner. Codex got it to showing the rockbox logo with buggy drivers stubbed out, but had clearly lost its mind in the meantime. I hadn’t been paying attention too closely, but as it had spun around it had:.

This flashing script - and many other tool scripts - would check the sha256 of the documentation files they depended on to ensure nothing had changed.

Industry observers note that it’s kind of beautiful in its own insane way: this seems to be an attempt to work around multiple agents and memory limits. Madness though.

Recent findings suggest that claude immediately threw that garbage away and wrote like a few python scripts to use instead. Auto mode in claude code helped too.

The subsequent TS17 port went from me plugging it in to a usable alpha build in about 4 hours with Opus 5.5 (there was little to re-use from the YP3 other than scripts and skills).

Recent findings suggest that this is one of the most valuable things it did. Rockbox has an existing one-way USB serial driver for logs. I had that extended to have dozens of little commands to drive the player, everything from injecting keypresses to taking screenshots to debugging the bluetooth radio.

This was critical for completely hands off development - I had it build a torture test suite in Python that would monkey-test the player for hours, pressing buttons at random. Many bugs were found doing this - including some in Rockbox upstream. At this point the player has hundreds of hours of bench testing under Rockbox - I could just leave it running and Claude would patiently watch the test logs for new failures to diagnose and fix.

An agent can reboot to recovery, flash firmware, reboot into Rockbox, run tests, see what is on the screen, hear what it is doing, completely on its own. Most of the development of this project happened while I was asleep.

For audio (and battery endurance testing) Claude had me set up a 3.5 mm splitter with one end going into the PC’s Line In and the other going into real headphones to provide an actual load.

Then I had it build a test suite and file that plays a variety of sweeps and test tones. I used an Apple lightning adapter to use as the ground truth for this setup, then used it to compare audio levels and frequency response.

My PC’s sound card is not high sensitivity equipment, but this is enough of a sanity check for me.

More charts that I don’t understand.

There were two tricky things to work out that Claude struggled to fix. The exact power off sequence took quite a few tries, probably because it was the only thing I had to be there to test, it couldn’t just work on it for hours overnight.

Industry observers note that the other crazy bug was that the FM radio sounded terrible. You could tune to a station, but the sound was distorted and clipped. Claude spent forever trying to figure out why, but eventually I noticed that the frequency it was tuned to did not match the station identifier over the air.

It has been revealed that it turns out the tuner had been set up with a slightly wrong clock source, so it was ~4 MhZ off. It just so happened to work out that when I tuned it to my test station, it could kind of lock on to another one, but sounded terrible.

I told Claude to port as many games as it could to Rockbox.

It has been revealed that this release adds THREE HUNDRED AND FIFTY SEVEN new plugins. That is not a typo: 357. Most of these are ports, a few are originals. Given the quantity here I haven’t done enough QA here.

Industry observers note that this is going to get its own blog post because it is deeply amusing. A ~1 million param model running on your MP3 player. Almost coherent, fine tuned to be aloof and dismissive of humanity. Weights are streamed from SD card. Crazy.

Recent findings suggest that A little tracker/chiptune editor for Rockbox. I haven’t had a ton of time to test this one. Probably needs ergonomic improvements.

It has been revealed that rockbox’s existing mpegplayer didn’t fit on the YP3 and I didn’t want to hack it up too much, so I had Claude write a upcoming one, with a nicer pixel art UI, MKV support. AVI, MKV, MP4; MPEG-1/2, MJPEG.

There are too many to list. Here is the full set of ports.

We got to stupid plugin numbers by writing compat shims/libraries for several popular open source players:.

Yes, you can pair a PS4 controller or keyboard to Rockbox. I wanted to see how much we could do with the existing Bluetooth stack.

I had it port some themes from the Rockbox website to work on this screensize, add a bluetooth status icon, and it generated 5 original themes: Ukiyo (my favorite), Asterism, Chaldani, Lavenia, Cyanotype.

Note: This is a WIP screenshot, there have been bug fixes & some of these got cut because of unclear licensing.

Note that heavy themes can cause some issues, so I would suggest sticking with lightweight ones.

Well, reverse engineering a completely undocumented chipset was one of the hardest things I could think of to do, and Claude can ace it. I’m planning on porting Rockbox to a bunch of other cheap MP3 players.

There are lots of clones that look like each other. The YP3 specifically:.

Also, these screens are made of cheese, you’ll want a screen protector.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on 28 October 2026.

Industry observers note that the US proposed latest tariffs on 14 trading partners on Wednesday. China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan are on the list. The Trump administration claims the duties target “structural excess capacity”, meaning factory output that subsidies keep high and that undercuts US manufacturers.

The US Trade Representative’s office announced the tariffs after an eight-month Section 301 investigation into 16 economies. David Lawder and Andrea Shalal reported the details for Reuters, citing a senior US official.

The other nine economies are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. The US spared Mexico and Norway, the last two economies in the investigation, for now. USTR planned to publish the exact rates in the Federal Register on Wednesday.

China would face a 20% tariff on most of its imports, Courtenay Brown reported for Axios. That comes on top of the roughly 25% tariffs from Trump’s first term, according to Reuters. For some Chinese goods, the total rate would reach 45%, according to AP.

Sources indicate that A senior US official told Axios the rate could rise to 40% if trade talks break down or China fails to meet its commitments. The 20% rate stays within the cap set by the trade truce with Beijing, which expires on 10 January, Reuters reported. About $30bn of Chinese imports under review for tariff cuts would be exempt.

It has been revealed that “We know that they don’t like these actions, but we are seeking stability with the Chinese. China is seeking stability with us,” the senior US official stated, according to Reuters.

The newly introduced tariffs will not surprise Beijing and are unlikely to undermine the truce, the official said, AP reported.

China’s foreign ministry rejected the idea of overcapacity but stopped short of threatening retaliation, Reuters reported.

“The so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false problem, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation,” foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

For the others, the proposals mostly target specific goods. They would raise existing tariffs by about 5 percentage points on average, the official told Axios. They would also stay within the caps in Trump’s trade deals: 15% for the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, and 19% for Malaysia, according to Reuters.

Sources indicate that vietnam faces a rate of up to 35%, while others face 20% or 25%, the BBC reported. Caps in Trump’s trade deals will lower some of those rates, the BBC mentioned.

In a recent development, the latest duties will not stack on top of the 10% and 12.5% forced-labour tariffs the US put on 60 trading partners in July. Nor will they stack on the separate tariffs on cars, steel and aluminium, AP reported.

It has been revealed that USTR’s notice pointed to unprofitable carmakers in China and Japan, according to Reuters’ live coverage. For the EU, it cited Germany’s and Ireland’s large goods surpluses with the US.

The duties are not final. They face a public comment period and a hearing, and may not take effect until January, the official told Reuters.

Sources indicate that the US singled out Brazil after trade talks stalled, AP reported. It proposed higher tariffs on raw and refined sugar and a latest 10% tariff on aircraft, which would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

The plan replaces broader tariffs that the Supreme Court struck down in February. It also follows Republican losses in this month’s midterm elections. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll after the vote, 62% of respondents stated they would support efforts to repeal Trump’s tariffs, Reuters reported.

Asian stocks fell sharply on Wednesday as reports of the plan added to worries about the tech sector, Semafor reported. MSCI’s global stock index fell 0.5%, according to Reuters.

Industry observers note that the announcement follows Trump’s summit in Shenzhen with Xi Jinping last week. Trump looks to host Xi next month at the G20 summit in Florida, AP reported.

The fresh duties sit alongside the existing US semiconductor tariff. Earlier this month, Trump said he would tax US companies that build data centres abroad.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eight years ago, I bought my first Philips Hue product: the Hue Go Portable Lamp.
  • Philips Hue is one of the few tech ecosystems I’ve genuinely enjoyed investing in, and one that has become more valuable to me over time.
  • Ahead of the shopping holiday, I asked Marco Merolla, Executive Vice President and Business Leader of Connected Lighting at Philips Hue, about the company's approach to affordability, product longevity and the future of smart lighting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eight years ago, I bought my first Philips Hue product: the Hue Go Portable Lamp. Eight years later, the bowl-shaped, battery-powered lamp still works, and it has quite a few friends.

Philips Hue is one of the few tech ecosystems I’ve genuinely enjoyed investing in, and one that has become more valuable to me over time. But Philips Hue does have a reputation for being expensive. That's why I consider Black Friday deals one of the best opportunities to either get started with Hue or expand an existing setup.

Ahead of the shopping holiday, I asked Marco Merolla, Executive Vice President and Business Leader of Connected Lighting at Philips Hue, about the company's approach to affordability, product longevity and the future of smart lighting.

His answers shed some light on why customers like me keep coming back, and where there's still room for improvement when it comes to connected smart homes.

I'm vehemently anti-substantial-light. One of my proudest domestic achievements is successfully converting my fiancé to the cause, too.

According to recent reports, my apartment is laden with lamps, most of which are from IKEA. I also have a Hue light strip running along the back of my Lovesac couch and Hue bulbs in the built-in pendant lights above my kitchen island. But generally, rather than buying smart-specific fixtures, I prefer picking out lamps that complement my mid-century modern decor and making them smart myself.

Sources indicate that merolla described smart lighting as a gradual progression rather than an all-at-once overhaul. Most people start with a single room or routine and build outward as they see how it fits their space. Still, I was curious how Hue reconciles its need to keep selling products with customers' expectations that their relatively expensive lights will last.

If you're just getting started with Philips Hue, this four-pack is an affordable way to turn the lamps you already own into smart lights, complete with adjustable white lighting, millions of colors and the option to expand your setup down the road.

“Our goal is not to encourage replacement for its own sake, but to give consumers meaningful reasons to expand and enhance their existing smart lighting setup as their needs change,” Merolla said.

The other side of that equation is lowering the barrier to entry without fragmenting the system. Hue's more affordable Essential range runs on the same underlying software and ecosystem connectivity as its flagship lights, trimming peak brightness and color performance to hit a friendlier price. It’s a smart option if you're outfitting an entire apartment and don't need top-tier output in every corner lamp..

Sources indicate that I've extensively tested competing smart lighting products in varying price ranges from Govee, Wyze and Nanoleaf. Govee, in particular, makes some incredibly fun lighting fixtures, and its adoption of Matter has made it a more compelling option for Apple Home users like myself.

It has been revealed that but I've experienced software glitches with these other brands over the years. Nearly a decade into my smart home journey, I simply don’t have patience for connected gadgets that don't work as expected 100% of the time. Sharing a home with someone less interested in technology makes reliability and simplicity even more key.

“Physical controls remain notable, since not everyone wants to reach for their phone every time they adjust the lights,” Merolla noted.

While you don't technically need a Bridge to get started with Hue, I'd recommend picking one up while it's on sale to unlock whole-home lighting control, advanced automations, Apple Home integration and more opportunities to expand your setup.

Recent findings suggest that despite my investment in Hue, I rarely need to open the app for everyday lighting controls. Between wall-mounted Hue dimmer switches and shortcuts I've configured in my iPhone's Control Center through Apple Home, the lights feel as immediate as traditional switches.

In a recent development, you don't actually need a Bridge to get started. Bluetooth-enabled Hue bulbs work directly with your phone for up to 10 lights. But upgrading to a Bridge unlocks remote access, advanced automations, Apple Home integration and entertainment synchronization, while scaling up to 50 lights and 12 accessories on the standard model.

If you're eyeing the newer Bridge Pro, you get triple the capacity, wireless placement without an Ethernet tether, and MotionAware, a feature that uses subtle signal shifts across your existing bulbs to detect movement without dedicated motion sensors.

If you're serious about building out your smart home, the Bridge Pro offers more room to expand, faster performance and MotionAware technology that can turn compatible Hue lights into motion sensors.

“The Hue Bridge continues to play an important role in delivering a robust, connected lighting experience, while innovations such as MotionAware demonstrate how lighting infrastructure can become more intelligent and responsive to people’s needs,” Merolla said.

If you're planning to expand beyond a few bulbs, I'd invest in the infrastructure now rather than revisit your setup later.

If you've already established a Hue ecosystem, the Philips Hue Play HDMI Sync Box is easily one of my favorite ways to get more out of it.

What I love about the experience is that it isn't limited to a light strip behind my TV. The lights I've already accumulated around my living space can react to what's happening on screen, making my apartment feel like one cohesive entertainment setup.

One of my absolute favorite smart home accessories, the 8K Sync Box lets you synchronize up to 10 compatible Philips Hue lights with what's happening on your TV through connected HDMI devices, making your entire living room feel like an extension of the screen.

Hue has also been finding new ways to make entertainment lighting more interesting. Earlier this year, it introduced Sports Live, which uses live soccer match data to trigger lighting effects. It doesn't even require a Sync Box if you already have a Bridge and compatible color lights.

It has been revealed that the Sync Box is admittedly a luxury, and it wouldn't be my first Hue purchase if I were starting from scratch. But it's exactly the kind of accessory I'd wait until Black Friday to buy.

As much as I appreciate Hue's reliability, I'd love to see more intelligence built into the experience. Whenever I add another lamp to my living room, for example, I have to revisit my entertainment area's lighting configuration. Smarter spatial mapping could make that process considerably easier.

The product that started my Philips Hue obsession eight years ago, this compact, bowl-shaped, battery-powered lamp is incredibly versatile for everything from setting the mood at dinner to adding a colorful accent to a bookshelf, and remains one of my favorite entry points into the Hue ecosystem.

Sources indicate that I'm not the only one looking for refinements. In a 2026 wishlist discussion on the Philips Hue subreddit, people called for more granular brightness controls, better Natural Light scene integration with third-party platforms and the ability to group multiple bulbs in a single fixture.

Merolla told me that the tech giant sees an opportunity to move beyond simply controlling individual devices.

“We believe the future of smart lighting is less about controlling individual devices and more about creating experiences that naturally respond to the way people live.”.

If I had to rebuild my smart home tomorrow, I'd probably start exactly where I did eight years ago: with a little Hue Go or a handful of smart bulbs.

The beauty of building a smart lighting ecosystem is that you don't need to buy everything at once. And with Black Friday discounts, you can take that first step (or if you’re like me, your next one) for considerably less.

#120566. Breaking: What the EU Quantum Act changes for quantum companies?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (939 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: What the EU Quantum Act changes for quantum companies?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The full text of the EU’s Quantum Act, published by the European Commission on Wednesday, confirms what drafts had suggested for weeks.
  • Indeed, something that Henna Virkkunen mentioned in the press conference this morning is that we don’t lack the bright minds, actually, we might be sitting on a mine, yet we still lack the capital and the context to be able to transform quantum research into commercial products.
  • We attract 5% of global private funding, against 50% in the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The full text of the EU’s Quantum Act, published by the European Commission on Wednesday, confirms what drafts had suggested for weeks. Brussels wants to turn Europe’s strong quantum research into an industry by steering public money towards European companies.

Indeed, something that Henna Virkkunen mentioned in the press conference this morning is that we don’t lack the bright minds, actually, we might be sitting on a mine, yet we still lack the capital and the context to be able to transform quantum research into commercial products.

We attract 5% of global private funding, against 50% in the US.

The 94-page proposal, however, sets aside no money for research or companies, leaving that to the EU’s next long-term budget.

According to the proposal, Europe is home to around a third of the world’s quantum companies, and its governments have also announced €8.6bn in public quantum funding, more than the €5.3bn announced in the US.

Yet, private investors have been far more cautious in Europe, with US quantum startups raising about €7bn in 2025, against €1.1bn for their EU rivals.

It has been revealed that at the heart of the Act sits the Quantum Europe Framework Initiative, which pulls national programmes under one EU strategy. Member states have largely run their own races until now, as France showed when it placed a €500M bet on homegrown champions.

Industry observers note that the initiative will be run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, the body that already manages Europe’s public supercomputers. It will fund grand challenges, contests aimed at the engineering problems that still hold the technology back. And it will also build shared testing and communication infrastructure inside the EU.

For companies, the Act creates a small number of innovation hubs offering engineering help, equipment, and training, plus at least one acceleration centre in every member state.

Projects that are ready for the market can be named strategic projects, which gives them easier access to EU funding for scaling up production.

It has been revealed that the procurement rule has the sharpest edges, because public bodies may only buy quantum technology from EU-controlled companies. The one exception is partners the EU has approved through agreements with their home countries. The rule reaches down to subcontractors, and the Commission can require certain critical parts to come only from EU-controlled suppliers.

The bar for counting as EU-controlled is high, as a firm qualifies only if no government, company, or citizen from outside the EU controls it.

Under that test, the European subsidiaries of US and Chinese groups would not qualify, and the same test decides who can use the new hubs and shared facilities, and who can take part in strategic projects.

In a recent development, the Act also tackles the security risk that has made quantum a priority for governments, since a powerful enough quantum computer could break today’s encryption. Six months after the law takes effect, central government bodies will have to buy quantum-safe products for their critical systems.

Cost alone cannot justify an exception.

Countries must report their progress every year, and the Commission can impose binding deadlines on those that fall behind. An EU roadmap from 2025 already asks governments to protect their most sensitive systems by the end of 2030.

And here we reach the most notable part: we have the minds, we have the network, but do we have money?

The Act’s own budget comes to about €71M between 2028 and 2034, and it only pays for running the latest system. It covers Commission staff, IT, and support for the new hubs and centres, rather than research or companies.

The money for research, infrastructure, and companies would come from the EU’s next long-term budget, which starts in 2028 and is still being negotiated. The text proposal names the successor to Horizon Europe and the planned European Competitiveness Fund as the likely sources, but states that the Act creates no automatic right to that funding.

Industry observers note that moreover, the Commission estimates that Europe’s quantum projects will need €12.9bn to €18.1bn between 2028 and 2034, to be met by the EU budget, national governments, and private investors. Officials have long described the law as a framework rather than a pot of money for exactly this reason.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest financial idea in the package, the Sovereign Tech Equity Fund, is only an option in the text. The Act says the EU may set it up but names no size, so the €50bn figure rests.

EU proposes €50bn Sovereign Tech Equity Fund for AI and quantum.

The fund is meant to back the EU’s chips and cloud laws as well, with large cheques for companies that have outgrown the EU’s scale-up funds.

In a recent development, another aspect that the proposal also does is set no target for how powerful Europe’s quantum computers should become. The gap stands out, given that the EU’s 2025 quantum strategy aims to make Europe the world leader by 2030.

And probably the most asked question is what should we do with this Act, and how will this help Europe become less dependent on the US and China?

The proposal now goes to the European Parliament and member states, which will debate and amend it, a process that usually takes around two years. And, if it survives in the actual form, the fresh structures would start in 2028, with the full programme running from 2030.

#120564. Breaking: Predicting LoRA size for any dataset

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2917 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engram ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Predicting LoRA size for any dataset

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engram

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that at Engram, we train lots of models.
  • LoRA has become the predominant approach for customizing models in industry.
  • In practice, smaller LoRAs enjoy a number of systems advantages, being lighter to load4, 5, faster to generate text from6, and easier to store on disk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at Engram, we train lots of models. We train models for individual users and update them when information changes. A major focus of our research is how to customize and adapt models efficiently at scale.

This post focuses on LoRA1. LoRA has become the predominant approach for customizing models in industry. While there exists a large body of knowledge on how to set the hyperparameters and train LoRA effectively2, 3, it’s still unclear how to set LoRA’s rank. Although it’s agreed-upon that LoRA underperforms full-finetuning on larger datasets, it’s not clear when this is the case. How big does a dataset have to be to require a larger LoRA?

In practice, smaller LoRAs enjoy a number of systems advantages, being lighter to load4, 5, faster to generate text from6, and easier to store on disk. For larger models, rank-1 can store quite a lot; some datasets, like RL data, can be represented in a small number of bits and often fit within a rank-one LoRA adapter (or smaller!7, 8, 9).

In this post, we develop a predictive theory and practical approach for sizing LoRA adapters to a new dataset. The idea is simple: the size of the LoRA required depends on how many bits it takes to encode the dataset under the base model. We use this idea to derive an exact formula for how many bits a single LoRA adapter can learn as a function of its rank.

We then extend our idea to measure the capacity of LoRA on full transformers. Since theory can’t predict the nonlinear behavior of deep transformers, we turn to an empirical solution: we generate synthetic datasets of exactly NNN bits under the base model and train on them to measure LoRA’s capacity. Our capacity predictions hold up on real datasets: across a variety of settings, we can accurately determine the necessary rank of the adapter.

We begin this post with a basic primer on the connection between information theory and language modeling. Remember that our goal is to find the smallest adapter that fits a given dataset. To do that, we need to measure adapters and datasets in the same unit: bits.

Language models assign probabilities to strings:.

A language model is, at its core, a text compressor10: a model that assigns high probability to data can encode it efficiently. And we’ve known this since the 1950s! By Shannon’s source coding theorem11, a model’s quality (its perplexity, or cross-entropy) corresponds directly to its effectiveness as a compressor. The number of bits needed to encode a string xxx under a model θ\thetaθ is its negative log-likelihood:.

Here’s an example of what it’s like to view training loss as bits. Given some fixed-size training dataset, we can directly convert loss to bits learned by θ\thetaθ12:.

Generating exactly N bits using an LLM.

Sources indicate that to measure the capacity of LLMs being trained with adapters, we need to generate data with a controllable number of bits. Prior work in this space creates data of fixed size with random generative processes, like randomly generated tables of facts13 or random strings of tokens.

Sources indicate that to generate truly random data from an LLM, we leverage a tool called arithmetic coding. Arithmetic coding gives us the ability to transform probability distributions into codes; it represents the entire code using a single floating point number in [0,1)[0, 1)[0,1) that we can turn into a sequence using pθp_\thetapθ​.

We take this one step further. A pretrained open-source model like Qwen or Inkling already provides likelihoods for text, so we can run arithmetic coding in reverse: start from NNN random bits and decode them into text. The result is a sample from pθp_\thetapθ​ whose code length under the model is NNN bits. One can think of this as an implementation of Neural Linguistic Steganography14 using randomly selected codes.

Sources indicate that here’s an example of arithmetic coding in use. The following panel allows you to generate strings with exact bit counts under SmolLM2:.

In a recent development, code lengths come out slightly longer than the number of encoded bits because tokens are indivisible. In this example, queen is worth eleven bits (surprising!), while little carries just two bits. Later in this post we will generate many strings like this to build a dataset of exactly known size, then train an adapter on it to measure how many bits it can learn.

Given a matrix WWW to adapt, LoRA works by training two matrices whose product is a low-rank enhancement to WWW:.

In a recent development, here WWW is an m×nm \times nm×n matrix being adapted and AAA and BBB are the matrices trained via LoRA. Since rrr is often much smaller than mmm and nnn, the total number of parameters trained by the LoRA is typically much smaller than training all of WWW.

The parameter α\alphaα is a rank-independent scaling factor; in this work, we fix α=256\alpha=256α=256 to avoid conflating rank with learning rate.

According to recent reports, prior work has estimated that the capacity of full transformer training scales roughly linearly with parameter count15, 16, 17. We don’t intuitively expect this to be true with LoRA, since some dimensions influence the model outputs more than others. Instead, we expect diminishing returns to capacity as rank increases. This is exactly what we see in practice, and it turns out we can predict the capacity curve quite cleanly using a simple statistical model.

Suppose we sample data from a model and then adapt one of its weight matrices to memorize that data. How much can we expect to increase the log-likelihood (and hence decrease the code length) with a rank-rrr adapter? To second-order, log⁡pθ(x)\log p_\theta(x)logpθ​(x) looks like an inverted bowl in parameter space. How high we can climb on that bowl can be determined from the gradient and Hessian at the point θ\thetaθ, and these are both random functions of the training data xxx. Since the data is sampled from pθp_\thetapθ​, the statistics of the gradient and Hessian are determined by the Fisher information matrix, which greatly simplifies the calculations.

After some algebra, we find that the capacity of a rank-rrr adapter is approximately,.

In a recent development, where σi(Z)\sigma_i(Z)σi​(Z) is the iii-th singular value of the random matrix ZZZ. The capacity grows roughly linearly at low rank,.

Sources indicate that but it plateaus as the rank increases and the singular values decrease. At full rank, the capacity is mn2ln⁡2\tfrac{mn}{2\ln 2}2ln2mn​ bits, recovering a classical result from Wilks’ theorem in statistics18.

For an 800M parameter Qwen3.5 model, which has 512×1024512 \times 1024512×1024 linear layers in its attention value projections (v_proj), the theory predicts about 378k bits, or 0.48 bits-per-parameter at full rank and 1.3-1.4 bits-per-parameter at low rank.

When we measure capacity using actual training, this prediction turns out to be quite accurate; C(r)C(r)C(r), the blue curve, is accurate at every rank:.

Recent findings suggest that theory predicts around 0.5-1.4 bpp when perturbing individual weight matrices. What about full transformers? When we adapt several matrices jointly, the capacity is more than the sum of its parts. We see super-additive scaling of capacity thanks to complementary interactions from adapting multiple weights at once19.

While the theory above cannot explain these super-additive effects yet, we do have a way to generate a dataset of a fixed size (measured above) and a way to measure how much a model learns from data (by checking its loss).

Extrapolating to the infinite-training regime. We fit a function to estimate the asymptote of the loss curve under infinite training, similar to20. This modeling allows us to train for a fixed number of steps and predict the asymptote of the loss under high compute, rather than perform the full training. It also allows us to avoid constantly sweeping learning rates, since different learning rates converge to the same capacity under infinite training.

We find a simple log-logistic curve fits our training runs well:.

Here TTT is the number of training steps, τ\tauτ is the step where the adapter has stored half its eventual bits, and ccc sets how sharp the rise is; we fit this on runs of 1k steps and up, and report bits∞\text{bits}_\inftybits∞​ as the adapter’s capacity.

Recent findings suggest that naively, one might expect the total capacity to be the sum of each adapter’s capacity, and hence the bits stored per parameter to remain roughly constant as we adapt more and more layers. However, as we increase the number of layers, total capacity actually rises from 1.5 bits-per-parameter to 3.3:.

For a fixed-depth model, we see that increasing the LoRA rank also increases total capacity. Our technique for generating data for θ\thetaθ across sizes allows us to easily measure the capacity of LoRAs across ranks:.

We can also easily study how capacity interacts with training. Although the majority of our results assume capacity in the infinite-training regime, we can swiftly model how even in the case of LoRA, capacity rises with the number of training steps21. This finding is intuitive, since training for longer stores more bits:.

According to recent reports, to test how much models forget about what they already know, we can measure likelihood on samples from the base model; this gives us a measurement of the total number of bits the model forgets during the training process. Across all the models trained for this post, we observe a remarkably predictable trend where models forget roughly as much as they learn:.

According to recent reports, this finding implies that training is quite efficient: as we add new information to a model, it forgets a comparable amount. A model that learns 10 KB of new information might forget 12 KB of old information. This setting provides a clean testbed for future research to investigate the connection between learning & forgetting.

Remember that our goal is to estimate the rank of LoRA required to fit some arbitrary SFT dataset. To do this, we need a method for measuring the size of datasets. In the previous section, we used log-likelihood under θ\thetaθ as a way to generate synthetic data of a precise size. Following the same logic, we can measure the log-likelihood of real data to compute its size under θ\thetaθ.

Industry observers note that we first extend the model’s context window to 2M tokens via YaRN22. If the data still doesn’t fit into context, we estimate its size in bits under the model by cutting it into windows of 2M tokens and summing the log likelihood:.

where x(1),…,x(K)x^{(1)}, \dots, x^{(K)}x(1),…,x(K) are consecutive 2M-token windows of the dataset DDD.

Although this gives us a slight overestimate for the total information content of a dataset, in practice we find the error to be small and the estimates useful enough to predict rank within 5% error.

Sources indicate that we now test our ability to properly allocate adapters and train. We test on datasets of varying sizes scattered across the public internet as well as our and our partners’ workspaces.

For each new dataset, we first measure its size in bits under the model and read the predicted rank rrr off the synthetic capacity curve. We then train LoRAs on the real dataset itself at ranks from r/2r/2r/2 to 2r2r2r, and report the measured rank as the smallest rank that stores 95% of the dataset.

Even though our capacity estimates assume the training data is drawn from the base model, our predictions are extremely accurate on real datasets: the orange dots, the smallest LoRAs required to fit each dataset in practice, fall almost on the blue line, our estimate of a given LoRA rank's capacity.

According to recent reports, this post described our work to automatically provision adapters of a fixed size by using information theory to estimate adapter capacity and relate it to the size of a given dataset. This gives a way to mint PEFT modules on-the-fly of the minimum size required for a given task.

In practice, we don’t always use LoRA. We’re exploring other options for parameter-efficient learning such as trainable prefixes23, sparse memory layers24, steering vectors25, GDN state, and trainable experts26. We find the landscape of PeFT methods contains a number of tradeoffs, and different modules work better for different tasks. We’re also working on other parts of this stack, such as more accurately estimating loss without training and understanding capacity in the finite-compute regime.

On a broader scale, examining how model capacity interacts with data size provides us a clean playground to investigate fundamental questions around how models learn.

Intuitively, the capacity of the adapter is the number of bits it can store about the data it is trained on. We formalize this concept as the decrease in code length of training data, on average over the training distribution. When the training distribution differs from the base model, the decrease in code length comes from a combination of learning the signal — the change in distribution — and noise — the particulars of the individual training samples. We can simplify our study of capacity by sampling from the base model, eliminating the signal so that any reduction in code length comes from memorizing the noise in the training samples. While this is unrealistic, it gives conservative worst-case estimates of capacity per parameter, and as we will empirically demonstrate, the theory is predictive in more realistic settings as well.

Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • These ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash fresh competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Recent findings suggest that amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is vital because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

It has been revealed that such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.
