But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES1. The Intelligence ExplosionAI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.2. Danger Without SuperintelligenceThe intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.3. A Useful AI FuturePowerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s crucial to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky promptly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a upcoming instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.” Explore the Superintelligence Debate In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead.

• Idea: A concept, argument, or vision.

• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development.

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress.

It has been revealed that introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”.

Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.

Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities.

Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.

François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.

Recent findings suggest that AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

In a recent development, claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

It has been revealed that an intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

In a recent development, pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

According to recent reports, but this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s vital to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky swiftly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

Industry observers note that to underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a fresh instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

In a recent development, though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the manufacturer’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

Sources indicate that these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

According to recent reports, in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Sources indicate that the misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Sources indicate that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its people because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted intends for achieving long-term objectives.

Sources indicate that the implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Sources indicate that even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the tech giant judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

According to recent reports, this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

It has been revealed that what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jay Clayton’s official portrait as US director of national intelligence, August 2026.

According to recent reports, hackers breached an unclassified system used by the CIA and at least two other US spy agencies, The Latest York Times reported on Tuesday. One of them was the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, run by Jay Clayton. The White House has just named Clayton its acting cyber director as well.

Recent findings suggest that the intrusions hit an open-source intelligence system, which looks for insights in public and commercially available material. Dustin Volz, Tyler Pager and Julian E. Barnes reported it for The New York Times, citing US officials and other people familiar with the matter. Classified material was not put at risk, the people said.

The National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was also affected, according to two of the people. One of them mentioned the matter had been resolved. It is not clear what information the hackers reached.

Sources indicate that some of the people told the Times they believed the hackers used Artex, an AI hacking tool released this year by a Chinese engineer. Investigators do not know who is responsible. Some early signs, including the use of Artex, suggest China may be behind it, two of the people remarked. Beijing routinely denies such allegations, according to the Times.

The FBI warned this month that the tool can break into networks in under three hours.

Industry observers note that an ODNI official told the Times there had been no disruptions to critical capabilities. The CIA declined to comment, and the NGA did not respond to the newspaper.

David DiMolfetta confirmed the breach for Nextgov/FCW, citing a person familiar with the matter. He also reported that hackers recently used the tool in an intrusion into the Defense Department’s Cyber Defense Command. One of two people familiar with that breach said it was low-impact. It is unclear whether it coincided with the spy agency hacks.

“If you can see what analysts are searching for and what topics they’re tracking, you get a solid look at U.S. intelligence priorities and blind spots without ever touching a classified file,” Ben Bernstein, a manager at cybersecurity firm Huntress, told Nextgov/FCW.

The breach follows a hack of the FBI’s crime database and a security incident at the Agriculture Department.

Recent findings suggest that clayton will lead the Office of the National Cyber Director as acting cyber director for now, Axios first reported. A White House official confirmed it to Nextgov/FCW on Monday. It is a third job for Clayton, who already oversees the spy agencies and coordinates the administration’s approach to AI.

Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies, named last week to replace Sean Cairncross, will instead seek Senate confirmation as the permanent director. She will be a senior adviser in the office in the meantime, according to Nextgov/FCW. Broad support for Davies persuaded Trump to nominate her, the official stated.

It has been revealed that the law does not let Davies act as director while her nomination is pending, Politico reported. It is unclear whether the Senate Homeland Security Committee, chaired by Rand Paul, will take up her nomination before the new Congress starts on 3 January, Politico said.

Clayton said in a statement that he was “excited to work more with Kirsten”, Nextgov/FCW reported.

He remarked he would help make her handover smooth.

On Sunday, Clayton told ABC’s This Week that no one coordinated last week’s outages and that no state sponsored them. Banks and the NSA have reportedly blamed some of them on rushed security patches.

Industry observers note that “These were what I would say is delays, outages and the like resulting from upgrades to systems which are absolutely necessary going forward. And we’re going to see more of that,” Clayton remarked.

Pressed on the FBI hack, he said cyber incidents had long been part of American life, and that the FBI was handling it as a routine incident. Reported cyber incidents had risen from about 750,000 in 2020 to more than a million, he said. He declined to discuss who was behind the FBI and Agriculture Department hacks.

On CNN the same day, Clayton mentioned Americans should expect more interruptions in service as organisations modernise their systems.

Fernandes, who rolled a spot-kick wide in a shoot-out against Leeds in midweek, was gifted the chance to open his pre-season account in Wroclaw, Poland.

His effort was on target this time, but Milan keeper Lorenzo Torriani dived to his right to beat the shot away.

Fernandes did at least get an assist, taking the second-minute corner which was powerfully headed home by Harry Maguire to give United the lead.

Amorim’s Milan equalised after a defensive mix-up allowed Gonçalo Ramos to break into the area and square for Samuel Chukwueze to roll home.

United were awarded their penalty just before half-time after Koni De Winter tugged back Youri Tielemans, but Torriani guessed correctly to leave Fernandes frustrated.

United retook the lead after Patrick Dorgu pounced on a loose backpass from Filippo Terracciano, but Milan equalised again when Chukwueze’s wayward shot was poked in by Alphadjo Cissè at the far post.

Marcus Rashford, who was frozen out by Amorim and loaned out to Aston Villa and then Barcelona, came on as a substitute on the hour for his first United appearance since returning from Spain.

But Milan went ahead in the 68th minute when Chukwueze’s cross was headed home by Ramos, and three minutes later former Chelsea midfielder Ruben Loftus-Cheek raced through to hit the fourth and cap a performance that underlines United’s need for reinforcements before their season starts in earnest next Saturday, away at Hull City.

Industry News: An annoying ‘mistake’ in macOS was actually prep for the latest MacBook Pro

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (483 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, you may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail.
  • Sources indicate that I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail.
  • Sources indicate that it turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail. The reason for this has now become clear, and Apple has done something both fun and clever in macOS 27 to resolve it ….

Sources indicate that I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail. Developer Norbert Heger pointed out this is because Apple changed the radius of the corners without changing the grabbable area.

Sources indicate that it turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it. The window expects this click to happen in an area of 19 × 19 pixels, located near the window corner. If the window had no rounded corners at all, 62% of that area would lie inside the window. But due to the huge corner radius in Tahoe, most of it – about 75% – now lies outside the window.

At the time, the radius change itself looked like an inexplicable mistake on Apple’s part, and the organization did revert it. However, Macworld’s Michael Simon appears to have discovered the reason for the original change.

The new rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii.

According to recent reports, so if you move a window to the corner of the new machine, it would fit perfectly. However, since Apple reverted the corner radius, it would no longer do so. The company solved this by a clever UI transition.

Recent findings suggest that what’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.

You can see this illustrated by a GIF in the Macworld piece. While the original change annoyed me, Apple’s solution is the perfect example of the tech giant sweating the details.

Amazon and Meta in talks to end the Muse blockade, Fortune reports

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, amazon and Meta are in talks over a deal that would let Meta’s Muse AI agent shop on Amazon.
  • The two companies have met several times, the people said.
  • Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from its store in September, saying the agent’s access would break its user agreements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jolly, the mascot of Meta’s Muse AI agent.

According to recent reports, amazon and Meta are in talks over a deal that would let Meta’s Muse AI agent shop on Amazon. It would end the block Amazon put on the shopping bot two months ago. Sebastian Herrera reported the talks for Fortune on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The two companies have met several times, the people said. How a deal would handle search results and advertising are two of the main issues. The talks are fluid, and nobody knows yet whether or when the two sides will agree. Any deal would likely need sign-off from both chief executives, the people said. Meta and Amazon declined to comment to Fortune.

Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from its store in September, saying the agent’s access would break its user agreements. In theory, Muse could shop on Amazon without its owners ever seeing the ads on Amazon’s website, according to Fortune.

In a recent development, advertising is now a $68.6bn business for Amazon, nearly 10% of its yearly revenue, Fortune reported. Amazon fears losing that money, the people remarked. It also doubts the quality of the search results Muse would show. Its executives also fear that shopping agents will weaken Amazon’s relationship with its customers.

In October, Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy said few customers buy through outside agents, because the experience is not yet good enough. He pitched Alexa for Shopping as Amazon’s own answer. This month, at a Semafor conference, he said Amazon had not ruled out letting outside agents in. They would have to offer a “fair exchange of value”, he said.

According to recent reports, the companies have worked together before. A 2023 deal lets Facebook and Instagram customers buy Amazon products without leaving Meta’s apps. Meta has also signed up Amazon rivals for Muse, including Shopify, Walmart and Best Buy, Fortune reported.

Recent findings suggest that muse carries no ads. But it already helps Meta’s ad business through Instagram, several people told Julia Boorstin of CNBC. Meta now prompts Instagram people to organise their saved posts in Muse, which also arrived in Instagram DMs this week.

About 20% of daily Instagram owners save at least one post a day, a person familiar with the details told CNBC. Many of those saves are shoppable items or ads. A senior Meta executive stated Muse cuts friction for shoppers and lets them return to items later.

“It gives advertisers a way to get more ROI for the dollars they’re already spending, and that’s all because Muse is helping people shop,” the executive told CNBC.

On Meta’s last earnings call, Mark Zuckerberg remarked 25% of Muse users shop through the agent. The average purchase is over $200. He has said Meta aims to take a small fee on those transactions.

In a recent development, muse handled 51% of all agent-made orders in the week to 22 November, CNBC reported. The figure comes from Forter Intelligence, an e-commerce analytics organization. Grok had 24% and ChatGPT 22%, with Google and the startup Instinct sharing the rest.

People told CNBC that Meta will likely add ads to Muse in time. But it is under no financial pressure to do so, they stated.

The Hoka Black Friday sale is heating up, with significant discounts available on some of the brand's most popular running shoes like the Clifton and Bondi.

Whether you're looking for a comfortable road shoe, a supportive trail shoe, or something that does both, you can find it in the Hoka sale right now.

It has been revealed that I’ve been testing and reviewing Hoka running shoes for over 10 years and have tried pretty much the brand's entire line-up, along with past versions of those shoes that sometimes offer better value in the sales. I’ve picked out what I think are the seven best deals on Hoka sneakers I’ve tested.

This is the cheapest I've seen the Arahi 8, which I think is very similar to the Hoka Arahi 9 based on my testing, so there's no need to pay more for the newer model if you're looking for a lightweight stability shoe. It's comfortable and has a smooth, supportive ride for daily training.

The Hoka Clifton 11 is basically the same shoe as the Hoka Clifton 10 based on my testing, so I'd definitely opt for the older shoe thanks to this deal, which reduces the Clifton 10 to the lowest price I've yet seen it. It's very comfortable for both walking and running, and a wide range of colors are on sale.

Sources indicate that the Skyward Laceless is not technically a running shoe, but it is probably the Hoka shoe I wear most often. It's a max-cushioned, slip-on sneaker that delivers a lot of comfort for long days on your feet, and I love wearing it when recovering from tough runs.

In a recent development, the Hoka Challenger 8 offers a similar ride and level of comfort to the Clifton 10 while having a more substantial outsole that grips on light trails as well as being comfortable on the road. It's a great all-rounder for runners who mix up the surfaces they run on, and several colors are still available in the Hoka sale.

According to recent reports, pretty much every color of the Bondi 9 is discounted in the Hoka sale right now, so you can take your pick. It's a max-cushioned cruiser that offers a little more comfort than even the Clifton provides.

The Hoka Speedgoat 7 is the latest model of Hoka's reliable trail-running shoe and offers a comfortable ride and secure grip across a wide variety of terrain. The colors and sizes included in the sale are limited, so you'll need to move as speedily as a goat to grab this deal.

While a springy, carbon plate trail shoe isn't something everyone needs, if you are tackling epic ultramarathons and want a fast and comfortable ride, the Hoka Tecton X3 is one of the best shoes available. I've never seen it this cheap before, and there are still plenty of sizes available.

Microsoft has explained more about why it took so long to resolve the issue and mentioned that it’s urgently working on latest approaches to resolve any future incidents in less than an hour ….

Code Red is a common term used to describe the highest priority response to a major problem, pulling a significant number of engineers off their current tasks in order to maximize the resources applied to fixing it.

The senior execs responsible for the service told staff that it was the most customer-impacting incident ever experienced, and has acknowledged that not only was the problem itself unacceptable, but so too was the time taken to resolve it. Reuters got sight of a memo sent to the team.

Industry observers note that it was the most ⁠customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to Silver’s memo.

One reason it took so long to work out what had happened was because the diagnostic data needed was “scattered across fragmented internal systems.” The memo claims 11 separate Teams chats exchanged more than 11,000 messages as they struggled to work out what exactly had gone wrong.

Microsoft is now working on five interrelated approaches to achieve a target resolution time of less than an hour for any future incidents of this nature.

BYD eyes a French plant days after a Dutch court bars its Ti7 from the EU

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD has entered exclusive talks to take over Ineos Automotive’s car plant in Hambach, France.
  • According to recent reports, BYD declared the Hambach talks in a statement on Tuesday, Daniel Ren reported for the South China Morning Post.
  • “Our commitment to Europe is long term.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD has entered exclusive talks to take over Ineos Automotive’s car plant in Hambach, France. It would be the Chinese carmaker’s second factory in Europe. The talks come days after a Dutch court barred BYD from selling its Ti7 SUV in the EU. The court found it infringes JLR’s design for the Land Rover Defender.

According to recent reports, BYD declared the Hambach talks in a statement on Tuesday, Daniel Ren reported for the South China Morning Post. It is still consulting works councils before any deal can close. Ineos builds its Grenadier off-roader at the site, according to Ineos.

“Our commitment to Europe is long term. Our proposed investment in Hambach reflects our confidence in France and our ambition to keep growing in Europe,” remarked Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice-president.

The District Court of The Hague issued the injunction on Friday, in a fast-track case brought by JLR. Nick Carey reported the ruling for Reuters.

“In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover. The characteristic and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7,” the court ruling noted.

The court also barred BYD from making the Ti7 at its new factory in Hungary until the case ends. That plant is due to start mass production early next year. The court said it had no jurisdiction over BYD’s UK affiliate, Reuters reported. Major carmakers in Europe rarely go to court over design rights. A ruling this early in a case is also uncommon.

In a recent development, JLR, owned by India’s Tata Motors, sued after BYD opened UK orders for the seven-seat Ti7. Deliveries are due in January. The Defender is JLR’s most popular model, with global sales of more than 100,000 in 2025.

BYD mentioned it strongly disagrees with the ruling and will appeal.

Sources indicate that “The BYD Ti7 is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights. We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision is incorrect,” the company said in a statement.

Sources indicate that JLR remarked it protects its intellectual property and takes legal action when necessary. It declined to comment further while proceedings continue.

Sources indicate that the injunction stays in place unless BYD wins its appeal. A final ruling on the claim is due next year, Kana Inagaki and Edward White reported for the Financial Times. BYD’s Hong Kong shares fell as much as 4% on Monday and closed 1.9% lower. JLR’s bailiffs raided BYD’s Dutch offices in August. Earlier this month, a Dutch court ordered JLR to destroy the seized files, saying the raid went too far.

The ruling does not apply in the UK. There the Ti7 starts at £47,995, against £64,315 for the cheapest five-door Defender 110, The Independent reported.

BYD’s share of the EU and UK car market rose to 2.7% this year from 1.2% last year, above JLR’s 0.9%, according to European carmakers’ association data cited by the FT. Chinese brands as a whole took a record 14.5% of European sales in September, market researcher Dataforce found, as Bloomberg reported. The EU has already moved to curb hybrid imports from China.

Industry observers note that BYD has said it will put a solid-state car on the road next year. JLR, meanwhile, cut 4,000 jobs in September.

Adyen co-founder Pieter van der Does retires as Ingo Uytdehaage takes over

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (402 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Dutch payments company Adyen will have a single chief executive from January.
  • It has been revealed that van der Does will stay on as an adviser.
  • “After 20 years, this is the right moment for me to step down on a positive note and with a very good feeling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pieter van der Does, co-founder of Adyen.

It has been revealed that the Dutch payments company Adyen will have a single chief executive from January. Co-founder Pieter van der Does leaves the co-CEO role on 31 December, and Ingo Uytdehaage, co-CEO since 2023, will run Adyen alone, Adyen noted on Monday, the company’s 20th anniversary.

It has been revealed that van der Does will stay on as an adviser. Adyen stated it has not changed its financial objectives.

“After 20 years, this is the right moment for me to step down on a positive note and with a very good feeling. Adyen has been my life’s work,” van der Does noted in the statement.

The two have worked side by side for more than 15 years, Uytdehaage mentioned. In a letter to staff, van der Does wrote that Adyen had planned the handover for more than three years, EU-Startups reported. The co-CEO model was part of that initiative.

According to recent reports, “Pieter built more than a firm. He built a culture that shapes how we make decisions, how we treat each other and how we put our merchants first, and it will outlast any one of us,” Uytdehaage stated.

Van der Does founded Adyen with Arnout Schuijff in 2006, after the two had worked together at the payments company Bibit. The name means “doing it again” in Surinamese, EU-Startups reported. Adyen listed in Amsterdam in 2018 and has grown by double digits every year since 2007, the company noted. It counts Meta, Uber, H&M, eBay and Microsoft among its customers.

According to recent reports, this year Adyen made its first acquisitions, moving beyond payments. It agreed to buy Talon.One, which lets merchants adjust promotions and prices, for €750mn. It also bought the billing platform Orb for $335mn, Sarah Jacob reported for Bloomberg.

Adyen expects net revenue to grow by 21% to 23% this year at constant currency. It recently named Niclas Neglén, the departing finance chief of rival Klarna, as its next CFO, Bloomberg reported.

It has been revealed that adyen competes with PayPal and Stripe, which Nuvei is chasing with its Payoneer deal. It is also among the firms in the ECB’s digital euro pilot.

Apple has iPads running macOS already, but don’t get too excited

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that with iPads running the same chips as Macs, many have wished Apple would give us the option of running macOS on them instead of the somewhat clunky iPadOS windowing system.
  • A new report says that Apple already has iPads running macOS internally, and that work on a giant iPad continues, but don’t hold your breath for a public launch of either ….
  • As iPad hardware has grown more powerful over the years, the software has struggled to keep up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that with iPads running the same chips as Macs, many have wished Apple would give us the option of running macOS on them instead of the somewhat clunky iPadOS windowing system. Apple’s previous arguments against converging devices have been somewhat weakened by the launch of the touchscreen MacBook Pro.

A new report says that Apple already has iPads running macOS internally, and that work on a giant iPad continues, but don’t hold your breath for a public launch of either ….

As iPad hardware has grown more powerful over the years, the software has struggled to keep up. We saw split-screen capabilities first, with full windowing finally coming to the devices in iPadOS 26 last year.

The UI is still rather clunky compared to macOS, however, leading a significant number of people to wish that Apple simply offered the option of using the more powerful operating system on its tablet devices.

In a recent development, I would be comfortable with 11" and 13" devices running macOS. Actually, I don’t require them to run macOS itself, but I do need them to run macOS apps. I wish the iPad could match a MacBook’s productivity. Running macOS on an iPad seems like a reasonable idea. The MacBook Air is now the better price choice, while those needing a powerhouse will always choose a MacBook Pro or Studio.

According to recent reports, some suggest that running macOS on iPad would reduce Mac sales, but I disagree. I own a nearly full-spec MacBook Pro 16" and expect to keep a machine like that, yet I also purchased a MacBook Air for lighter travel. I would prefer an iPad over the Air, but I cannot choose it because it lacks the apps I require. If it supported them, I would buy the iPad Pro with all accessories, and Apple would gain more revenue from me. I appreciate the concept of owning an iPad, but right now it lacks the value needed to justify paying more for a device that simply does less than a MacBook Air.

In a podcast Q&A, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says that Apple is already doing this internally, but there’s no sign of any plans to make it available outside the firm.

It has been revealed that apple has iPads internally running macOS, and they’ve had that for some time. The fact that they have the underlying architecture of Apple Silicon that’s the same on the iPad and the Mac gives them the flexibility in order to test these types of things.

Industry observers note that in terms if they’re actually going to do it – would they bring macOS to the iPad itself – at this point I don’t think that’s going to happen anytime soon. I’ve checked into this and there’s no ongoing operating system project right now in terms of a brand upcoming operating system for the iPad – there is no work being done to consumerize macOs on the iPad.

Gurman indicates Apple seems set to continue to make piecemeal changes over time to bring iPad capabilities closer to those of the Mac but is showing no signs of full convergence.

He reiterated that work on a long-rumored giant-sized folding iPad continues.

Sources indicate that the other thing I want to say is that I’m really excited for this potential of Project J312. That is, this giant 19-inch, 20-inch foldable iPad. And it’s basically like a gigantic iPhone Duo with no display on the outside.

According to recent reports, however, he states there’s no guarantee it will ever launch, saying the timings have already slipped from 2027 through 2028 to 2029, but both cost and yield complications may still kill the project. If it does launch, it’s expected to cost anywhere from $3,000 to $5,000.

#120538. Asian data centres look to US buyers as US chip rules bite, Bloomberg notes

Asian data centres look to US buyers as US chip rules bite, Bloomberg notes

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Data centres across Asia are trying to sell computing power meant for Chinese customers to buyers in the US.
  • Industry observers note that liquid Compute is a Newly introduced York startup building an exchange for AI computing capacity.
  • According to recent reports, “All the neoclouds based in Asia-Pacific selling to Tencent and other companies, or in Singapore or Taiwan with Chinese companies as offtakers, have excess capacity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Data centres across Asia are trying to sell computing power meant for Chinese customers to buyers in the US. Washington has closed a loophole that let Chinese firms rent Nvidia’s top chips abroad. Newley Purnell reported it for Bloomberg on Wednesday, citing Ronit Jain, chief executive of Liquid Compute.

Industry observers note that liquid Compute is a Newly introduced York startup building an exchange for AI computing capacity. It says it tracks more than 200 data centre companies.

According to recent reports, “All the neoclouds based in Asia-Pacific selling to Tencent and other companies, or in Singapore or Taiwan with Chinese companies as offtakers, have excess capacity. They’re trying to broker it into the US,” Jain told Bloomberg.

He declined to name the sellers or the buyers.

A B300, Nvidia’s top graphics processor, rented for $7.72 an hour at the end of October, Liquid Compute’s index highlights. By Tuesday the price had fallen 7% to $7.19. A year ago it was $4.55, and it rose steadily until last month, Jain said. He expects prices to keep falling. Data centres in Asia-Pacific are trying to place their spare capacity in the US and Western Europe, he said.

Industry observers note that not every sign points to a glut. New B300 orders now take 26 to 40 weeks to arrive, the Taiwanese newspaper China Times reported, citing supply chain sources. GB300 orders take 14 to 26 weeks. The delays only hit new orders.

The remote access rule took effect last Thursday, Owen Walker and Arjun Neil Alim reported for the Financial Times. It covers data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil that supply significant computing power to Chinese customers. They now need US licences to buy advanced American chips, and have 90 days to get them.

In a recent development, malaysia has told 117 approved data centre projects to comply, the FT reported. It also told them to cut ties with seven companies the US added to its blacklist this week. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries are among them. Malaysia has received just under $100bn of data centre funding in the past five years, according to its trade ministry.

“We do not want Singapore to be used and abused as a conduit by companies to circumvent America’s export controls,” Singapore’s prime minister, Lawrence Wong, stated on Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that lenders may now hold back. Banks will likely withhold unpaid loans to projects aimed at Chinese customers, noted Zhan Kai, a partner at Dacheng Law Offices in Shanghai. He spoke to the FT.

According to recent reports, in China, the squeeze reveals up in the grey market. Joshua Yang visited Shenzhen’s Huaqiangbei electronics market for The Washington Post. Vendors there quoted $3mn to $3.4mn for a server with eight B300s. One vendor said the same server cost $2mn two months ago. An equivalent server sells for about $500,000 to $600,000 in the US, Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, told the Post. The Post could not verify the chips on offer.

The shift follows weeks of turmoil at Nvidia, which brought Jensen Huang back as chief executive on Monday.

At Tom's Guide we use a diverse panel of sleep experts to test the most popular mattresses you can find online. We combine repeatable, scientific lab measurements with extended at-home sleep trials. Their review process is also editorially independent and free from brand influence.

Rather than relying solely on first impressions, we use standardized, objective lab tests to generate reliable, unbiased data. For instance, we use thermal imaging camera tests to see how well a mattress regulates temperature, and use accelerometers to test how well a mattress isolates motion.

In a recent development, lab numbers do not tell the whole story, so a lead reviewer sleeps on each mattress at home for at least three weeks — the typical time it takes for a person's body to adjust to a upcoming bed. We also gather feedback from a testing panel made up of people with different body types and sleeping positions to account for subjective comfort.

You can find out more about how we test mattresses in our mattresses by reading up on our mattress methodology.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • iOS 27.3 includes many new features for Apple’s built-in apps, but it also introduces design changes on the iPhone across Calendar, Safari, Music, and more.
  • Apple is always iterating on the design of its software.
  • As seen above, Health introduces brand fresh Insights, Longevity, and Browse tabs that replace the previous options and include a variety of fresh UI elements like a top navigation row, personalized prompts and coaching, educational videos, and a lot more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27.3 includes many new features for Apple’s built-in apps, but it also introduces design changes on the iPhone across Calendar, Safari, Music, and more. Here’s what’s new.

Apple is always iterating on the design of its software. While major overhauls like iOS 26’s Liquid Glass don’t come along often, the company makes smaller design changes all the time via software updates. In iOS 27.3, which will launch to all consumers next month, Apple has design changes coming to four popular apps: Health, Calendar, Safari, and Music.

The Health app gets the biggest design changes.

As seen above, Health introduces brand fresh Insights, Longevity, and Browse tabs that replace the previous options and include a variety of fresh UI elements like a top navigation row, personalized prompts and coaching, educational videos, and a lot more.

As the side-by-side above indicates, the buttons for search and creating a latest event have moved out of the top-right corner and into the bottom of the screen.

Calendar also now highlights the year at the top of the screen next to the current month, and has updated the ‘Today’ button to show the current date instead.

In a recent development, safari introduces an optional latest design for tabs: Vertical Tabs. You can enable these inside Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Safari for a different approach to tabs across iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Here’s an example of vertical tabs on iPhone Duo.

Vertical Tabs won’t be for everyone, but they’ve proven popular in other browsers, so it’s great to see Safari add the option.

  • HP’s revenue rose 9.3% to $16.0bn in its fiscal fourth quarter, HP said on Tuesday.
  • “In the fourth quarter, we continued to grow our higher-value businesses, with AI PCs reaching nearly 60% of shipments, while taking steps to address memory and storage cost pressures,” said Bruce Broussard, HP’s interim CEO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that HP and Hewlett Packard Enterprise split from Hewlett-Packard in 2015. This week both told investors that memory costs are squeezing their profits. HPE’s shares had their worst day since the split. HP gave a cautious outlook for its fresh fiscal year.

HP’s revenue rose 9.3% to $16.0bn in its fiscal fourth quarter, HP said on Tuesday. AI PCs made up nearly 60% of shipments, but total PC units fell 29%. Adjusted earnings per share fell 10.8% to $0.83.

“In the fourth quarter, we continued to grow our higher-value businesses, with AI PCs reaching nearly 60% of shipments, while taking steps to address memory and storage cost pressures,” said Bruce Broussard, HP’s interim CEO.

In a recent development, for fiscal 2027, HP expects adjusted earnings of $3.15 to $3.45 a share, against $3.33 this year. It also raised its quarterly dividend to $0.31.

“While our fiscal 2027 outlook reflects a prudent view of continued cost and demand pressures, we have a strong track record of addressing challenges,” mentioned Karen Parkhill, HP’s chief financial officer.

PC makers have been dealing with memory costs for months. HP, Asus and Acer were moving production back to China in October to cut them.

HPE’s revenue jumped about 50% to $14.5bn in the quarter, driven by AI servers, it reported on Monday. Its Cloud and AI division grew 68.6% to $11.3bn. It raised its sales outlook for the latest fiscal year to $59.4bn to $63.1bn.

But HPE expects the division’s operating margin to shrink to 14% from 18.4%, Dina Bass reported for Bloomberg. The shares fell 16% to $40.19 on Tuesday. It was their biggest one-day drop since HPE began trading in November 2015. The stock had doubled this year.

“We expect supply of memory, NAND, and many other critical components to remain constrained through at least the second half of calendar 2028,” Antonio Neri, HPE’s chief executive, said on the earnings call.

According to recent reports, neri told Bloomberg Television that the turmoil at Nvidia had not changed customers’ behaviour. Nvidia brought Jensen Huang back as CEO on Monday. Rising component costs have already pushed server makers to raise their prices.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (350 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

Windows Loudness Equalization, reverse-engineered and ported to PipeWire

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (350 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that windows' Loudness Equalization for PipeWire, reverse engineered from WMALFXGFXDSP.dll.
  • To install only one part, use make -C modules/loudness, make -C modules/limiter or make -C app.
  • Open Loudness Equalization from your application menu, or run pw-loudness-eq.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that windows' Loudness Equalization for PipeWire, reverse engineered from WMALFXGFXDSP.dll. It evens out the volume of each application, so quiet and loud parts play at a similar level.

Requires PipeWire ≥ 1.4, and GTK 3 for the window.

To install only one part, use make -C modules/loudness, make -C modules/limiter or make -C app. To uninstall, run sudo make uninstall and restart the same services.

Open Loudness Equalization from your application menu, or run pw-loudness-eq.

The settings live in a PipeWire metadata object, so they can also be scripted:.

Changes apply immediately and are kept across restarts.

Industry observers note that defaults are in /usr/share/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/60-loudness-eq.conf. To override them, copy it to ~/.config/pipewire/pipewire.conf.d/.

Settings changed at runtime are saved in ~/.local/state/pw-loudness-eq/state.conf and take precedence over this file.

The loudness module sets audioconvert.filter-graph.90 on each app's playback stream, so the plugin runs inside that stream, before its volume and before mixing, like a Windows stream effect.

In a recent development, the limiter module does what Windows' audio engine does on every playback device: after the mix and the software volume, it runs the output through a look-ahead limiter. It's always on, independent of Loudness Equalization, as on Windows.

Not processed: JACK clients, streams with more than 8 channels, and Flatpak apps that use PipeWire directly (those going through PulseAudio are processed).

A broadband automatic gain control. Despite the name, it doesn't equalize the spectrum.

The boost can push pure tones such as a whistle well above full scale; the limiter catches that.

Ported from CAudioLimiter in AudioEng.dll. audiodg.exe puts it on every render device, after its effects, before the device.

It has been revealed that on Windows the device's software volume comes before the limiter; in PipeWire it comes after the device's filter graphs. So the plugin gets the volume of each channel (kept in sync by the module), measures peaks on the signal as it will be after the volume, and applies only its gain. Once PipeWire applies the volume, the result is the same as Windows'. Hardware volume comes after the limiter on both.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Ariane 6 upper stage being lifted onto DLR’s P5.2 test stand, February 2021.

Amazon is moving its next SpaceX launch for Amazon Leo forward to December. On Tuesday, Europe’s Ariane 6 put 36 more of its satellites into orbit. An Amazon official told Stephen Clark of Ars Technica that the Falcon 9 flight was originally due next year. Several more Falcon 9 debuts will follow in quick succession.

SpaceX also runs Starlink, the network Amazon Leo is built to compete with. Starlink has more than 11,000 satellites, according to Ars.

It has been revealed that the Ariane 6 lifted off from French Guiana at about 6:15am New York time, Summer Maxwell reported for Bloomberg. It released all 36 satellites about two hours later. It was the rocket’s 10th flight and Arianespace’s fourth for Amazon. Arianespace has now debuted 136 Amazon satellites.

The launch came nine days after a Vulcan rocket failure destroyed 40 Amazon Leo satellites. United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan is Amazon’s main launch provider. It cannot fly until an investigation led by the US Federal Aviation Administration ends. Blue Origin’s Fresh Glenn has not flown since May, and its return to flight has slipped to early next year.

Industry observers note that amazon Leo now has 432 satellites in orbit, Ars reported. Amazon has booked 108 releases to deploy 3,232 satellites, and 17 have flown so far, with one failure. Amazon has not yet started its internet service, Bloomberg reported. In 2025 it had said the service would start that year.

Amazon added six Ariane 6 launches in September, taking its total with Arianespace to 24. Arianespace intends to raise the rocket’s cadence to 12 launches a year by about 2030, according to Bloomberg.

Recent findings suggest that europe’s factories can support up to nine or ten Ariane 6 flights a year, Ars reported. Arianespace is likely to reach six this year, with one more before the end of December. European ministers are weighing looks to build more Ariane 6 rockets, and a decision could come next month.

Recent findings suggest that amazon built its 1,000th satellite in October. Hundreds now wait in storage for a ride to orbit, according to Ars.

  • In a recent development, how about the emphatic scoreline – surely that was it?
  • So what was it that should have those with pretensions of ripping Arsenal’s crown from their grasp shuffling uncomfortably?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that was it the early goal that should have put Arsenal’s rivals on red alert? No. While Ricardo Calafiori’s intervention was dramatic, it wasn’t that. Was it the seamless introduction of the newly introduced signings, then? No, it wasn’t that either, despite the excellence of Bruno Guimarães and Christos Tzolis.

In a recent development, how about the emphatic scoreline – surely that was it? Again, the answer is no. Three unanswered goals against Manchester City will always grab a headline, but scorelines do not always define the nature of a performance or a team’s capabilities.

So what was it that should have those with pretensions of ripping Arsenal’s crown from their grasp shuffling uncomfortably? One word: hunger. The reason this was such an ominous afternoon for the chasing pack is the fact Mikel Arteta’s team played with intensity of a team with everything to prove.

Title wins can sometimes sate ambition. Players don’t always want to climb the same mountain again, not least if reaching the peak was initially so draining, but everywhere you looked on a day when Cardiff was painted red and white was evidence that Arsenal remain ravenous for success.

First Guimarães pounced out of the shadows to mug Jérémy Doku, leaving him in a heap. Then there was Gabriel Magalhães thundering into a befuddled Doku, celebrating in front of City’s fans as if he had scored, before Ben White flung himself in front of the Belgian, denying a clear-cut scoring opportunity.

Ben White to the rescue with an incredible block 🦸📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/ZK0cNnFz5N.

Another notable incident was Martin Odegaard, not long after he had glossed a fabulous display with a third goal, sprinting 30 yards to spook Gianluigi Donnarumma and make the Italian hurry his clearance. The victory was good, the trophy was nice, but the energy heartened Arteta more than anything.

“They are really good examples,” Arteta said. “The way the team tracks back is unbelievable, especially when, fitness-wise, we aren’t there yet. We had desire and composure on the ball. When you put your soul and your heart into every action, this is what happens. We want to do it again.

“The desire comes from them thinking: ‘I want to live that moment again. I want to have all the moments again and I want them to be even bigger.’ We know what it is going to take. We have never done it [retain the Premier League] at this football club. We know it will demand something special.”.

You could flip that and say it will take something special from the chasers. George Graham and Arsène Wenger could never hold on to the biggest prize during their reigns and you must return to Herbert Chapman, in Arsenal’s thriving 1930s, to find the only manager who went back-to-back.

It can feel premature (and can be foolish) to go out on a limb before the first weekend, but there was just something about them that felt different. Often in the past they have been overtly tentative when playing City, but they came out of their corner this time swinging – and they landed.

Enzo Maresca revealed afterwards that he “really didn’t like” how Arsenal had scored their first goal and that was putting it mildly, as there were 10 passes – broken only by the ball bouncing off Elliott Anderson’s shins – before Myles Lewis-Skelly ushered Calafiori into wreak havoc.

You had to go back to 1968, when City played West Brom, to find the last first-minute goal – City’s Bobby Owen was the scorer that day – and how Calafiori enjoyed it, shaking his fist in delight as Arsenal’s noisy fans reminded everyone of their status.

Riccardo Calafiori gives Arsenal the lead after just 24 seconds 🤯The assist from Myles Lewis-Skelly 👏📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/aU0UsCB1Xs.

It has been revealed that here was a rude awakening for Anderson, City’s newly introduced £116m man. He was ever so slightly off the pace and that allowed Lewis-Skelly to slip a beautiful ball in behind the FA Cup winners’ defence and invite Calafiori to do the rest, which he did with assurance.

Recent findings suggest that when Maresca watches back the video, he will see Abdukodir Khusanov sleeping and Phil Foden failing to press, but that should not detract from the quality of Arsenal’s interchanging – and it should also make whoever is hawking Lewis-Skelly around to clubs to think again. Why would he leave this?

It should not have been the case that a goal so soon should have governed how the game progressed, but that is exactly what happened as Arsenal completely dominated. Whenever they lost possession, they recovered it as a matter of urgency. Without Pep Guardiola on the touchline, City were like Samson after Delilah shaved his hair, devoid of all power.

In a recent development, city, in contrast to their opponents, demonstrated a complete lack of desire and the second goal arrived when Odegaard was allowed time to flip a ball to the back post, where new boy Tzolis was arriving. The Greek headed back into the six-yard area and Kai Havertz did the rest.

Kai Havertz finishes off a well-worked move to double Arsenal's lead 🤩📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/tGkxCIBV8F.

Arsenal were criticised – fairly – during their title-winning campaign for being too physical and relying on gamesmanship, but if Havertz and Odegaard can stay fit for a prolonged period, the difference in style will be like night and day.

Recent findings suggest that throw in Tzolis, who was tricky and dynamic in Cardiff, to the mix and there will be another enhancement. He looks considerably better than Gabriel Martinelli, with more end product, and Bukayo Saka will do more down the right than Noni Madueke, who started here.

Maresca knew, with his team lacking fitness, that it would be difficult to overhaul the deficit once they had gone two goals behind but, really, he was lucky that Arsenal did not administer a genuine hiding which, at one stage, seemed as though they might.

Goal number three arrived just after the interval, again Lewis-Skelly and Tzolis were involved, combining to enable Odegaard to waltz into the area, hoodwinking Donnarumma so he sat down before sliding a contemptuous finish beyond him.

Take a bow, Martin Ødegaard 😮‍💨Arsenal are flying against Man City!📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/cMHbIyJ90D.

Had they gone through the gears, there could have been more, but it didn’t matter. What Arsenal showed was far more significant than a couple of more goals when the game was being disrupted by substitutions. The tackles, the running, energy and commitment – that is what brought Arteta joy.

“I’m extremely happy with the performance, the result and winning the first trophy,” Arteta purred.

You would be brave to say it will be their last.

The league champions kick-off the domestic season with a resounding and stylish victory. Shades of 1998 and 2004 when they swept Manchester United aside in this fixture as title winners, only to fail to defend the crown in the season that followed. So maybe it is unwise to make bold forecasts, but it could not have gone better for Arteta. Odegaard, Lewis-Skelly and Tzolis caught the eye, and Arsenal had their usual solidarity defensively. City just completely off the pace, one to write off and move on.

In case any Arsenal fan had forgotten that last season ended with them losing a Champions League final on penalties, City fans are on hand to remind them. They have one European Cup to Arsenal’s zero. Away from the tin foil trophies, I’m sure much bottle-related mirth is on the cards, especially now broadcasters and fans are aware of the viral possibilities. Too aware, I would argue.

The pool of players who can improve the Premier League champions and Champions League finalists is a small one, but it is still fair to point out that Arsenal’s summer has not gone smoothly. They pursued Morgan Rogers and Vinicius Junior without success, and Arteta’s desire to take the team to a “different dimension” has so far gone unfulfilled., certainly in the forward positions.

Arsenal still look strong, but have they passed up a chance to pull away from the rest? Sam Wallace takes a look at their summer so far.

It would have been less stressful for Guardiola to go once he realised the great side of Kevin De Bruyne was nearing its end. Instead he opted to oversee a rebuild that gives his successor a greater chance of immediate success, going close to the title last season in what was effectively year one for a re-emerging City side. Guardiola must have known he was signing Gianluigi Donnarumma, Antoine Semenyo, Marc Guéhi and Rayan Cherki for someone else’s long-term benefit.

The Community Shield returns to Cardiff’s Principality Stadium for the first time since 2006, and a different dynamic is at play between Arsenal and Manchester City.

When the two clubs played at Wembley in this fixture three years ago, it felt like a more significant occasion for Arsenal as they sought to prove that the gap was closing to Pep Guardiola’s champions.

Now it is Arsenal and Mikel Arteta who have a league title behind them, while Enzo Maresca is the manager hoping to build credibility as City turn the page post-Pep Guardiola.

In a recent development, in truth, these two teams will look very different by the time the season gathers pace in autumn. World Cup exertions mean Elliot Anderson, Erling Haaland, Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka will be minimally involved in this game, while transfer plans remain up in the air for both camps.

Sources indicate that city appear bound to lose Rodri, in addition to Bernardo Silva and Tijjani Reijnders in central midfield. Rodri’s sale would expedite a move for Lille’s Ayyoub Bouaddi, and possibly Enzo Fernandez despite Chelsea’s insistence that the deadline to sign him for £120m has passed.

Arsenal are also open for business, hoping to add a right-sided defender to help them cope with William Saliba’s absence. The £75m purchase of Bruno Guimarães means the champions’ midfield options look formidable, but so far it has been another summer without a level-raising forward signing. Christos Tzolis in and Leandro Trossard out looks canny business, but falls into the category of like for like.

Although Arsenal held their nerve to see off City in the title race, they failed to win in three attempts against their rivals, including a limp defeat in the Carabao Cup final at Wembley. Arsenal also failed to win, or score, against Liverpool in the Premier League last season so their record in the big games is an area for improvement.

The victors this afternoon will claim to have laid a marker down, the losers will write the game off as a warm up exercise.

Industry News: Cloudflare wants AI agents to search websites, not crawl them

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (348 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cloudflare’s illustration shows robots searching a website through a magnifying glass, above an on/off switch.
  • According to recent reports, cloudflare has launched Search for Agents in beta for all customers, including free ones.
  • Recent findings suggest that cloudflare has debuted a switch that turns a website on its network into a search engine for AI agents, the manufacturer noted on Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cloudflare’s illustration shows robots searching a website through a magnifying glass, above an on/off switch.

According to recent reports, cloudflare has launched Search for Agents in beta for all customers, including free ones. Switching it on indexes a site and adds a search endpoint on its own domain, advertised on every page, so AI agents can search the site instead of crawling it page by page.

Recent findings suggest that cloudflare has debuted a switch that turns a website on its network into a search engine for AI agents, the manufacturer noted on Wednesday. Search for Agents is in beta and open to every customer, including those on the free proposal.

Once it is on, Cloudflare crawls and indexes the site, then puts a search endpoint at a standard address on the site’s own domain. Every page also carries hidden tags telling visiting agents the search exists. That way, agents can search the site instead of crawling it page by page.

The search returns matching text from the site, not an AI-written answer. Cloudflare says the agent already has its own AI model, so it only needs the source material.

Site owners keep their existing defences. Agents still face each site’s bot settings and firewall rules, which Cloudflare has tightened against AI crawlers this year. It has also worked with OpenAI to help ChatGPT find upcoming pages faster.

In a recent development, the launch is Cloudflare’s latest move to shape how agents use the web. In August it released Kitesurf, a browser for AI agents.

Recent findings suggest that daily requests from AI agents on its network grew over 1,700% in a year, Cloudflare noted in October. Chief executive Matthew Prince has said bot traffic could reach 1,000 times human levels.

Use is billed under Cloudflare’s AI Search pricing, which starts charging on December 1, with some usage included each month. Free plans come with tighter limits.
